patterns.diagnosis: Git can't auto-merge changes in `{1}`. You need to resolve manually.
fixes: Edit to keep the right version, remove the markers.
Then `git add {1}` and `git commit` (or `git merge --continue`).
Abort if you want out: `git merge --abort`.

patterns.title: Detached HEAD
patterns.diagnosis: You checked out a specific commit/tag, not a branch. New commits won't belong to any branch.
fixes: If you want to keep work here: `git switch -c new-branch`.
If you just wanted to peek: `git switch main` to return.

patterns.title: Branch diverged from upstream
patterns.diagnosis: You and the remote each have commits the other doesn't.
fixes: Rebase to put your commits on top: `git pull --rebase`.
Merge if you prefer: `git pull` (creates a merge commit).

patterns.match: nothing to commit, working tree clean
patterns.title: Nothing to commit
patterns.diagnosis: Git sees no changes. Either you didn't edit anything, or the changes aren't staged (or are ignored).
fixes: Check `git status`.
Did your file match `.gitignore`?
Run `git add <files>` if you have unstaged changes.

patterns.title: Empty author identity
patterns.diagnosis: Git needs a name to attribute commits to.
fixes: Set it: `git config --global user.name "Your Name"`.
And email: `git config --global user.email "you@example.com"`.

patterns.match: Please tell me who you are
patterns.title: Identity not configured
patterns.diagnosis: Git needs `user.name` and `user.email` before committing.
fixes: `git config --global user.name "Your Name"`.
`git config --global user.email "you@example.com"`.

patterns.title: Could not read Username (no TTY)
patterns.diagnosis: Git tried to prompt for credentials but there's no terminal.
fixes: Use SSH instead of HTTPS for git remotes.
Configure a credential helper: `git config --global credential.helper store`.
Use a token in the URL (not recommended — leaks in shell history).

patterns.match: The remote end hung up unexpectedly
patterns.title: Remote hung up
patterns.diagnosis: Network dropped or remote rejected the connection.
fixes: Retry — could be transient.
For large pushes, increase buffer: `git config http.postBuffer 524288000`.
Try SSH instead of HTTPS.

patterns.match: error: failed to fetch some refs
patterns.title: Fetch failed
patterns.diagnosis: Some refs couldn't be retrieved from remote.
fixes: Check network connectivity.
Authentication issue? Test with `git ls-remote <url>`.
Specific refs deleted on remote? Try `git fetch --prune`.

patterns.title: Push rejected — file too large
patterns.diagnosis: `{1}` exceeds GitHub's 100MB limit.
fixes: Remove the file from history: `git filter-repo` or BFG Repo-Cleaner.
Use Git LFS for large binaries: `git lfs track '*.zip'`.
Add the file to `.gitignore` going forward.

patterns.match: LF will be replaced by CRLF
patterns.title: LF/CRLF line ending warning
patterns.diagnosis: Git's auto-conversion will change line endings on checkout.
fixes: Usually harmless — just a notice.
Configure `core.autocrlf` for your platform (`input` on Linux/Mac, `true` on Windows).
Add `.gitattributes` with explicit line endings for cross-platform repos.

patterns.title: Ambiguous argument
patterns.diagnosis: Git can't tell whether your argument is a branch, file, or ref.
fixes: Use `--` to separate refs from paths: `git checkout HEAD -- file`.
Spell out the full ref: `refs/heads/foo` vs `foo`.

patterns.title: Object file is empty
patterns.diagnosis: An object in `.git/objects/` is corrupt (zero bytes).
fixes: Try `git fsck`.
Delete the bad file and `git fetch` to re-download.
Worst case, re-clone.

patterns.match: git: '([^']+)' is not a git command
patterns.title: git: not a git command — `{1}`
patterns.diagnosis: `{1}` isn't a built-in or installed subcommand.
fixes: Check spelling — `git stauts` → `git status`.
Did you mean one of the suggestions Git printed?
Some commands need extras (`git lfs` needs git-lfs installed).

patterns.title: Submodule has uncommitted changes
patterns.diagnosis: Submodule `{1}` has local edits.
fixes: Enter the submodule and commit/discard those changes.
Or skip with `--ignore-submodules`.

patterns.title: Pre-commit hook failed
patterns.diagnosis: A hook rejected your commit.
fixes: Read the hook output — it usually says exactly what to fix.
Fix and re-stage, then commit again.
Skip the hook only if you know what you're doing: `--no-verify`.

patterns.title: Commit message hook failed
patterns.diagnosis: Your commit message didn't pass the hook (often Conventional Commits or DCO).
fixes: Re-write the message to match the convention.
Common format: `type(scope): description`.

patterns.match: gpg failed to sign the data
patterns.title: gpg failed to sign commit
patterns.diagnosis: Git is configured to GPG-sign but signing failed.
fixes: Check your signing key: `gpg --list-secret-keys`.
Set the right key: `git config user.signingkey <key>`.
Make sure gpg-agent is running.
Disable signing temporarily: `git commit --no-gpg-sign`.

patterns.title: Index lock exists
patterns.diagnosis: Another git process is running, or a stale lock remains.
fixes: Wait for any other git command to finish.
If stale: `rm .git/index.lock`.

patterns.match: Please use -f if you really want to clean
patterns.title: git clean needs -f
patterns.diagnosis: Git won't delete files without confirmation.
fixes: Add `-f`: `git clean -fd`.
Preview first: `git clean -n`.

patterns.match: fatal: A branch named '([^']+)' already exists
patterns.title: Branch already exists — `{1}`
patterns.diagnosis: You can't create a branch with a name that's taken.
fixes: Switch to it: `git switch {1}`.
Or pick a new name.
Force-overwrite (destructive): `git branch -f {1}`.

patterns.title: Rebase conflict
patterns.diagnosis: Rebasing hit a conflict.
fixes: Resolve the conflict, then `git add` and `git rebase --continue`.
Skip the offending commit: `git rebase --skip`.
Abort: `git rebase --abort`.

patterns.match: error: The branch '([^']+)' is not fully merged
patterns.title: Branch not fully merged
patterns.diagnosis: Deleting `{1}` would lose commits not on any other branch.
fixes: Make sure those commits are merged elsewhere.
Force-delete if you're sure: `git branch -D {1}`.

patterns.title: Clone destination exists
patterns.diagnosis: `{1}` is already there and not empty.
fixes: Pick a different directory: `git clone <url> other-name`.
Or remove the existing directory first.

patterns.match: warning: There are too many unreachable loose objects
patterns.title: Too many loose objects
patterns.diagnosis: Git's storage has accumulated cruft.
fixes: Run `git gc` (garbage collect).
For deeper cleanup: `git gc --aggressive --prune=now`.

patterns.title: Clone failed mid-transfer
patterns.diagnosis: Network dropped or remote sent bad data.
fixes: Retry — usually transient.
Try shallow clone first: `git clone --depth 1`, then fetch the rest.
Increase buffer: `git config http.postBuffer 524288000`.

patterns.match: There is no tracking information for the current branch|no upstream branch
patterns.title: No upstream branch
patterns.diagnosis: This branch isn't tracking a remote, so `git pull` doesn't know where to fetch.
fixes: Set it: `git push -u origin <branch>`.
Or `git branch --set-upstream-to=origin/<branch>`.

patterns.title: Tag already exists
patterns.diagnosis: Tag `{1}` is already in the repo.
fixes: Use a different tag name.
Force-replace (rarely a good idea): `git tag -f {1}`.

patterns.title: No changes added to commit
patterns.diagnosis: You have edits but didn't `git add` them.
fixes: Stage specific files: `git add <files>`.
Or stage everything: `git add -A`.
Use `git commit -a` to stage all tracked changes.

patterns.title: Unmerged paths
patterns.diagnosis: There's an in-progress merge or rebase to finish.
fixes: Resolve the conflicts and `git add` the resolved files.
Continue: `git merge --continue` or `git rebase --continue`.
Abort: `git merge --abort` or `git rebase --abort`.

patterns.match: fatal: unable to access .* Could not resolve host
patterns.title: Couldn't reach git host
patterns.diagnosis: DNS or network can't reach the git remote.
fixes: Check network.
Try `ping github.com`.
Corporate proxy? Configure `http.proxy`.

patterns.match: fatal: unable to access .*: Failed to connect to .* proxy
patterns.title: Git proxy connection failed
patterns.diagnosis: Git's proxy setting points somewhere unreachable.
fixes: Check `git config --get http.proxy`.
Unset if not needed: `git config --global --unset http.proxy`.

patterns.match: fatal: '([^']+)' does not appear to be a git repository
patterns.title: Remote isn't a git repo
patterns.diagnosis: `{1}` URL doesn't point to a repo.
fixes: Double-check the URL.
Authentication failed? Some hosts return 'not a repo' instead of 'access denied'.

patterns.title: ECONNREFUSED — connection refused
patterns.diagnosis: Nothing is listening at that address:port. Server is down or you're hitting the wrong host/port.
fixes: Confirm the server is running.
Verify host and port.
Check firewalls.

patterns.title: ETIMEDOUT — operation timed out
patterns.diagnosis: A network operation took longer than allowed.
fixes: Retry with backoff.
Increase the timeout if appropriate.
Test reachability with `ping` / `curl -v`.

patterns.title: EHOSTUNREACH — no route to host
patterns.diagnosis: The OS can't find a route to the target host.
fixes: Check routing: `traceroute host` or `ip route`.
VPN required? Connect it.
Firewall dropping packets?

patterns.title: ENETUNREACH — network unreachable
patterns.diagnosis: Your machine has no path to that network at all.
fixes: Check that you have a working network interface.
Test with `ping 8.8.8.8`.
VPN or interface down?

patterns.title: EAI_AGAIN — DNS temporary failure
patterns.diagnosis: DNS resolution failed but might succeed if retried.
fixes: Retry after a moment.
Check that your DNS server is reachable.
Try a public resolver (1.1.1.1, 8.8.8.8).

patterns.title: EAI_NONAME — name unknown
patterns.diagnosis: Hostname doesn't exist in DNS.
fixes: Check spelling.
Confirm the domain resolves: `dig hostname`.
If internal, are you on the right network/VPN?

patterns.title: ENOTFOUND — DNS lookup failed
patterns.diagnosis: Couldn't resolve the hostname.
fixes: Check the URL.
Test with `nslookup`.
Verify DNS settings.

patterns.title: EPIPE — broken pipe
patterns.diagnosis: Wrote to a stream whose reader closed.
fixes: Often harmless — the reader (e.g. `head`) finished early.
Listen for the `error` event on the stream to avoid an unhandled exception.

patterns.title: EISDIR — path is a directory
patterns.diagnosis: You treated a directory as a file.
fixes: Append a filename.
If listing, use `readdir`/`ls` style.

patterns.title: ENOTDIR — not a directory
patterns.diagnosis: Some component of the path is a file, not a directory.
fixes: Inspect the path with `ls -l`.
Did a path concatenation produce something weird?

patterns.title: EEXIST — file already exists
patterns.diagnosis: A create operation hit something that already exists.
fixes: Pick a different name.
Delete the existing file if you mean to replace it.
Use a flag that allows overwriting if available.

patterns.match: ENOSPC: no space left|No space left on device
patterns.title: ENOSPC — disk full
patterns.diagnosis: No free space on the target filesystem.
fixes: Check usage: `df -h`.
Clean caches, logs, old downloads.
Check inodes too: `df -i`.

patterns.title: EROFS — read-only filesystem
patterns.diagnosis: You can't write here — the filesystem is mounted read-only.
fixes: Check the mount with `mount | grep <path>`.
Write somewhere writable (home dir, /tmp).
On macOS, some system paths are read-only by design.

patterns.title: Out of memory
patterns.diagnosis: Process exhausted available RAM and was killed.
fixes: Stream data instead of loading it all into memory.
Increase memory limit (container/VM).
Profile memory use to find leaks.

patterns.title: HTTP 401 — Unauthorized
patterns.diagnosis: Request lacked valid credentials.
fixes: Provide auth headers (token, basic auth).
Token expired? Refresh it.
Check the auth method the API expects.

patterns.title: HTTP 403 — Forbidden
patterns.diagnosis: You're authenticated but not allowed.
fixes: Account may lack permission for this resource.
Some 403s mean the IP/origin is blocked.
Check the response body — it often explains why.

patterns.title: HTTP 404 — Not Found
patterns.diagnosis: The URL doesn't exist on the server.
fixes: Check the path spelling.
Verify the API version in the URL.
Resource may have been deleted or moved.

patterns.title: HTTP 429 — Too Many Requests
patterns.diagnosis: You hit a rate limit.
fixes: Back off and retry after the time in `Retry-After`.
Reduce request rate.
Cache responses to make fewer calls.

patterns.title: HTTP 500 — Internal Server Error
patterns.diagnosis: The server crashed handling your request.
fixes: Not usually your fault — but check whether your input is malformed.
Check the server's logs.
Retry — could be transient.

patterns.title: HTTP 502 — Bad Gateway
patterns.diagnosis: A reverse proxy got a bad response from the upstream server.
fixes: Upstream service may be down or crashing.
Retry — often transient during deploys.
Check upstream health if you own it.

patterns.title: HTTP 503 — Service Unavailable
patterns.diagnosis: Server is overloaded, in maintenance, or has no upstream available.
fixes: Retry with backoff.
Check status page if it's a third-party service.

patterns.title: HTTP 504 — Gateway Timeout
patterns.diagnosis: Reverse proxy gave up waiting for the upstream.
fixes: Upstream is slow or hung.
Increase proxy timeout if you control it.
Optimize the upstream operation.

patterns.match: duplicate key value violates unique constraint
patterns.title: SQL — duplicate key
patterns.diagnosis: Insert/update broke a unique constraint.
fixes: Check the value — does a row with that key exist?
Use `ON CONFLICT` (Postgres) or `INSERT IGNORE` (MySQL).
Use upsert logic where appropriate.

patterns.title: SQL — foreign key violation
patterns.diagnosis: You referenced a row that doesn't exist (or tried to delete a row that's referenced).
fixes: Insert the parent row first.
Or use `ON DELETE CASCADE` if appropriate.
Check ID values match between tables.

patterns.title: SQL — relation `{1}` doesn't exist
patterns.diagnosis: The table/view `{1}` isn't in the current schema.
fixes: Check spelling and schema (`schema.table`).
Run pending migrations.
Maybe you're connected to the wrong database.

patterns.title: SQL — permission denied
patterns.diagnosis: Your DB user lacks privileges on that object.
fixes: `GRANT SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE ON <table> TO <user>;`.
Check whether you're connected as the right user.

patterns.match: Cannot connect to the Docker daemon
patterns.title: Docker daemon not reachable
patterns.diagnosis: The Docker daemon isn't running or your user can't talk to it.
fixes: Start Docker: `systemctl start docker` (Linux) or open Docker Desktop.
Linux: add user to `docker` group, then log out and back in.
Check `DOCKER_HOST` env var.

patterns.title: Docker — image not found
patterns.diagnosis: Docker couldn't find the requested image (typo, private registry, or doesn't exist).
fixes: Check spelling and tag.
`docker login` for private registries.
Search: `docker search <name>`.

patterns.match: port is already allocated|bind: address already in use
patterns.title: Docker — port already allocated
patterns.diagnosis: Another container or process is using that port.
fixes: Find: `docker ps` or `lsof -i :PORT`.
Stop the conflicting container or pick a different host port.

patterns.match: permission denied while trying to connect to the Docker daemon socket
patterns.title: Docker — socket permission denied
patterns.diagnosis: Your user doesn't have access to `/var/run/docker.sock`.
fixes: Add user to docker group: `sudo usermod -aG docker $USER`, then log out/in.
Or run with `sudo` (less ideal).

patterns.title: K8s — ImagePullBackOff
patterns.diagnosis: Kubelet can't pull the container image.
fixes: Check image name and tag in the manifest.
If private registry: add a `imagePullSecrets` to the pod spec.
`kubectl describe pod <pod>` for the underlying error.

patterns.title: K8s — CrashLoopBackOff
patterns.diagnosis: Container starts then crashes repeatedly.
fixes: `kubectl logs <pod> --previous` for the last crash log.
Common causes: bad config, missing env var, app exits immediately.
Check the container's command and args.

patterns.title: K8s — pod stuck Pending
patterns.diagnosis: Pod can't be scheduled. Usually no node with enough resources or missing volumes.
fixes: `kubectl describe pod <pod>` and look at Events.
Check node CPU/memory capacity.
If using PVCs, make sure they're Bound.

patterns.title: K8s — pod OOMKilled
patterns.diagnosis: Container exceeded its memory limit and was killed.
fixes: Raise the memory limit if the app legitimately needs it.
Investigate the memory profile — likely a leak.
Set `requests` and `limits` based on observed usage.

patterns.title: K8s — forbidden for user `{1}`
patterns.diagnosis: RBAC denied the action.
fixes: Check role bindings for `{1}`.
`kubectl auth can-i <verb> <resource>` to test.
Bind a role: `kubectl create rolebinding ...`.

patterns.title: SSL handshake failed
patterns.diagnosis: Couldn't agree on TLS parameters with the server.
fixes: Server may require a newer TLS version — update client.
Check the cert isn't expired.
Try `openssl s_client -connect host:443` for details.

patterns.title: SSL cert expired
patterns.diagnosis: The server's TLS certificate is past its valid-until date.
fixes: Server admin needs to renew.
As a temporary client-side workaround for testing, skip verification (don't ship).
Open the URL in a browser to confirm.

patterns.title: SSL — self-signed cert
patterns.diagnosis: The server presents a cert not signed by a trusted CA.
fixes: For dev with self-signed certs: trust the cert in your store.
Don't use `--insecure` / `verify=False` in production.

patterns.title: DNS — NXDOMAIN
patterns.diagnosis: DNS authoritative server says this name doesn't exist.
fixes: Check spelling.
Wait for DNS propagation if you just created the record.
Try a different resolver.

patterns.title: DNS — SERVFAIL
patterns.diagnosis: Resolver couldn't answer because of an upstream problem.
fixes: Try a different DNS server.
Wait a bit — could be transient.
If you own the domain, check DNSSEC and name-server config.

patterns.match: Could not find a version that satisfies the requirement
patterns.title: pip — no compatible version
patterns.diagnosis: pip can't find a version of the package that fits your constraints / Python version / platform.
fixes: Check the package supports your Python version.
Loosen any version pin.
Try `--pre` to allow pre-releases.

patterns.title: Disk full
patterns.diagnosis: Out of disk space (or inodes).
fixes: `df -h` to find the full volume.
Clean caches, logs, old containers.
`df -i` to check inode usage.

patterns.title: Too many open files
patterns.diagnosis: Process exceeded FD limit.
fixes: `ulimit -n 4096` to raise.
Close file handles promptly.
Pool connections instead of opening fresh ones each time.

patterns.title: Address already in use
patterns.diagnosis: Another process owns that port.
fixes: Find with `lsof -i :PORT` or `netstat`.
Kill the old process or pick another port.

patterns.title: Disk quota exceeded
patterns.diagnosis: User account hit their disk quota (separate from physical space).
fixes: Clean up your home directory.
Ask admin to raise the quota.

patterns.title: I/O error
patterns.diagnosis: Low-level disk/IO failure.
fixes: Check `dmesg` for hardware errors.
Filesystem may need `fsck`.
If on a network share, check connectivity.

patterns.title: Stale file handle
patterns.diagnosis: On NFS: the file was deleted/replaced from another client.
fixes: Re-open the file.
Reduce `noac`/refresh interval on the NFS mount.

patterns.title: DNS timeout
patterns.diagnosis: DNS server didn't respond in time.
fixes: Try another resolver.
Check network.

patterns.title: TLS protocol version mismatch
patterns.diagnosis: Client and server can't agree on a TLS version.
fixes: Update client (old curl / Python / OpenSSL won't support modern TLS).
Server too old? It may need to support TLS 1.2+.

patterns.title: TLS — unknown issuer
patterns.diagnosis: Server's cert is signed by a CA the client doesn't trust.
fixes: Update CA bundle (`certifi`, system store).
If it's an internal CA, add it to the trust store.

patterns.title: No route to host
patterns.diagnosis: Network has no path to the destination.
fixes: Check routes: `ip route` / `route -n`.
VPN required?
Firewall dropping?

patterns.title: Connection reset by peer
patterns.diagnosis: Remote side sent RST — abrupt close.
fixes: Retry — often transient.
Check server logs for crashes.

patterns.title: Partial write
patterns.diagnosis: Wrote fewer bytes than requested. Often disk full or pipe closed.
fixes: Check disk space.
Loop until all bytes written if writing manually.

patterns.title: File too large
patterns.diagnosis: Exceeds filesystem max file size or process limit.
fixes: Split the file.
Some filesystems (FAT32) have small file-size limits.

patterns.title: Text file busy
patterns.diagnosis: You tried to write to an executable that's currently running.
fixes: Stop the running program first.
Or write to a temp name and rename atomically.

patterns.title: E2BIG — argument list too long
patterns.diagnosis: Same as the bash one — the args don't fit.
fixes: Use `xargs` or `find -exec ... +`.

patterns.title: EINVAL — invalid argument
patterns.diagnosis: A syscall got a bad argument.
fixes: Check the call's parameters.
Some calls fail with EINVAL on certain unsupported flag combos.

patterns.title: ELOOP — symlink loop
patterns.diagnosis: Symlinks form a cycle.
fixes: `readlink -f <path>` to follow.
Break the cycle.

patterns.title: ENOLCK — no locks available
patterns.diagnosis: File locking unavailable (often on network filesystems without locking).
fixes: Use a different filesystem.
Mount NFS with `lock` option.

patterns.title: ENOSYS — not implemented
patterns.diagnosis: The kernel/library doesn't implement that call.
fixes: Library version mismatch?
Containers may filter syscalls — check seccomp profile.

patterns.title: EAGAIN — try again
patterns.diagnosis: Non-blocking call had nothing to return right now.
fixes: Wait and retry, or use `select`/`poll` to wait for readiness.

patterns.title: EINTR — interrupted syscall
patterns.diagnosis: A signal interrupted a blocking call.
fixes: Retry the call.
Most modern libraries handle this for you.

patterns.title: Seccomp blocked operation
patterns.diagnosis: Sandbox blocked a syscall.
fixes: Relax the seccomp profile (carefully).
Run with `--security-opt seccomp=unconfined` in Docker (only for debugging).

patterns.title: AWS — credentials missing
patterns.diagnosis: AWS SDK can't find credentials.
fixes: Set env vars: `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID`, `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`.
Or configure `~/.aws/credentials`.
Or use an IAM role on EC2/ECS.

patterns.title: AWS — access denied
patterns.diagnosis: IAM denied the call.
fixes: Check the policy attached to the role/user.
Confirm region and account.
Read the error — it usually names the missing permission.

patterns.title: AWS — throttled
patterns.diagnosis: You're calling too fast for the service's limits.
fixes: Use exponential backoff (most SDKs do automatically).
Request a service quota increase if legitimate.

patterns.title: GCP — quota exceeded
patterns.diagnosis: Hit a Google Cloud quota.
fixes: Check quotas in the console.
Request increase if needed.

patterns.title: MongoDB — duplicate key
patterns.diagnosis: Insert/update violated a unique index.
fixes: Use upsert.
Pick a unique value.

patterns.title: Postgres — too many connections
patterns.diagnosis: DB hit its max_connections.
fixes: Use a connection pool (PgBouncer).
Close idle connections.
Raise `max_connections` if hardware can take it.

patterns.title: MySQL — lock wait timeout
patterns.diagnosis: Transaction waited too long for a row lock.
fixes: Shorten transactions.
Look for contended rows / hot keys.
Tune `innodb_lock_wait_timeout`.

patterns.match: ERR max number of clients reached
patterns.title: Redis — max clients reached
patterns.diagnosis: Hit `maxclients`.
fixes: Close idle connections.
Use a pool.
Raise `maxclients` config.

patterns.title: Kafka — offset out of range
patterns.diagnosis: Consumer asked for an offset that's no longer in the topic.
fixes: Reset offset to earliest/latest.
Increase retention if you need older messages.

patterns.title: gRPC — deadline exceeded
patterns.diagnosis: RPC didn't complete within its deadline.
fixes: Increase the deadline if reasonable.
Check why the server is slow.

patterns.title: gRPC — unavailable
patterns.diagnosis: Couldn't reach the gRPC service.
fixes: Check the service address.
Retry — often transient.

patterns.title: OAuth — invalid_grant
patterns.diagnosis: Refresh/auth code rejected. Expired, revoked, or already used.
fixes: Re-authorize from scratch.
Check clock skew on the client (JWT iat/exp).

patterns.title: JWT expired
patterns.diagnosis: Your auth token is past its expiration.
fixes: Refresh the token.
Re-authenticate.

patterns.title: Signature verification failed
patterns.diagnosis: A signed payload didn't verify. Wrong key, tampering, or formatting.
fixes: Confirm both sides use the same key/algorithm.
Don't re-encode the payload between sign and verify.

patterns.title: npm audit — vulnerabilities
patterns.diagnosis: Some dependencies have known security advisories.
fixes: `npm audit fix` to auto-fix what's safe.
Review remaining advisories carefully — not every CVE applies to your use.

patterns.title: Headless Chrome failed to launch
patterns.diagnosis: Puppeteer/Playwright couldn't start the browser.
fixes: Install missing system libraries (most distros need `--no-sandbox` or extras).
Try `--no-sandbox` in args (only in sandboxed envs).
On Linux, install: `libnss3`, `libatk-bridge2.0-0`, etc.

patterns.title: TypeError — int isn't iterable
patterns.diagnosis: You wrote `for x in n:` where `n` is an int. To loop a number of times, use `range(n)`.
fixes: Use `range(n)` to iterate `n` times.
Convert to string `str(n)` to iterate digits.

patterns.match: TypeError: object of type 'int' has no len\(\)
patterns.title: TypeError — int has no len()
patterns.diagnosis: You called `len(n)` on a number.
fixes: Convert to string first: `len(str(n))` to count digits.
Or apply `len` to the actual collection you meant.

patterns.title: zlib error
patterns.diagnosis: Decompression failed — data corrupt or wrong format.
fixes: Verify the source data is actually gzip/zlib compressed.
Check for truncated downloads.

patterns.title: OSError EINVAL
patterns.diagnosis: An OS call got an argument it considered invalid.
fixes: Check path encoding (especially on Windows with non-ASCII).
Some operations need specific flags.

patterns.title: ZeroDivisionError — float division by zero
patterns.diagnosis: You did `x / 0.0` with floats.
fixes: Use `math.inf` or `nan` semantics: `numerator / denom if denom else float('inf')`.

patterns.match: TypeError: not all arguments converted during string formatting
patterns.title: TypeError — leftover args in % formatting
patterns.diagnosis: Old-style `%` formatting has more args than placeholders.
fixes: Wrap multiple args in a tuple: `'%s %s' % (a, b)`.
Switch to f-strings.

patterns.title: TypeError — number format needed
patterns.diagnosis: `%d`/`%f` got a non-number.
fixes: Convert: `'%d' % int(x)`.

patterns.title: AttributeError — str.decode (Python 3)
patterns.diagnosis: Python 3 strings don't have `.decode` — that's a bytes method.
fixes: If you have bytes, `.decode('utf-8')`.
If you already have a str, you don't need to decode anything.

patterns.title: AttributeError — bytes.encode
patterns.diagnosis: Bytes don't have `.encode`. You probably want `.decode` to get a str.
fixes: Use `.decode('utf-8')` to turn bytes into str.

patterns.title: TypeError — __init__ returned non-None
patterns.diagnosis: `__init__` mustn't return anything other than None.
fixes: Remove the `return` statement.
If you want to construct and return, use `__new__` or a classmethod factory.

patterns.title: decimal — invalid operation
patterns.diagnosis: A `Decimal` operation got bad input or hit a trap.
fixes: Validate the string before constructing `Decimal(s)`.
Set a more lenient `getcontext()` if needed.

patterns.title: React — too many re-renders
patterns.diagnosis: A component keeps calling `setState`/state-setter inside render or in an effect with bad deps, causing an infinite loop.
fixes: Don't call setters unconditionally in the render body.
Check `useEffect` deps — missing them can cause loops.
Memoize functions and values that go into deps.

patterns.match: Can't perform a React state update on an unmounted component
patterns.title: React — setState on unmounted component
patterns.diagnosis: An async callback fired after the component unmounted.
fixes: Track a mounted flag with `useRef` and skip the setter if unmounted.
Cancel pending requests in the effect cleanup.
Use AbortController with fetch.

patterns.match: Functions are not valid as a React child
patterns.title: React — rendered a function
patterns.diagnosis: You rendered a function instead of calling it.
fixes: Call it: `{render()}`, not `{render}`.
If you meant a component, capitalize and use JSX: `<Render />`.

patterns.title: Node engine incompatible
patterns.diagnosis: Module declares Node engines that don't match yours.
fixes: Upgrade Node via `nvm`.
Or pick an older module version that supports your Node.

patterns.title: Node — self-signed cert
patterns.diagnosis: Node rejected a self-signed TLS cert.
fixes: Trust the cert in `NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS`.
For dev only: `NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED=0` (don't ship!).

patterns.title: EPERM — operation not permitted
patterns.diagnosis: On Windows often a file is open in another process. On Unix, missing capability.
fixes: Close anything that has the file open.
Antivirus on Windows can hold files briefly — retry.

patterns.title: Promise.all needs an iterable
patterns.diagnosis: `Promise.all` got something that isn't iterable.
fixes: Pass an array of promises.
Use `Object.values(map)` if you have an object of promises.

patterns.title: Node deprecation — punycode
patterns.diagnosis: Node has deprecated the built-in `punycode` module.
fixes: Install the userland version: `npm install punycode`.
Or check if your dependency has an update that removes its use.

patterns.title: Git — too many arguments
patterns.diagnosis: Subcommand got more args than it accepts.
fixes: Check the command syntax.
Quote arguments with spaces.

patterns.title: Git — invalid path
patterns.diagnosis: Path `{1}` isn't valid (e.g. contains `..`, or Windows reserved chars).
fixes: Rename the file.
On Windows, watch for `CON`, `PRN`, `AUX`, etc.

patterns.title: Git rename failed
patterns.diagnosis: Git's working-tree rename failed — usually permissions or a file lock.
fixes: Close anything that has the file open.
Check filesystem permissions.

patterns.title: Git — corrupt loose object
patterns.diagnosis: Object file in `.git/objects/` is damaged.
fixes: Run `git fsck`.
Re-fetch from remote to repair.
Re-clone as a last resort.

patterns.title: Author identity unknown
patterns.diagnosis: Git needs user.name and user.email.
fixes: `git config --global user.name 'You'`.
`git config --global user.email 'you@example.com'`.

patterns.match: The current branch .* has no upstream branch
patterns.title: No upstream — first push
patterns.diagnosis: You haven't set an upstream branch yet.
fixes: `git push -u origin <branch>` to set it on first push.
After that, plain `git push` works.

patterns.title: kill — invalid signal
patterns.diagnosis: Signal name/number isn't recognized.
fixes: List signals: `kill -l`.
Common: `TERM`, `KILL`, `HUP`, `INT`, `QUIT`.

patterns.title: Unterminated command substitution
patterns.diagnosis: `$(...)` or backticks not closed.
fixes: Balance parens / backticks.
Watch for nested substitutions.

patterns.title: pipefail mention
patterns.diagnosis: Pipefail makes pipelines fail when any stage does.
fixes: `set -o pipefail` is recommended at the top of scripts.
Combined with `set -eu` for safer scripts.

patterns.title: Keychain locked
patterns.diagnosis: macOS keychain is locked — you need to unlock it.
fixes: Unlock from Keychain Access app.
`security unlock-keychain`.

patterns.title: HTTP 407 — proxy auth required
patterns.diagnosis: Your proxy needs credentials.
fixes: Set credentials in the proxy URL: `http://user:pass@proxy:port`.
Or configure your client's proxy auth settings.

patterns.title: DNS — REFUSED
patterns.diagnosis: The DNS server refused to answer (likely policy / ACL).
fixes: Try a different resolver.
If you control the server, check its ACLs.

patterns.title: Address family not supported
patterns.diagnosis: Tried to use IPv6 on a system without IPv6, or vice versa.
fixes: Force IPv4: `curl -4`, `python -c 'socket.AF_INET'`.
Check that the interface supports the family.

patterns.title: Tip — setrecursionlimit
patterns.diagnosis: You're raising the recursion limit. Make sure the deep recursion is really intended.
fixes: Verify the algorithm — could it be iterative?
Very deep recursion risks stack overflow at the OS level.

patterns.title: URIError — malformed URI
patterns.diagnosis: `decodeURIComponent` (or similar) got an invalid encoding like `%G1`.
fixes: Validate input before decoding.
Wrap in try/catch and fall back to the raw value.

patterns.title: PendingDeprecationWarning
patterns.diagnosis: A future Python release plans to remove this. You have time, but plan ahead.
fixes: Read the warning text for the replacement.
Bump your code now while it's easy.

patterns.title: ValueError — math domain error
patterns.diagnosis: A `math` function got an input outside its valid range — typically `math.sqrt` of a negative number, `math.log` of zero or a negative, or `math.acos`/`asin` of a value outside [-1, 1].
fixes: Guard the input: check `if x >= 0` before `math.sqrt(x)`, or `if x > 0` before `math.log(x)`.
For square roots of negatives, switch to `cmath.sqrt(x)` to get a complex result.
Clamp domain-limited args: `math.acos(max(-1, min(1, x)))` to absorb tiny floating-point overshoots.
patterns.example_fix:
import math
val = math.sqrt(x) if x >= 0 else 0

patterns.match: ValueError: could not convert string to float: '([^']*)'
patterns.title: ValueError — that string isn't a float
patterns.diagnosis: `float()` got `'{1}'`, which doesn't look like a number. Common culprits: stray whitespace, commas as thousands separators, a currency symbol, or an empty string from blank input.
fixes: Strip and clean first: `float(s.strip().replace(',', ''))`.
If `'{1}'` could be empty, default it: `float(s) if s.strip() else 0.0`.
Validate with a try/except so one bad row doesn't crash the whole loop.

patterns.match: TypeError: string indices must be integers
patterns.title: TypeError — indexing a string with a string
patterns.diagnosis: You wrote something like `s['key']` but `s` is a string, and strings can only be indexed by integers. This almost always means a variable you thought was a dict (or a row/JSON object) is actually a plain string.
fixes: Print `type(s)` right before the line — you probably have a `str` where you expected a `dict`.
If you parsed JSON, make sure you used `json.loads(...)` (returns objects), not `json.dumps(...)` (returns a string).
When looping a dict with `for x in d:` you get the keys (strings); use `for k, v in d.items():` to get values.

patterns.match: TypeError: list indices must be integers or slices, not ([\w.]+)
patterns.title: TypeError — indexing a list with a {1}
patterns.diagnosis: You indexed a list using a `{1}` instead of an integer. Usually this is treating a list like a dict (`lst['name']`) or using a float/string index by accident.
fixes: If you meant a dictionary lookup, the variable is a list — check where it was built.
Cast a numeric index to int: `lst[int(i)]`.
To find an item by value, search instead: `[x for x in lst if x['name'] == 'foo']`.

patterns.title: TypeError — can't unpack that
patterns.diagnosis: You tried `a, b = something` but `something` is a `{1}`, which can't be unpacked. Often a function returned a single value (or `None`) where you expected a tuple.
fixes: Check the return value of the function on the right-hand side — does it actually return multiple values?
If it can return `None`, handle that case before unpacking.
If you only need one value, drop the second target: `a = something`.

patterns.match: ValueError: list\.remove\(x\): x not in list
patterns.title: ValueError — removing an item that isn't there
patterns.diagnosis: `list.remove(x)` raises when `x` isn't in the list. The value may have already been removed, or it doesn't match exactly (e.g. `'5'` vs `5`, or trailing whitespace).
fixes: Check membership first: `if x in lst: lst.remove(x)`.
Make sure the types match — `lst.remove(5)` won't find `'5'`.
If you're removing inside a loop, iterate over a copy (`for x in lst[:]:`) so indices don't shift.

patterns.title: ValueError — str.index() couldn't find it
patterns.diagnosis: `str.index(sub)` raises when `sub` isn't present. Unlike `str.find`, which returns -1, `index` throws.
fixes: Use `str.find(sub)` and check for `-1` if a missing substring is normal.
Guard with `if sub in s:` before calling `s.index(sub)`.
Watch case and whitespace — `'Hello'.index('hello')` fails; normalize with `.lower()` first.

patterns.match: TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of '([^']+)' and '([^']+)'
patterns.title: TypeError — can't order those two types
patterns.diagnosis: Python tried to compare a `{1}` with a `{2}` using `<` (often while sorting), but it doesn't know how to order them. Usually a mix of numbers and strings, or `None` sneaking into the data.
fixes: Make the values one type before sorting: `sorted(items, key=lambda x: str(x))` or `key=int`.
If `None` may appear, filter it out or sort with `key=lambda x: (x is None, x)`.
Sorting a list of dicts? Pass an explicit `key=` so you compare a single field, not the whole dict.

patterns.match: TypeError: object of type '([^']+)' has no len\(\)
patterns.title: TypeError — {1} has no len()
patterns.diagnosis: You called `len()` on a `{1}`, which doesn't have a length. Common with `int`, `float`, generators, or `None`.
fixes: If `{1}` is an int and you wanted its digit count, convert: `len(str(n))`.
Generators have no len — materialize first with `len(list(gen))`.
If `{1}` is `NoneType`, a function probably returned nothing where you expected a collection.

patterns.match: TypeError: argument of type '([^']+)' is not iterable
patterns.title: TypeError — `in` on a non-iterable
patterns.diagnosis: You used `x in y` where `y` is a `{1}` that can't be searched. The `in` operator needs the right-hand side to be a container (list, str, dict, set), not an int or None.
fixes: Check the right side of `in` — print `type(y)`; it's likely an `int` or `None`.
If you meant to test equality, use `==` not `in`.
Wrap a single value as a container if needed: `x in [y]`.

patterns.title: SyntaxError — return outside a function
patterns.diagnosis: A `return` statement is sitting at module level or in a block that isn't inside a `def`. Usually an indentation slip pulled it out of the function body.
fixes: Indent the `return` so it's inside the function it belongs to.
At module level, use `sys.exit()` or just an expression instead of `return`.
Check that the enclosing `def` line wasn't accidentally commented out or mis-indented.

patterns.title: SyntaxError — break outside a loop
patterns.diagnosis: `break` only works inside a `for` or `while` loop. It's currently outside one — often due to wrong indentation or a loop that got refactored away.
fixes: Make sure the `break` is indented inside the loop body.
If you wanted to exit a function, use `return` instead.
To stop the whole program, use `sys.exit()`.

patterns.title: SyntaxError — continue outside a loop
patterns.diagnosis: `continue` only makes sense inside a `for`/`while` loop. It's outside one, usually because of an indentation mistake.
fixes: Indent the `continue` so it lives inside the loop body.
If the loop was removed, delete the now-orphaned `continue`.
Don't put `continue` inside a `try/finally` that escapes the loop in older Pythons.

patterns.title: SyntaxError — yield outside a function
patterns.diagnosis: `yield` can only appear inside a function (which makes it a generator). It's at module level or wrongly indented.
fixes: Wrap the `yield` logic in a `def` so it becomes a generator function.
Check indentation — the `yield` may have fallen out of its function body.
If you wanted an expression, you may have meant `return` or a list comprehension instead.

patterns.title: SyntaxError — assigning to a literal
patterns.diagnosis: You tried to assign to a constant like `5 = x` or `'a' = b`. The target on the left of `=` must be a name, not a literal value. Often a flipped assignment or a `==` typed as `=`.
fixes: Swap the sides — the variable goes on the left: `x = 5`.
If you meant a comparison, use `==` not `=`.
Check for a stray number/string where a variable name should be.

patterns.match: SyntaxError: cannot assign to function call
patterns.title: SyntaxError — assigning to a function call
patterns.diagnosis: You wrote something like `foo() = 5`. You can't assign to the result of a call. This often happens when `[]` indexing got typed as `()`.
fixes: If you meant to index, use brackets: `lst[0] = 5`, not `lst(0) = 5`.
Assign the call result to a variable instead: `result = foo()`.
Check for a `==` that should be there, or a misplaced `=`.

patterns.title: IndentationError — unexpected indent
patterns.diagnosis: A line is indented more than the surrounding code expects, without an opening statement (like `if:` or `def:`) to justify it. Often a stray space/tab at the start of a line.
fixes: Remove the extra leading whitespace so the line lines up with its siblings.
Make your editor show whitespace and use 4 spaces per level consistently (never mix tabs and spaces).
Check the line just above — if it should have opened a block, it may be missing its colon.

patterns.title: IndentationError — unexpected unindent
patterns.diagnosis: A line is dedented to a level that doesn't match any open block. Python can't tell where the current block ends.
fixes: Align the line with one of the existing indentation levels.
Check for a missing or extra line above that threw the block off.
Use spaces only — a mix of tabs and spaces makes levels look aligned when they aren't.

patterns.match: ModuleNotFoundError: No module named '([^']+)'; '([^']+)' is not a package
patterns.title: ModuleNotFoundError — {2} isn't a package
patterns.diagnosis: You tried `from {2} import ...` or `import {1}`, but `{2}` is a single module file, not a package (a folder with `__init__.py`). You can't import a submodule out of a plain module.
fixes: If `{2}` is your own file, you probably meant `from {2} import name`, not `import {2}.something`.
A name clash with a local file shadowing a real package? Rename your file (e.g. don't call it `email.py`, `json.py`).
To make `{2}` a package, turn it into a folder with an `__init__.py`.

patterns.title: OverflowError — math result too large
patterns.diagnosis: A `math` function produced a number too big for a float, e.g. `math.exp(1000)`. Floats top out around 1.8e308.
fixes: Work in log space: keep `math.log(x)` values instead of the raw exponentials and add instead of multiply.
Clamp the input range before calling `math.exp`/`math.pow`.
For arbitrary precision use the `decimal` module or pure-Python ints (which are unbounded).

patterns.match: TypeError: sequence item (\d+): expected str instance, ([\w.]+) found
patterns.title: TypeError — join got a non-string item
patterns.diagnosis: `str.join` needs every item in the iterable to be a string, but item {1} is a `{2}`. One element (often an int or None) isn't text.
fixes: Convert every element to str: `', '.join(str(x) for x in items)`.
Item {1} is a `{2}` — find where it entered the list and stringify it there.
Filter out `None` first if blanks are expected: `', '.join(str(x) for x in items if x is not None)`.

patterns.match: AttributeError: '([^']+)' object has no attribute '([^']+)'\. Did you mean: '([^']+)'\?
patterns.title: AttributeError — typo for `{3}`?
patterns.diagnosis: A `{1}` has no `.{2}` — Python suggests you meant `.{3}`. This is almost always a method/attribute spelling slip.
fixes: Use the suggested name: `.{3}` instead of `.{2}`.
Check the docs for the exact method name on `{1}`.
Print `dir(obj)` to list every available attribute on the object.

patterns.title: KeyError — missing environment variable {1}?
patterns.diagnosis: A key `{1}` is missing. If you read it from `os.environ['{1}']`, the environment variable isn't set in this shell/process.
fixes: Use `os.environ.get('{1}')` (returns `None`) or `os.environ.get('{1}', default)` to avoid the crash.
Set the variable before running: `export {1}=value` (or add it to a `.env` loaded by python-dotenv).
If this is a plain dict, the key was never inserted — check spelling and where it should be set.

patterns.match: TypeError: '([^']+)' object cannot be interpreted as an integer
patterns.title: TypeError — {1} where an int was needed
patterns.diagnosis: A spot that needs a whole number (like `range()`, `round(x, n)`, list repetition, or an index) got a `{1}`. Usually a float, string, or None slipped in.
fixes: Convert to int: `range(int(n))`.
If `{1}` is a float from division, use `//` for integer division, or wrap with `int(...)`.
Check that the value isn't a numeric string like `'5'` — parse it first.

patterns.match: TypeError: '([^']+)' object does not support item deletion
patterns.title: TypeError — can't `del` an item from that
patterns.diagnosis: You used `del thing[i]` but `{1}` doesn't allow item deletion — tuples and strings are immutable, for example.
fixes: If you need to remove items, use a mutable type like `list`.
Build a new value without the item instead: `t = t[:i] + t[i+1:]`.
For strings, use `.replace(...)` or slicing rather than `del`.

patterns.title: TypeError — __str__ didn't return a string
patterns.diagnosis: Your class's `__str__` method returned a `{1}` instead of a `str`. `__str__` must always return text.
fixes: Wrap the return in `str(...)` or use an f-string: `return f'{self.value}'`.
If you returned another object, return its string form instead.
Same rule applies to `__repr__` — it must return a `str` too.

patterns.title: TypeError — subscripting a class on old Python
patterns.diagnosis: You wrote a generic type hint like `list[int]` or `dict[str, int]` (or subscripted a class directly), but this Python is older than 3.9 where built-in generics became subscriptable.
fixes: On Python 3.7/3.8, import from typing: `from typing import List, Dict` and use `List[int]`.
Add `from __future__ import annotations` at the top of the file so hints are evaluated lazily.
Or upgrade to Python 3.9+ where `list[int]` works directly.
If this isn't a type hint, you indexed a class object by mistake — instantiate it first.

patterns.match: RuntimeError: Set changed size during iteration
patterns.title: RuntimeError — set changed while looping
patterns.diagnosis: You added to or removed from a set while iterating over it. Python forbids resizing a set mid-loop.
fixes: Iterate over a copy: `for x in set(s):` or `for x in list(s):`.
Collect changes in a separate set, then apply them after the loop.
Use a set comprehension to build the new set in one shot instead of mutating in place.

patterns.title: TypeError — naive vs aware datetimes
patterns.diagnosis: You compared or subtracted a timezone-naive datetime with a timezone-aware one. Python won't mix them.
fixes: Make both aware: attach a tz with `dt.replace(tzinfo=timezone.utc)` or `dt.astimezone(...)`.
Or make both naive by stripping tz: `dt.replace(tzinfo=None)` (only if you're sure of the zone).
Prefer `datetime.now(timezone.utc)` over `datetime.now()` so everything is aware from the start.
patterns.example_fix:
from datetime import datetime, timezone
now = datetime.now(timezone.utc)

patterns.match: ValueError: time data '([^']*)' does not match format '([^']*)'
patterns.title: ValueError — date string doesn't match format
patterns.diagnosis: `strptime` tried to parse `'{1}'` with format `'{2}'`, but they don't line up — wrong separators, swapped day/month, or extra characters.
fixes: Match the format codes to the actual string: `%Y-%m-%d` for `2026-05-28`, `%d/%m/%Y` for `28/05/2026`.
Strip stray whitespace or timezone suffixes before parsing.
For mixed/unknown formats, use `dateutil.parser.parse(s)` which auto-detects.
patterns.example_fix:
from datetime import datetime
dt = datetime.strptime(s, "%Y-%m-%d")

patterns.title: sqlite3 — no such table {1}
patterns.diagnosis: The query references a table `{1}` that doesn't exist in the connected database — it was never created, you connected to the wrong file, or migrations didn't run.
fixes: Run your `CREATE TABLE {1} (...)` before querying it.
Check the database path you passed to `sqlite3.connect(...)` — a typo creates a fresh empty DB.
List existing tables to confirm: `SELECT name FROM sqlite_master WHERE type='table';`.

patterns.match: sqlite3\.IntegrityError: (UNIQUE constraint failed|NOT NULL constraint failed): ([\w.]+)
patterns.title: sqlite3 — {1}
patterns.diagnosis: An insert/update violated a constraint on `{2}`. A UNIQUE failure means a duplicate value; a NOT NULL failure means you left a required column empty.
fixes: For UNIQUE: check before inserting, or use `INSERT OR IGNORE` / `INSERT OR REPLACE`.
For NOT NULL: supply a value for `{2}` (or give the column a `DEFAULT`).
Use an upsert if you want to update existing rows: `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT(...) DO UPDATE SET ...`.

patterns.match: TypeError: Object of type ([\w.]+) is not JSON serializable
patterns.title: TypeError — {1} can't be JSON-encoded
patterns.diagnosis: `json.dumps` hit a `{1}`, which it doesn't know how to serialize. Common offenders: `datetime`, `Decimal`, `set`, `bytes`, numpy types, and custom objects.
fixes: Convert the value first: `dt.isoformat()`, `float(decimal_val)`, `list(my_set)`.
Pass a `default=` handler: `json.dumps(obj, default=str)` for a quick fix.
For dataclasses, use `dataclasses.asdict(obj)` before dumping.

patterns.title: pytest — fixture {1} not found
patterns.diagnosis: A test asked for a fixture named `{1}`, but pytest can't find one. Either it's misspelled, not decorated with `@pytest.fixture`, or it lives somewhere pytest doesn't look.
fixes: Define it: `@pytest.fixture\ndef {1}(): ...`, and check the spelling matches the test parameter.
Put shared fixtures in a `conftest.py` so all tests in that directory can see them.
If it's from a plugin, make sure the plugin is installed and not disabled with `-p no:...`.

patterns.match: TypeError: super\(type, obj\): obj must be an instance or subtype of type
patterns.title: TypeError — bad super() arguments
patterns.diagnosis: An explicit `super(SomeClass, obj)` call got a class/object pair that don't match — `obj` isn't an instance of `SomeClass`. Usually a copy-paste slip in the super() arguments.
fixes: In Python 3, just use the no-argument form inside a method: `super().__init__(...)`.
If you must be explicit, pass the right pair: `super(CurrentClass, self)`.
Make sure `CurrentClass` actually appears in `type(self).__mro__`.

patterns.match: IndexError: index (\d+) is out of bounds for axis (\d+) with size (\d+)
patterns.title: numpy — index {1} out of bounds (axis {2})
patterns.diagnosis: You indexed numpy axis {2} at position {1}, but that axis only has {3} elements (valid indices 0..{3}-1). Off-by-one or a wrong axis assumption.
fixes: Remember indices are 0-based — the last valid index on axis {2} is {3} minus one.
Check the array's shape with `arr.shape` before indexing.
If you swapped dimensions, you may be indexing the wrong axis — `arr[row, col]` order matters.

patterns.match: SyntaxError: invalid syntax\. Perhaps you forgot a comma\?
patterns.title: SyntaxError — missing comma
patterns.diagnosis: Python's newer parser noticed two values sitting side by side with no operator between them, usually inside a list, tuple, dict, or function call. You almost certainly dropped a comma.
fixes: Look at the caret in the traceback — add a comma between the two items it points at.
Check multi-line collections; the missing comma is often at the end of one of the lines.
Don't forget a trailing comma is fine in Python and avoids this when editing lists.

patterns.title: SyntaxError — unclosed bracket
patterns.diagnosis: You opened a `{1}` but never closed it. Python read to the end of the file still expecting the matching closer.
fixes: Find the `{1}` the traceback points to and add its matching close bracket.
Count your openers and closers — an editor with bracket matching highlights the mismatch fast.
A stray bracket inside a string or comment can confuse you; check those too.

patterns.title: SyntaxError — unclosed f-string brace
patterns.diagnosis: An f-string has an opening `{` with no matching `}`. The expression part of an interpolation was left open.
fixes: Close the interpolation with `}`: `f"value is {x}"`.
To print a literal brace, double it: `f"{{not a slot}}"`.
Check nested quotes inside the braces — they can mask where the brace should close.

patterns.match: SyntaxError: f-string expression part cannot include a backslash
patterns.title: SyntaxError — backslash inside f-string (pre-3.12)
patterns.diagnosis: On Python before 3.12, the `{...}` part of an f-string can't contain a backslash, so escapes like `\n` aren't allowed directly inside the braces.
fixes: Move the backslash out: assign it to a variable first, then interpolate the variable.
Use `chr(10)` for a newline inside the expression instead of `\n`.
Upgrade to Python 3.12+, which removed this restriction.

patterns.title: SyntaxError — '{1}' in the wrong place
patterns.diagnosis: `{1}` was used outside the construct it belongs to. `return`/`yield` only work inside a function; `break`/`continue` only inside a loop.
fixes: Check your indentation — the `{1}` may have fallen out of the function or loop body.
If you meant to exit a function, make sure the `def` is actually wrapping this line.
For `break`/`continue`, confirm you're inside a `for` or `while`.

patterns.match: TypeError: ([\w.]+)\(\) takes (\d+) positional arguments? but (\d+) were given
patterns.title: TypeError — too many arguments (often missing self)
patterns.diagnosis: `{1}()` accepts {2} positional argument(s) but you passed {3}. In a method this usually means you forgot `self`, or you're passing one extra value.
fixes: If `{1}` is a method, add `self` as the first parameter: `def {1}(self, ...)`.
Count the arguments at the call site against the definition — drop the extra one.
If the count is one more than expected on a method call, you're likely calling it on the class instead of an instance.

patterns.match: TypeError: ([\w.]+)\(\) got multiple values for argument '([^']+)'
patterns.title: TypeError — argument '{2}' passed twice
patterns.diagnosis: `{1}()` received `{2}` both positionally and as a keyword, so Python got two values for the same parameter.
fixes: Drop either the positional value or the `{2}=...` keyword — not both.
This is common when `self`/`cls` shifts the positions; check whether you're double-passing the first real argument.
Match each call-site argument to exactly one parameter.
patterns.example_fix:
greet("hi")            # or  greet(msg="hi")
# not  greet("hi", msg="hi")

patterns.match: TypeError: string indices must be integers(?:, not '([^']+)')?
patterns.title: TypeError — bad string index
patterns.diagnosis: You indexed a string with something that isn't an integer (often a string key). This frequently means a value you thought was a dict is actually a string — e.g. JSON parsed wrong, or you're looping over a dict's keys.
fixes: If you expected a dict, check what the variable really holds (`print(type(x))`).
Iterating a dict yields keys; use `for k, v in d.items()` to get values.
Index strings with integers or slices: `s[0]`, `s[1:4]`.
patterns.example_fix:
for k, v in record.items():
    print(v["name"])   # v is a dict, not the outer string

patterns.match: TypeError: 'float' object cannot be interpreted as an integer
patterns.title: TypeError — float where an int is required
patterns.diagnosis: Something that demands a whole number (like `range`, list indexing, or `*` repetition) got a float. Division with `/` always yields a float in Python 3.
fixes: Use `//` for integer division: `range(n // 2)` instead of `range(n / 2)`.
Wrap with `int(...)` when you really want truncation.
Index and `range` need ints — convert the float first.
patterns.example_fix:
for i in range(n // 2):   # not  range(n / 2)
    ...

patterns.title: TypeError — wrong argument count for built-in
patterns.diagnosis: `{1}` expected {2} argument(s) but got {3}. A builtin or C-level function is being called with the wrong number of values.
fixes: Check the function's signature in the docs and match the count.
Watch for an accidental extra comma turning one argument into a tuple.
If wrapping with `*args`, confirm the unpacked length is what the function wants.

patterns.match: AttributeError: '([^']+)' object has no attribute '([^']+)'\. Did you mean to assign to it
patterns.title: AttributeError — reading an attribute that was never set
patterns.diagnosis: You read `.{2}` on a `{1}`, but it was never assigned. Often it's only set inside a method that hasn't run yet, or only in some code paths.
fixes: Initialize `self.{2}` in `__init__` so it always exists.
Make sure the method that sets `.{2}` actually runs before you read it.
Guard the read with `getattr(obj, "{2}", default)` if it's genuinely optional.

patterns.title: AttributeError — using 'with' on a non-context-manager
patterns.diagnosis: You used `with` on a `{1}`, but it isn't a context manager. Common when you `with` something already opened, or a plain object that doesn't support the protocol.
fixes: Use `with open(path) as f:` — don't wrap an already-open file or a non-manager.
Confirm the object defines `__enter__`/`__exit__` (or use `contextlib.contextmanager`).
If it's a lock/connection, check the library's docs for the right `with` target.
patterns.example_fix:
with open("data.txt") as f:
    data = f.read()

patterns.title: AttributeError — calling a non-list method on a list
patterns.diagnosis: Lists don't have `.{1}`. You may be expecting a string, dict, or numpy/pandas method on a plain list, or you meant a list method with a different name.
fixes: For strings: convert with `" ".join(lst)` or index an element first.
Lists have `.append`, `.extend`, `.sort`, `.pop` — not `.{1}`.
If you wanted a DataFrame/array method, build that object first (`pd.DataFrame(lst)` / `np.array(lst)`).

patterns.title: AttributeError — method called on an int
patterns.diagnosis: Integers don't have `.{1}`. A value you expected to be a string/list/object is actually an `int`.
fixes: Check the variable's type with `print(type(x))`.
If you need string methods, convert first: `str(n).{1}(...)`.
A reassignment earlier may have overwritten an object with a number.

patterns.match: ValueError: I/O operation on closed file
patterns.title: ValueError — file used after closing
patterns.diagnosis: You read or wrote a file after it was closed. With `with open(...)`, the file closes at the end of the block, so using the handle outside the block fails.
fixes: Do all reads/writes inside the `with` block, while the file is still open.
If you need the data later, read it into a variable inside the block.
Don't reuse a file object after calling `.close()` on it.
patterns.example_fix:
with open("f.txt") as f:
    data = f.read()   # use it here
print(data)            # not f.read() out here

patterns.match: ImportError: cannot import name '([^']+)' from partially initialized module '([^']+)'
patterns.title: ImportError — circular import
patterns.diagnosis: Module `{2}` imported `{1}` before `{2}` finished loading. Two modules import each other, so one sees the other half-built.
fixes: Move the import inside the function that needs it (deferred/local import).
Restructure so the shared code lives in a third module both can import.
Import the module object (`import {2}`) and reference `{2}.{1}` lazily instead of `from`-importing the name at top level.

patterns.match: ImportError: ([^ ]+): cannot open shared object file: No such file or directory
patterns.title: ImportError — missing native shared library
patterns.diagnosis: A C-extension package needs the native library `{1}`, but the OS loader can't find it. The Python wheel is installed but a system dependency is missing.
fixes: Install the system package that provides `{1}` (e.g. via apt/brew/yum).
Add its directory to `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` if it's installed somewhere non-standard.
Reinstall the Python package after the system lib is present so it links correctly.

patterns.title: ImportError — NumPy ABI / version mismatch
patterns.diagnosis: A package was built against a different NumPy version than the one installed (the NumPy 1.x vs 2.x ABI break is the usual cause).
fixes: Pin compatible versions: either `numpy<2` or upgrade the dependent package for NumPy 2.
Reinstall in a clean virtualenv so everything links against one NumPy.
Force a rebuild: `pip install --no-binary :all: <package>` if a stale wheel is to blame.
patterns.example_fix: pip install "numpy<2"   # or upgrade the package that needs >=2

patterns.title: RuntimeError — collection mutated while looping
patterns.diagnosis: You added to or removed from a `{1}` while iterating over it. Python won't let the container resize mid-loop.
fixes: Iterate over a copy: `for x in list(coll):` or `for k in list(d.keys()):`.
Collect items to remove, then delete them after the loop.
Build a new filtered collection instead of mutating in place.

patterns.match: RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded in comparison
patterns.title: RecursionError — runaway recursion
patterns.diagnosis: A function kept calling itself past Python's stack limit (default ~1000). Either the base case is never hit, or the problem is genuinely too deep for recursion.
fixes: Add or fix the base case so recursion actually terminates.
Make sure each call moves toward the base case (shrinking input).
Rewrite as an iterative loop for large inputs, or raise the limit with `sys.setrecursionlimit(...)` cautiously.

patterns.title: OSError — filename too long
patterns.diagnosis: The path or filename exceeds the filesystem limit (often 255 chars per component). Frequently a URL or huge string got used as a filename.
fixes: Shorten the name, or hash it (`hashlib.md5(name.encode()).hexdigest()`) for a fixed-length filename.
If you accidentally passed file *contents* where a path was expected, fix the argument.
Split deeply nested paths so no single component is too long.

patterns.title: FileExistsError — path already exists
patterns.diagnosis: You tried to create `{1}` but it already exists — typically `os.mkdir` on an existing directory, or opening with `'x'` mode on an existing file.
fixes: Use `os.makedirs('{1}', exist_ok=True)` to ignore an existing directory.
Check first with `os.path.exists('{1}')` before creating.
Open with `'w'` to overwrite, or `'a'` to append, instead of `'x'`.

patterns.title: MySQL 1054 — unknown column
patterns.diagnosis: MySQL can't find a column named `{1}` while resolving the `{2}` clause. Usually a typo, a column that lives on a different table, or an alias referenced before it exists.
fixes: Run `DESCRIBE your_table;` (or `SHOW COLUMNS FROM your_table;`) and confirm `{1}` is spelled exactly right — names can be case-sensitive on Linux.
If `{1}` belongs to a joined table, qualify it: `tablename.{1}` so MySQL looks in the right place.
You can't use a SELECT-list alias in `WHERE` (it's evaluated before SELECT) — repeat the expression or move it to `HAVING`.
patterns.example_fix: SELECT u.id, u.email FROM users u WHERE u.email = 'a@b.com';

patterns.title: MySQL 1146 — table doesn't exist
patterns.diagnosis: MySQL looked for `{1}` and found nothing. Either the table name/schema is wrong, you're connected to the wrong database, or the name's case doesn't match (table-name case sensitivity follows `lower_case_table_names`).
fixes: Run `SHOW TABLES;` to see the exact names, then `USE the_right_db;` if you're in the wrong schema.
Qualify the table with its database: `SELECT * FROM mydb.tablename;`.
On Linux, table names are case-sensitive — make sure `{1}` matches the on-disk name exactly.

patterns.match: ERROR 1064 \(42000\): You have an error in your SQL syntax
patterns.title: MySQL 1064 — SQL syntax error
patterns.diagnosis: The parser hit something it couldn't understand. The message usually quotes the text 'near ...' — that's roughly where parsing broke, so the real mistake is often the token just before it.
fixes: Look at the snippet after 'near' in the full error — the problem is usually right before that point (a missing comma, stray quote, or unclosed paren).
Check for reserved words used as identifiers (`order`, `group`, `rank`) — wrap them in backticks: `` `order` ``.
Make sure each statement ends with `;` and string literals use straight single quotes, not smart quotes.
patterns.example_fix: SELECT `order`, total FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid';

patterns.title: MySQL 1062 — duplicate key
patterns.diagnosis: You tried to insert/update a row whose value `{1}` collides with an existing row on the unique index `{2}`. The constraint is doing its job — that value already exists.
fixes: Check first with `SELECT * FROM tbl WHERE col = '{1}';` to see the existing row.
Use `INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE` if you want to update instead of fail.
Use `INSERT IGNORE` to silently skip the duplicate, or `REPLACE INTO` to overwrite it.
If the duplicate is unexpected, the unique index `{2}` may be on the wrong column — review the table definition.
patterns.example_fix:
INSERT INTO users (email) VALUES ('{1}')
ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE updated_at = NOW();

patterns.match: ERROR 1452 \(23000\): Cannot add or update a child row: a foreign key constraint fails
patterns.title: MySQL 1452 — foreign key constraint fails
patterns.diagnosis: You inserted/updated a child row whose foreign-key value has no matching row in the parent table. InnoDB refuses to create an orphan reference.
fixes: Insert the parent row first, then the child — the referenced id must already exist.
Verify the FK value: `SELECT * FROM parent WHERE id = <your_value>;` should return a row.
If you're loading data and order is hard to control, you can temporarily `SET FOREIGN_KEY_CHECKS=0;`, load, then `SET FOREIGN_KEY_CHECKS=1;` (re-validate afterward).

patterns.title: MySQL 1452 — named foreign key constraint fails
patterns.diagnosis: The foreign-key constraint `{1}` rejected the write because the referenced parent row doesn't exist. The child can't point at a parent that isn't there.
fixes: Find the constraint's columns with `SHOW CREATE TABLE child_table;` and check which value is unmatched.
Insert or confirm the parent row before writing the child.
If you're deleting parents, set the FK to `ON DELETE CASCADE` or `ON DELETE SET NULL` so children are handled automatically.

patterns.title: MySQL 1366 — incorrect value for column
patterns.diagnosis: The value `{2}` can't be stored in column `{3}` as a `{1}`. Usually you're pushing text into a numeric column, or a string with the wrong character encoding.
fixes: Check the column type with `DESCRIBE tbl;` — `{3}` likely expects a number but got `'{2}'`.
Clean or cast the value before inserting (`CAST('{2}' AS UNSIGNED)`), or fix the source data.
For encoding issues, ensure the connection charset matches the column: `SET NAMES utf8mb4;`.

patterns.match: ERROR 1364 \(HY000\): Field '([^']+)' doesn't have a default value
patterns.title: MySQL 1364 — field needs a value
patterns.diagnosis: Column `{1}` is `NOT NULL` with no default, but your INSERT didn't supply it (strict SQL mode rejects this instead of silently inserting a blank).
fixes: Include `{1}` in the INSERT column list and provide a value.
Give the column a default in the schema: `ALTER TABLE tbl ALTER {1} SET DEFAULT '...';`.
If a blank is genuinely acceptable, make it nullable: `ALTER TABLE tbl MODIFY {1} VARCHAR(255) NULL;` (or relax strict mode, less ideal).

patterns.match: ERROR 1242 \(21000\): Subquery returns more than 1 row
patterns.title: MySQL 1242 — subquery returns more than one row
patterns.diagnosis: A scalar subquery (used with `=`, `<`, etc.) returned multiple rows, but only one value is allowed in that position.
fixes: Switch the operator to `IN` if you intend to match any of several rows: `WHERE x IN (SELECT ...)`.
Constrain the subquery to a single row with `LIMIT 1` or a tighter `WHERE`.
Use an aggregate (`MAX`, `MIN`) so the subquery is guaranteed to return one value.
patterns.example_fix: WHERE price = (SELECT MAX(price) FROM products WHERE cat_id = 3);

patterns.match: ERROR 1140 \(42000\)|ERROR 1055 \(42000\): .*not in GROUP BY clause and contains nonaggregated column '([^']+)'
patterns.title: MySQL 1055 — column not in GROUP BY (only_full_group_by)
patterns.diagnosis: With `only_full_group_by` enabled, every selected column must either be in `GROUP BY` or wrapped in an aggregate. Column `{1}` is neither, so the value would be ambiguous.
fixes: Add `{1}` to the `GROUP BY` clause.
Wrap it in an aggregate if you only need one representative value: `MAX({1})` or `ANY_VALUE({1})`.
If the column is functionally dependent on the GROUP BY key, MySQL 5.7+ usually allows it — otherwise list it explicitly.

patterns.match: ERROR 1093 \(HY000\): You can't specify target table '([^']+)' for update in FROM clause
patterns.title: MySQL 1093 — can't update a table you're selecting from
patterns.diagnosis: MySQL forbids UPDATE/DELETE on `{1}` while a subquery in the same statement also reads from `{1}`. It can't safely modify and scan the same table at once.
fixes: Wrap the subquery in a derived table so MySQL materializes it first: `... IN (SELECT id FROM (SELECT ... FROM {1}) AS t)`.
Rewrite as a self-join UPDATE instead of a correlated subquery.
On modern MySQL/MariaDB, a CTE often sidesteps the restriction too.
patterns.example_fix: DELETE FROM {1} WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM (SELECT id FROM {1} WHERE dup=1) AS t);

patterns.match: ERROR 1205 \(HY000\): Lock wait timeout exceeded; try restarting transaction
patterns.title: MySQL 1205 — lock wait timeout
patterns.diagnosis: Your transaction waited longer than `innodb_lock_wait_timeout` (default 50s) for a row lock held by another transaction, so it gave up.
fixes: Find the blocker: query `INFORMATION_SCHEMA.INNODB_TRX` / `performance_schema.data_locks` to see who holds the lock.
Keep transactions short — commit promptly and don't leave one open while waiting on user input.
Access rows in a consistent order across your app to avoid lock contention; retry the transaction on timeout.

patterns.match: ERROR 1213 \(40001\): Deadlock found when trying to get lock; try restarting transaction
patterns.title: MySQL 1213 — deadlock detected
patterns.diagnosis: Two transactions each held a lock the other needed, forming a cycle. InnoDB detected it and rolled back one of them (the cheaper victim) to break the deadlock.
fixes: Make the application retry the transaction — deadlocks are expected and the rolled-back side should just run again.
Acquire locks in a consistent order everywhere (e.g. always lock parent before child) to prevent cycles.
Inspect `SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS;` (LATEST DETECTED DEADLOCK section) to see exactly which statements clashed.

patterns.title: MySQL 1045 — access denied
patterns.diagnosis: Authentication failed for `{1}` connecting from `{2}` — wrong password, or no grant matching that user@host pair.
fixes: Double-check the password; reset it with `ALTER USER '{1}'@'{2}' IDENTIFIED BY 'newpass';` as an admin.
MySQL accounts are user+host — a grant for `'{1}'@'localhost'` won't cover `'{1}'@'{2}'`. Create the right one or use `'%'`.
Run `FLUSH PRIVILEGES;` after granting, and confirm with `SELECT user, host FROM mysql.user;`.

patterns.match: ERROR 2002 \(HY000\): Can't connect to (local )?MySQL server (through socket|on) '([^']+)'
patterns.title: MySQL 2002 — can't connect to server
patterns.diagnosis: The client couldn't reach the server at `{3}`. Either mysqld isn't running, the socket/host is wrong, or a firewall is blocking the port.
fixes: Confirm the server is up: `systemctl status mysql` (or `mysqld`) / `brew services list`.
If it's a socket path issue, point the client at TCP: `mysql -h 127.0.0.1 -P 3306 -u root -p`.
Check the socket path matches the server's `--socket` setting in `my.cnf`, and that port 3306 isn't firewalled.

patterns.title: Postgres — relation does not exist
patterns.diagnosis: Postgres couldn't find a table/view named `{1}`. Common cause: the identifier was created with quotes (so it's case-sensitive), it's in a schema not on your `search_path`, or it's simply misspelled.
fixes: List tables with `\dt` in psql, or query `information_schema.tables` to confirm the name.
Unquoted identifiers fold to lowercase — if you ran `CREATE TABLE "Users"`, you must query `"Users"`, not `users`.
Qualify with the schema (`SELECT * FROM myschema.{1};`) or add the schema to `search_path`.

patterns.title: Postgres — column does not exist
patterns.diagnosis: No column named `{1}` is visible in the current query. Often it's a typo, a quoted (case-sensitive) name, or you used double quotes around a string literal — Postgres treats `"x"` as an identifier, not text.
fixes: String literals use single quotes: `WHERE name = 'value'`. Double quotes mean a column/table name.
Check the real column names with `\d tablename` in psql.
If the column came from a joined table and is ambiguous, qualify it: `t.{1}`.
patterns.example_fix: SELECT * FROM users WHERE status = 'active';  -- single quotes for text

patterns.match: ERROR:  syntax error at or near "([^"]+)"
patterns.title: Postgres — syntax error at or near
patterns.diagnosis: Postgres's parser failed at the token `{1}`. The real mistake is usually just before `{1}` (a missing comma, an unclosed parenthesis, or a reserved word used as a name).
fixes: Inspect the SQL immediately before `{1}` — that's where the grammar broke.
If `{1}` is a reserved word being used as a column/table name (`user`, `order`, `limit`), double-quote it: `"{1}"`.
Check for a stray/missing comma in a SELECT or column list, and that all parentheses are balanced.

patterns.match: ERROR:  duplicate key value violates unique constraint "([^"]+)"
patterns.title: Postgres — unique constraint violation
patterns.diagnosis: An insert/update would create a duplicate that the unique constraint/index `{1}` forbids. That key value already exists in the table.
fixes: Use `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (col) DO NOTHING` or `DO UPDATE SET ...` for an upsert.
Query for the existing row first to confirm what's colliding (the DETAIL line names the value).
If a serial/identity sequence is out of sync after a manual insert, reset it: `SELECT setval('tbl_id_seq', (SELECT MAX(id) FROM tbl));`.
patterns.example_fix:
INSERT INTO users (email) VALUES ('a@b.com')
ON CONFLICT (email) DO UPDATE SET seen_at = now();

patterns.match: ERROR:  insert or update on table "([^"]+)" violates foreign key constraint "([^"]+)"
patterns.title: Postgres — foreign key violation
patterns.diagnosis: A write to `{1}` referenced a parent row that doesn't exist, so constraint `{2}` blocked it. Postgres won't allow a dangling reference.
fixes: Insert the referenced parent row first; the DETAIL line shows which key value is missing.
Verify the value exists in the parent: `SELECT * FROM parent WHERE id = <value>;`.
If you're deleting parents and want children handled automatically, define the FK with `ON DELETE CASCADE` or `ON DELETE SET NULL`.

patterns.match: ERROR:  null value in column "([^"]+)" (of relation "([^"]+)" )?violates not-null constraint
patterns.title: Postgres — not-null constraint violation
patterns.diagnosis: Column `{1}` is `NOT NULL`, but the row you wrote left it NULL (either omitted, or an expression evaluated to NULL).
fixes: Provide a value for `{1}` in the INSERT/UPDATE.
Give the column a default: `ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN {1} SET DEFAULT '...';`.
If NULLs are legitimately allowed, drop the constraint: `ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN {1} DROP NOT NULL;`.
Watch for joins/subqueries that produce NULL when no row matches — use `COALESCE(expr, fallback)`.

patterns.title: Postgres — invalid input syntax for type
patterns.diagnosis: Postgres tried to coerce `"{2}"` into a `{1}` and failed — the text isn't a valid literal of that type (e.g. a non-numeric string into integer, or a malformed date).
fixes: Make sure the value matches the column type; clean stray characters or whitespace before inserting.
For dates, use ISO format `'YYYY-MM-DD'` (or cast explicitly: `'{2}'::date`).
If a column has the wrong type for your data, fix it with `ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN ... TYPE ... USING ...`.

patterns.title: Postgres — operator does not exist (type mismatch)
patterns.diagnosis: There's no `{2}` operator defined between `{1}` and `{3}`. Postgres is strict about types and won't implicitly compare, say, text to integer.
fixes: Cast one side so the types line up: `col::text = '5'` or `col = '5'::int`.
Quote literals correctly — a bare number compared to a text column needs `'5'`, and text needs single quotes.
If you meant string concatenation, use `||` (Postgres) rather than `+`.

patterns.match: ERROR:  column "([^"]+)" must appear in the GROUP BY clause or be used in an aggregate function
patterns.title: Postgres — column must appear in GROUP BY
patterns.diagnosis: You selected `{1}` alongside aggregates, but it's neither grouped nor aggregated, so its value is ambiguous per group.
fixes: Add `{1}` to the `GROUP BY` clause.
Wrap it in an aggregate if you just need one value per group: `max({1})`.
If you want a representative row per group, consider `DISTINCT ON (...)` instead of `GROUP BY`.

patterns.title: Postgres — relation already exists
patterns.diagnosis: `CREATE TABLE`/`CREATE INDEX` failed because `{1}` is already defined in the schema.
fixes: Use `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS {1} (...)` to make the create idempotent.
Drop the old one first if you intend to replace it: `DROP TABLE IF EXISTS {1};` (this deletes its data).
If two migrations both create `{1}`, reconcile them so only one owns the object.

patterns.match: ERROR:  current transaction is aborted, commands ignored until end of transaction block
patterns.title: Postgres — transaction aborted
patterns.diagnosis: An earlier statement in this transaction errored, so Postgres rejects every following command until you `ROLLBACK` (or `COMMIT`, which also rolls back).
fixes: Issue `ROLLBACK;` to end the failed transaction, then re-run your statements after fixing the original error.
Scroll up to the FIRST error in the block — that's the real cause; everything after is just this follow-on message.
Wrap risky steps in `SAVEPOINT`/`ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT` so one failure doesn't poison the whole transaction.

patterns.title: Postgres — deadlock detected
