patterns.diagnosis: Two transactions each waited on a lock the other held. Postgres aborted one to break the cycle (the DETAIL line names the conflicting processes).
fixes: Retry the aborted transaction — deadlocks are normal under concurrency.
Lock rows/tables in a consistent order across all code paths to avoid cycles.
Use `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` deliberately and keep transactions short to shrink the lock window.

patterns.match: ERROR:  more than one row returned by a subquery used as an expression
patterns.title: Postgres — subquery returned multiple rows
patterns.diagnosis: A subquery used where a single scalar value was expected returned several rows.
fixes: Use `IN (SELECT ...)` instead of `= (SELECT ...)` if multiple matches are valid.
Add a `LIMIT 1` (with an `ORDER BY`) or a tighter `WHERE` so it returns exactly one row.
Aggregate the subquery: `(SELECT max(x) FROM ...)`.

patterns.title: Postgres — permission denied
patterns.diagnosis: Your role lacks the needed privilege on {1} `{2}`. Authentication worked, but authorization (the GRANTs) doesn't allow this action.
fixes: Grant the privilege as an owner/superuser: `GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON {2} TO your_role;`.
For schemas you also need `GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA ... TO your_role;`.
Set defaults for future objects: `ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES IN SCHEMA public GRANT SELECT ON TABLES TO your_role;`.

patterns.match: FATAL:  password authentication failed for user "([^"]+)"
patterns.title: Postgres — password authentication failed
patterns.diagnosis: Postgres rejected the credentials for role `{1}` — wrong password, or `pg_hba.conf` requires a different auth method than the client offered.
fixes: Reset the password as a superuser: `ALTER ROLE {1} WITH PASSWORD 'newpass';`.
Check `pg_hba.conf` — the matching line must use `md5`/`scram-sha-256` for password auth (and reload with `SELECT pg_reload_conf();`).
Confirm you're hitting the right host/port/database; a wrong dbname can surface as an auth failure on some setups.

patterns.match: psql: error: connection to server (?:on socket "[^"]+"|at "[^"]+").*failed: Connection refused
patterns.title: Postgres — connection refused
patterns.diagnosis: Nothing accepted the connection at that host/port. The server is probably stopped, not listening on that address, or blocked by a firewall.
fixes: Check the server is running: `pg_isready -h host -p 5432` or `systemctl status postgresql`.
Ensure `listen_addresses` in `postgresql.conf` includes your host (use `'*'` for all) and restart.
Confirm the port (default 5432) is open and `pg_hba.conf` has a line allowing your client IP.

patterns.title: SQLite — UNIQUE constraint failed
patterns.diagnosis: An insert/update violated the UNIQUE constraint on `{1}` — that value already exists in the table.
fixes: Use `INSERT OR IGNORE` to skip the duplicate, or `INSERT OR REPLACE` to overwrite the existing row.
Use upsert: `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT({1}) DO UPDATE SET ...` (SQLite 3.24+).
Query the existing row first to decide whether to insert or update.

patterns.title: SQLite — NOT NULL constraint failed
patterns.diagnosis: Column `{1}` is `NOT NULL` but the write left it NULL — either omitted from the INSERT or set to NULL explicitly.
fixes: Supply a value for `{1}` in your INSERT/UPDATE.
Add a default in the schema so omitted inserts still work: `... {1} TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT ''`.
If NULLs are valid, recreate the column without `NOT NULL` (SQLite can't drop the constraint in place — rebuild the table).

patterns.title: SQLite — no such table
patterns.diagnosis: SQLite has no table named `{1}`. Common causes: the schema was never created, you opened the wrong/empty database file, or an in-memory DB was reset.
fixes: List existing tables with `.tables` in the sqlite3 shell.
Run your `CREATE TABLE` migrations against the same DB file your app uses (check the path).
An `:memory:` database starts empty every connection — create the schema each time, or use a file-backed DB.

patterns.title: SQLite — database is locked
patterns.diagnosis: Another connection holds a write lock on the SQLite file and yours timed out waiting. SQLite allows only one writer at a time.
fixes: Make sure other connections COMMIT/close promptly — long-open write transactions block everyone.
Enable WAL mode for better read/write concurrency: `PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL;`.
Raise the wait time: `PRAGMA busy_timeout = 5000;` (milliseconds) so writers retry instead of failing instantly.

patterns.title: MySQL 1241 — operand column count mismatch
patterns.diagnosis: A row/subquery comparison expected `{1}` column(s) but got a different number. Usually a subquery selects the wrong number of columns, or a row constructor `(a, b)` is compared against a mismatched list.
fixes: Make the subquery select exactly `{1}` column(s) to match the left side of the comparison.
For `IN` with a row value, both sides must have the same arity: `WHERE (a, b) IN (SELECT a, b FROM ...)`.
If you only need one value, trim the SELECT list down to a single column.

patterns.match: error: Your local changes to the following files would be overwritten by checkout:\s*\n?\s*([^\n]+)
patterns.title: Checkout blocked by uncommitted changes
patterns.diagnosis: Git won't switch branches because `{1}` has uncommitted edits that the target branch would clobber.
fixes: Commit the work first: `git add -A && git commit -m 'wip'`.
Or stash it: `git stash`, switch, then `git stash pop` to bring changes back.
Throw the changes away if you don't want them: `git checkout -- {1}` (irreversible).
patterns.example_fix:
git stash
git checkout other-branch
git stash pop

patterns.match: fatal: The current branch ([^\s]+) has no upstream branch
patterns.title: Branch has no upstream set
patterns.diagnosis: You ran a bare `git push` on `{1}`, but Git doesn't know which remote branch to push to.
fixes: Set it on first push: `git push -u origin {1}`.
After that, plain `git push` works for `{1}`.
To set upstream without pushing: `git branch --set-upstream-to=origin/{1} {1}`.

patterns.match: fatal: pathspec '([^']+)' did not match any files
patterns.title: git add couldn't find that path
patterns.diagnosis: `git add {1}` failed — there's no file or directory named `{1}` relative to where you ran the command.
fixes: Check the path with `ls {1}` or `git status` for the real filename.
If you meant a file deeper in the tree, run the command from the repo root or use the full relative path.
Quote globs so the shell doesn't expand them: `git add '*.js'`.

patterns.match: fatal: Unable to create '([^']+)/\.git/shallow\.lock': File exists
patterns.title: Stale shallow lock blocking fetch
patterns.diagnosis: A leftover lock file in `{1}/.git` (from an interrupted shallow fetch/clone) is stopping the current operation.
fixes: Remove the stale lock: `rm -f {1}/.git/shallow.lock`.
Make sure no other git process is running on the repo first (`ps aux | grep git`).
Retry the fetch — also clear `.git/index.lock` if that complains next.

patterns.match: error: cannot rebase: You have unstaged changes
patterns.title: Rebase needs a clean tree
patterns.diagnosis: Git won't start a rebase while you have unstaged (and/or staged) changes in the working tree.
fixes: Commit the changes: `git commit -am 'wip'`.
Or stash them: `git stash`, rebase, then `git stash pop`.
Check what's dirty with `git status` first.
patterns.example_fix:
git stash
git rebase main
git stash pop

patterns.match: fatal: You have not concluded your merge \(MERGE_HEAD exists\)
patterns.title: An unfinished merge is blocking you
patterns.diagnosis: A previous merge is still in progress — `MERGE_HEAD` exists — so Git won't let you start another operation.
fixes: Finish it: resolve conflicts, `git add` the files, then `git commit`.
Or abort and go back: `git merge --abort`.
Check state with `git status` to see what's still unmerged.

patterns.match: fatal: Exiting because of an unfinished merge
patterns.title: Pull blocked by an unfinished merge
patterns.diagnosis: You tried to pull, but a prior merge never completed. Git stops so you don't pile changes on top.
fixes: Resolve the open conflicts, `git add` them, and `git commit` to finish the merge.
Or discard the merge attempt: `git merge --abort`.
Run `git status` to see which files are still unmerged.

patterns.match: fatal: cannot lock ref '([^']+)': is at [0-9a-f]+ but expected [0-9a-f]+
patterns.title: Ref moved under you during fetch/push
patterns.diagnosis: The ref `{1}` changed on the remote between when Git read it and tried to update it — someone pushed concurrently.
fixes: Just retry: `git fetch` or `git pull` again.
If it persists, prune stale refs: `git remote prune origin`.
Run `git gc` to clean up packed-refs if a local ref is corrupt.

patterns.match: error: unable to unlink old '([^']+)': Permission denied
patterns.title: Can't replace a file during checkout
patterns.diagnosis: Git tried to overwrite `{1}` but the OS denied permission — the file is locked, read-only, or open in another program.
fixes: Close any program holding `{1}` open (editor, server, build watcher).
Fix permissions/ownership: `chmod u+w {1}` or `sudo chown $USER {1}`.
On Windows, antivirus or a running process can lock files — stop it and retry.

patterns.match: fatal: refusing to merge unrelated histories|fatal: Need to specify how to reconcile divergent branches
patterns.title: Pull doesn't know merge vs rebase
patterns.diagnosis: Newer Git versions refuse to pull when local and remote diverged unless you say whether to merge or rebase.
fixes: Merge this time: `git pull --no-rebase`.
Rebase this time: `git pull --rebase`.
Set a default once: `git config --global pull.rebase false` (merge) or `true` (rebase).

patterns.title: Git can't resolve that revision
patterns.diagnosis: `{1}` isn't a valid commit, branch, tag, or range — it may be misspelled or the range syntax is wrong.
fixes: Verify with `git log --oneline` or `git branch -a` that the name exists.
For ranges use two dots: `git log main..feature`, not a single name.
If a file and a revision share a name, disambiguate with `--`: `git log {1} -- path/`.

patterns.match: fatal: Could not read from remote repository
patterns.title: Can't reach the remote
patterns.diagnosis: Git couldn't connect to the remote — usually wrong URL, missing SSH key access, or no permission to that repo.
fixes: Check the URL: `git remote -v` and fix with `git remote set-url origin <url>`.
Test SSH auth: `ssh -T git@github.com`.
Make sure your account actually has access to the repository.

patterns.title: Branch to delete doesn't exist
patterns.diagnosis: `git branch -d {1}` failed because there's no local branch named `{1}`.
fixes: Check the exact name: `git branch` (local) or `git branch -a` (incl. remotes).
To delete a remote-tracking branch instead: `git branch -dr origin/{1}`.
To delete the branch on the remote: `git push origin --delete {1}`.

patterns.title: Rebase target doesn't exist
patterns.diagnosis: `git rebase {1}` failed because `{1}` isn't a valid branch or commit to rebase onto.
fixes: Fetch first if it's a remote branch: `git fetch origin` then `git rebase origin/main`.
Check the exact name with `git branch -a`.
For an interactive rebase of recent commits, use a count: `git rebase -i HEAD~3`.

patterns.match: fatal: It is not possible to ([a-z]+) more than once
patterns.title: Stash/cherry-pick step already done
patterns.diagnosis: Git refused to `{1}` again because that operation is already in progress or there's nothing left to act on.
fixes: Check current state with `git status`.
If something is mid-flight, finish it (`--continue`) or cancel it (`--abort`).
Re-read the exact command — you may be repeating a step that already succeeded.

patterns.title: Add/add conflict — both sides created the file
patterns.diagnosis: Both branches independently created `{1}`, so Git can't tell which version to keep.
fixes: Open `{1}`, merge the two versions by hand, then `git add {1}`.
Keep one side wholesale: `git checkout --ours {1}` or `git checkout --theirs {1}`, then `git add {1}`.
Finish with `git commit` once all conflicts are resolved.

patterns.match: error: commit ([0-9a-f]+) is a merge but no -m option was given
patterns.title: Reverting a merge needs a parent
patterns.diagnosis: `{1}` is a merge commit with two parents, so `git revert` needs to know which parent line to keep as mainline.
fixes: Pick the mainline parent (usually 1): `git revert -m 1 {1}`.
Use `-m 2` if you want to keep the merged-in side as mainline instead.
Confirm parents with `git show {1}` (look at the `Merge:` line).

patterns.match: fatal: ambiguous argument '([^']+)': unknown revision or path not in the working tree
patterns.title: Git can't tell if that's a revision or a path
patterns.diagnosis: `{1}` matches neither a known revision nor a tracked path, or it's ambiguous between the two.
fixes: If `{1}` is a file path, separate it: `git log -- {1}`.
If it's a branch/commit, verify it exists with `git branch -a` or `git log --oneline`.
Fetch first if it's a remote ref you don't have locally yet.

patterns.title: Remote repo not found (or no access)
patterns.diagnosis: GitHub returned 'not found' — the repo URL is wrong, the repo is private and you lack access, or it was deleted/renamed.
fixes: Double-check the URL spelling/case: `git remote -v`.
For private repos, confirm you're authenticated and have access (SSH key or token).
If it was renamed, update the remote: `git remote set-url origin <new-url>`.

patterns.match: remote: Support for password authentication was removed
patterns.title: GitHub no longer accepts account passwords
patterns.diagnosis: GitHub dropped password auth over HTTPS — you must use a personal access token (PAT) or SSH.
fixes: Create a PAT in GitHub settings and use it as the password when prompted.
Better: switch the remote to SSH — `git remote set-url origin git@github.com:user/repo.git`.
Cache credentials with `git config --global credential.helper store` or the OS keychain helper.

patterns.match: fatal: refusing to remove '([^']+)' recursively without -r
patterns.title: git rm needs -r for directories
patterns.diagnosis: You tried to `git rm {1}`, but it's a directory and Git won't recurse into it without `-r`.
fixes: Add the recursive flag: `git rm -r {1}`.
To untrack but keep the files on disk: `git rm -r --cached {1}`.
Then commit the removal: `git commit -m 'remove {1}'`.

patterns.match: fatal: the following file has staged content different from both the file and the HEAD
patterns.title: git rm blocked by staged changes
patterns.diagnosis: A file you're trying to remove has staged edits that differ from both HEAD and the working copy, so Git protects them.
fixes: Force the removal if you mean it: `git rm -f <file>`.
Or unstage first to inspect: `git reset HEAD <file>`.
Use `git status` to see exactly which file is involved.

patterns.match: error: Pulling is not possible because you have unmerged files
patterns.title: Pull blocked by unresolved conflicts
patterns.diagnosis: There are leftover merge conflicts; Git won't pull more changes until you resolve them.
fixes: Resolve each conflicted file, then `git add` it.
Commit to finish: `git commit`.
Or bail out of the merge entirely: `git merge --abort`.

patterns.match: fatal: '([^']+)' is not a commit and a branch '([^']+)' cannot be created from it
patterns.title: Can't branch from a non-commit
patterns.diagnosis: `git checkout -b {2} {1}` failed because `{1}` doesn't resolve to a commit you can branch from.
fixes: Fetch the source ref first: `git fetch origin {1}`.
Use the full remote ref: `git checkout -b {2} origin/{1}`.
Verify `{1}` exists with `git branch -a` or `git log --oneline`.
patterns.example_fix:
git fetch origin
git checkout -b {2} origin/{1}

patterns.match: fatal: detected dubious ownership in repository at '([^']+)'
patterns.title: Repo owned by a different user
patterns.diagnosis: Git refuses to operate on `{1}` because the directory is owned by a different user than the one running Git (common with sudo or shared mounts).
fixes: Mark it safe: `git config --global --add safe.directory {1}`.
Or fix ownership: `sudo chown -R $USER {1}`.
Avoid running git under sudo — that's a frequent cause.

patterns.match: hint: You've added another git repository inside your current repository
patterns.title: Accidentally adding a nested repo (gitlink)
patterns.diagnosis: A subdirectory has its own `.git`, so Git wants to track it as a submodule (a single gitlink) instead of its files.
fixes: If you didn't mean a submodule, remove the inner `.git`: `rm -rf <subdir>/.git` then re-add.
Untrack the gitlink: `git rm --cached <subdir>` and re-`git add <subdir>`.
If it really should be a submodule, use `git submodule add <url> <subdir>`.

patterns.match: error: Untracked working tree file '([^']+)' would be overwritten by merge
patterns.title: Merge would clobber an untracked file
patterns.diagnosis: The incoming merge brings a file named `{1}`, but you already have an untracked `{1}` that Git won't silently overwrite.
fixes: Back up or move your local `{1}` out of the way, then merge.
Or commit it first if it belongs in the repo: `git add {1} && git commit -m 'add {1}'`.
Delete it if it's disposable: `rm {1}`, then retry the merge.

patterns.match: fatal: Not possible to fast-forward, aborting
patterns.title: Pull can't fast-forward
patterns.diagnosis: You're configured for fast-forward-only pulls, but local commits diverge from the remote so a fast-forward is impossible.
fixes: Merge the divergence: `git pull --no-rebase`.
Or rebase your commits on top: `git pull --rebase`.
Inspect the split first: `git log --oneline --graph HEAD..@{u}`.

patterns.match: fatal: unable to write new index file
patterns.title: Can't write the index
patterns.diagnosis: Git couldn't write `.git/index` — usually the disk is full, the file is read-only, or permissions are wrong.
fixes: Check free space: `df -h .` and free some up.
Fix permissions on the repo: `sudo chown -R $USER .git`.
Remove a stale lock if present: `rm -f .git/index.lock`.

patterns.title: A branch and tag share a name
patterns.diagnosis: `{1}` exists as both a branch and a tag (or two refs), so Git can't tell which one you mean.
fixes: Be explicit: `refs/heads/{1}` for the branch, `refs/tags/{1}` for the tag.
Rename or delete one of them: `git tag -d {1}` or `git branch -m {1} newname`.
List refs to see the clash: `git show-ref {1}`.

patterns.match: fatal: bad config line (\d+) in file ([^\s]+)
patterns.title: Malformed git config
patterns.diagnosis: Line {1} of `{2}` isn't valid config syntax — often a stray bracket, missing `=`, or a hand-edit gone wrong.
fixes: Open `{2}` and inspect line {1} for a typo or unclosed `[section]` header.
Validate with `git config --list --show-origin` (it errors on the bad spot).
Set values via `git config` instead of hand-editing to avoid syntax slips.

patterns.match: error: insufficient permission for adding an object to repository database
patterns.title: No write permission to the object store
patterns.diagnosis: Git can't write into `.git/objects` — the directory is owned by another user or is read-only (common after a sudo commit).
fixes: Fix ownership recursively: `sudo chown -R $USER .git`.
Check the perms: `ls -ld .git/objects`.
Stop running git commands under sudo so files keep your ownership.

patterns.match: fatal: cannot create directory at '([^']+)': Permission denied
patterns.title: Checkout can't create a directory
patterns.diagnosis: Git tried to create `{1}` during checkout but the OS denied permission — the parent dir isn't writable by you.
fixes: Fix permissions on the parent: `chmod u+w <parent>` or `sudo chown -R $USER .`.
Make sure no file already exists where Git wants a directory named `{1}`.
Re-run the checkout once permissions are corrected.

patterns.match: error: Your local changes to the following files would be overwritten by merge
patterns.title: Merge blocked by uncommitted changes
patterns.diagnosis: Incoming merge changes overlap files you've edited but not committed; Git stops to protect your work.
fixes: Commit your work: `git commit -am 'wip'`, then merge.
Or stash it: `git stash`, merge, then `git stash pop`.
Discard local edits if unwanted: `git checkout -- <file>` (irreversible).
patterns.example_fix:
git stash
git merge origin/main
git stash pop

patterns.match: fatal: could not lookup name for submodule '([^']+)'
patterns.title: Submodule missing from .gitmodules
patterns.diagnosis: Submodule `{1}` is referenced in the index but has no matching entry in `.gitmodules`, so Git can't resolve its URL/path.
fixes: Re-sync submodule config: `git submodule sync` then `git submodule update --init`.
Check `.gitmodules` has a `[submodule "{1}"]` block with `path` and `url`.
If it's stale, remove the gitlink: `git rm --cached {1}` and re-add the submodule.
patterns.example_fix:
git submodule sync
git submodule update --init --recursive

patterns.match: fatal: refusing to fetch into branch '([^']+)' checked out at
patterns.title: Can't fetch into the current branch
patterns.diagnosis: You tried to fetch directly into `{1}`, but it's the branch currently checked out — Git won't update it underneath you.
fixes: Use a normal pull instead: `git pull` (fetch + integrate safely).
Or switch to a different branch before fetching into `{1}`.
For bare-style updates, fetch into a tracking ref and merge: `git fetch origin {1}` then `git merge FETCH_HEAD`.

patterns.match: Cannot connect to the Docker daemon at (unix://[^\s\.]+|tcp://[^\s\.]+)\.? Is the docker daemon running\??
patterns.title: Docker daemon not reachable
patterns.diagnosis: The Docker CLI tried to talk to the daemon at `{1}` but got no response. The daemon isn't running, or your user can't reach that socket.
fixes: Start the daemon: `sudo systemctl start docker` (Linux) or open Docker Desktop (Mac/Windows).
Check it's up: `sudo systemctl status docker` or `docker info`.
Permission issue? Add yourself to the group: `sudo usermod -aG docker $USER`, then log out and back in.
Wrong endpoint? Unset or fix `DOCKER_HOST` if it points at a stale `{1}`.
patterns.example_fix:
sudo systemctl start docker
docker info

patterns.match: permission denied while trying to connect to the Docker daemon socket at unix://([^\s:]+)
patterns.title: Permission denied on Docker socket
patterns.diagnosis: Your user lacks permission to read/write `{1}`. The socket is owned by root and the `docker` group; you're in neither.
fixes: Add your user to the docker group: `sudo usermod -aG docker $USER`.
Apply the new group without a full logout: `newgrp docker`.
Or run the command with `sudo docker ...` (less convenient).
Verify: `id -nG` should list `docker`.

patterns.match: pull access denied for ([^,]+), repository does not exist or may require 'docker login'
patterns.title: Pull access denied
patterns.diagnosis: Docker couldn't pull `{1}`. Either the image name/tag is wrong, the repo is private and you're not logged in, or the registry path is mistyped.
fixes: Double-check the name and tag — typos like `ubunto` or a missing namespace are common.
Private image? Authenticate: `docker login` (or `docker login <registry>`).
For a non-Docker-Hub registry, include the host: `registry.example.com/{1}`.
Confirm the tag exists on the registry; `:latest` may not be published.

patterns.match: manifest for ([^\s]+) not found: manifest unknown
patterns.title: Image manifest / tag not found
patterns.diagnosis: The repository exists but the specific tag in `{1}` doesn't. You're requesting a version that was never pushed or has been deleted.
fixes: List available tags on the registry (Docker Hub page, or `docker search` / registry API).
Pin to a tag you know exists instead of assuming `:latest`.
Check for a typo in the tag portion after the colon.
If you just built it locally, you may need to `docker push` it first.

patterns.match: failed to solve: ([^:]+): no such file or directory
patterns.title: COPY/ADD source missing in build context
patterns.diagnosis: During `docker build`, a `COPY`/`ADD` referenced `{1}` which isn't inside the build context. Files outside the context directory (or excluded by `.dockerignore`) can't be copied.
fixes: Make sure `{1}` exists relative to the build context (the path you passed to `docker build`, usually `.`).
Check `.dockerignore` — it may be excluding `{1}`.
Run `docker build` from the right directory, or pass the correct context path as the final argument.
Paths in COPY are relative to the context root, not the Dockerfile location.
patterns.example_fix: COPY ./app /app   # ./app must be under the build context

patterns.title: RUN step failed during build
patterns.diagnosis: A `RUN` instruction `{1}` exited with code {2}, aborting the build. The command itself failed inside the image layer.
fixes: Run the failing command manually in a shell of the base image: `docker run -it <base> sh` then paste `{1}`.
If it's a package install, refresh indexes first (e.g. `apt-get update && apt-get install -y ...` in one RUN).
Check the build log above this line — the real error message is there.
Add `--progress=plain` to `docker build` to see full output of `{1}`.

patterns.match: Bind for 0\.0\.0\.0:(\d+) failed: port is already allocated
patterns.title: Host port already in use
patterns.diagnosis: Docker tried to publish host port {2} but another process (often a previous container) already holds it.
fixes: Find what's using it: `docker ps` (look for the published port) or `sudo lsof -i :{2}`.
Stop the conflicting container: `docker stop <id>`, or remove leftovers: `docker rm -f <id>`.
Or map to a different host port: `-p {2}1:{2}` (left side is the host).
Clean up dangling containers: `docker container prune`.

patterns.match: OCI runtime create failed:.*exec: "([^"]+)": executable file not found in \$PATH
patterns.title: Container entrypoint binary not found
patterns.diagnosis: The container's command `{1}` isn't on the PATH inside the image. The CMD/ENTRYPOINT points at a binary that doesn't exist there.
fixes: Verify `{1}` is installed in the image (it may live in a different base than you expect).
Use an absolute path in CMD/ENTRYPOINT, e.g. `/usr/local/bin/{1}`.
Alpine images use `sh`, not `bash` — `{1}` may simply not be present; install it or switch base.
Check the binary's architecture matches the image (arm64 vs amd64).

patterns.match: standard_init_linux\.go:\d+: exec user process caused: exec format error
patterns.title: Exec format error — wrong architecture
patterns.diagnosis: The image's binary was built for a different CPU architecture than the host (e.g. an amd64 image on arm64, or a script missing its shebang).
fixes: Pull/build for the right platform: `docker run --platform linux/amd64 ...` or `docker build --platform linux/arm64 ...`.
For multi-arch builds use buildx: `docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 ...`.
If it's a script entrypoint, add a shebang line (`#!/bin/sh`) and make it executable.
On Apple Silicon, emulation needs QEMU — ensure Docker Desktop's Rosetta/QEMU support is enabled.

patterns.match: Error response from daemon: Conflict\. The container name "/?([^"]+)" is already in use by container
patterns.title: Container name already in use
patterns.diagnosis: You asked for a container named `{1}` but one already exists with that name (running or stopped).
fixes: Remove the old one: `docker rm {1}` (add `-f` if it's still running).
Or pick a different `--name`.
Auto-clean on exit with `--rm` so the name frees up: `docker run --rm --name {1} ...`.
List by name to inspect: `docker ps -a --filter name={1}`.

patterns.title: Docker out of disk space
patterns.diagnosis: The Docker storage volume is full. Old images, stopped containers, build cache, and dangling volumes accumulate quickly.
fixes: Reclaim space: `docker system prune -a` (removes unused images — be careful).
Clear build cache specifically: `docker builder prune`.
Remove dangling volumes: `docker volume prune`.
Check usage first: `docker system df`. On Docker Desktop you may also need to grow the disk image in settings.
patterns.example_fix:
docker system df
docker system prune -a

patterns.match: failed to resolve reference "([^"]+)": failed to do request:.*(?:dial tcp|timeout|no such host)
patterns.title: Registry unreachable / DNS failure
patterns.diagnosis: Docker couldn't reach the registry to resolve `{1}` — a network, DNS, or proxy problem rather than a missing image.
fixes: Check connectivity: `curl -I https://registry-1.docker.io/v2/`.
Behind a proxy? Configure it in `~/.docker/config.json` or the daemon's `http-proxy.conf`.
DNS broken inside the daemon? Set `dns` in `/etc/docker/daemon.json` and restart Docker.
For a private/insecure registry, add it to `insecure-registries` in `daemon.json`.

patterns.title: Unknown Dockerfile instruction
patterns.diagnosis: Line {1} of the Dockerfile has `{2}`, which isn't a valid instruction. Usually a typo or a continuation line that lost its `\`.
fixes: Check the spelling of `{2}` — valid instructions are FROM, RUN, COPY, ADD, CMD, ENTRYPOINT, ENV, ARG, WORKDIR, EXPOSE, etc.
A multi-line `RUN` needs `\` at the end of each continued line; a missing one makes the next line look like an instruction.
Inline comments must be on their own line starting with `#`, not appended after a command.
Make sure the file really is a Dockerfile and not, say, a shell script.

patterns.match: failed to compute cache key:.*"/?([^"]+)" not found: not found
patterns.title: Build cache key references missing path
patterns.diagnosis: BuildKit couldn't hash `{1}` for a COPY/ADD because the path doesn't exist in the build context. Same root cause as a missing COPY source.
fixes: Confirm `{1}` exists relative to the build context root.
Inspect what's actually in context — `.dockerignore` may exclude `{1}`.
Generate any built artifacts (e.g. `dist/`, `target/`) before running `docker build`.
Glob patterns in COPY must match at least one file or the step fails.

patterns.match: Error response from daemon: driver failed programming external connectivity on endpoint
patterns.title: Port mapping / networking failed to program
patterns.diagnosis: Docker couldn't set up the iptables/network rules for a published port. Often a stale port binding, an iptables conflict, or the daemon's networking needs a reset.
fixes: Stop whatever holds the port and retry; clean up old containers: `docker container prune`.
Restart the Docker daemon to reprogram networking: `sudo systemctl restart docker`.
If you manage iptables manually, ensure Docker's chains weren't flushed.
As a last resort recreate the bridge network the container uses.

patterns.match: invalid reference format(?:: repository name must be lowercase)?
patterns.title: Invalid image reference format
patterns.diagnosis: The image name you passed is malformed. Repository names must be lowercase, and the `name:tag` / `registry/name:tag` syntax must be exact.
fixes: Lowercase the repository part — `MyApp` must be `myapp`.
Don't put a space around the colon: `node:18`, not `node :18`.
If you meant a tag, separate with `:`; for a registry use a `/` host prefix.
Quote the argument if a shell variable expanded to something empty.

patterns.match: Error response from daemon: failed to create shim task: OCI runtime create failed.*cgroup
patterns.title: Container failed to start — cgroup error
patterns.diagnosis: The OCI runtime couldn't set up cgroups for the container. Common after a kernel/cgroup v2 mismatch or a systemd/cgroup driver conflict.
fixes: Align the cgroup driver: set `"exec-opts": ["native.cgroupdriver=systemd"]` in `/etc/docker/daemon.json` and restart Docker.
Reboot after kernel/cgroup changes so v1/v2 hierarchies are consistent.
Update Docker and the OCI runtime (`runc`) to recent versions.
On WSL2, restart the distro: `wsl --shutdown` then reopen.

patterns.match: Error response from daemon: lstat /var/lib/docker/overlay2/([0-9a-f]+):? no such file or directory
patterns.title: Corrupted overlay2 layer
patterns.diagnosis: Docker's overlay2 storage references layer `{1}` that's missing on disk — usually from an unclean shutdown or disk-full event that corrupted the layer store.
fixes: Remove the affected image and re-pull/rebuild it.
Prune broken state: `docker system prune` (and `docker image prune`).
If widespread, stopping the daemon and clearing `/var/lib/docker/overlay2` orphans is a last resort (destroys all images).
Make sure the disk isn't full — `df -h` — which is the usual cause.

patterns.match: toomanyrequests: You have reached your pull rate limit
patterns.title: Docker Hub pull rate limit hit
patterns.diagnosis: Docker Hub rate-limits anonymous and free-tier pulls per IP/account. You've exceeded the window's quota.
fixes: Authenticate to get the higher logged-in limit: `docker login`.
Cache/mirror images via a pull-through registry to avoid repeat pulls.
Pin and reuse digests so CI doesn't re-pull `:latest` constantly.
Wait for the 6-hour window to reset, or upgrade the Docker Hub plan.

patterns.match: container_linux\.go:\d+: starting container process caused.*chdir to cwd \("([^"]+)"\)
patterns.title: WORKDIR does not exist in container
patterns.diagnosis: The container tried to start in working directory `{1}`, but that path doesn't exist in the image filesystem.
fixes: Add `WORKDIR {1}` in the Dockerfile — it creates the dir if missing.
If you set `-w {1}` on `docker run`, make sure the image actually has that path.
Verify with `docker run --rm <image> ls -la <parent-dir>`.
Don't point WORKDIR at a file or a not-yet-mounted volume path.

patterns.title: Pod can't pull its image
patterns.diagnosis: Kubernetes failed to pull the container image for pod `{1}` and is backing off ({2}). The image name/tag is wrong, the registry needs credentials, or the node can't reach it.
fixes: Read the real cause: `kubectl describe pod {1}` — see the Events section.
Fix the image name/tag in the manifest if it's a typo.
Private registry? Create an `imagePullSecret` and reference it in the pod spec or service account.
Confirm the node has network access to the registry.

patterns.title: Pod crash-looping
patterns.diagnosis: The container in pod `{1}` keeps starting and exiting, so Kubernetes restarts it with increasing back-off. The app crashes on startup.
fixes: Read the logs: `kubectl logs {1}` and `kubectl logs {1} --previous` (the crashed instance).
`kubectl describe pod {1}` shows exit codes and OOMKilled/probe events.
Common causes: bad config/env, missing dependency, failing liveness probe, or exiting code 0 too fast.
If a probe kills it, loosen `initialDelaySeconds`/`failureThreshold` until startup completes.

patterns.title: Kubernetes resource not found
patterns.diagnosis: The API server has no `{1}` named `{2}` in the targeted namespace. Either it doesn't exist, was deleted, or you're looking in the wrong namespace.
fixes: Check the namespace: `kubectl get {1} -A | grep {2}` (resources are namespaced).
Pass the right namespace: `kubectl get {1} {2} -n <namespace>`.
List what exists: `kubectl get {1}` to catch typos in `{2}`.
If you just applied a manifest, confirm it succeeded with `kubectl apply` returning no errors.

patterns.match: Error from server \(Forbidden\): ([\w.]+) is forbidden: User "([^"]+)" cannot ([\w]+)
patterns.title: RBAC permission denied
patterns.diagnosis: User/service account `{2}` is not authorized to `{3}` on `{1}`. RBAC has no Role/ClusterRole binding granting it.
fixes: Check what you can do: `kubectl auth can-i {3} {1}`.
Grant access with a Role + RoleBinding (namespace) or ClusterRole + ClusterRoleBinding (cluster-wide).
Bind it to `{2}`: `kubectl create rolebinding <name> --role=<role> --user={2}`.
For a pod's service account, bind the role to that ServiceAccount, not your user.

patterns.title: Pod unschedulable — not enough resources
patterns.diagnosis: None of the {1} nodes can fit the pod because its `{2}` request exceeds remaining capacity. The pod stays Pending.
fixes: Lower the pod's `resources.requests.{2}` if it's over-asking.
Check node capacity: `kubectl describe nodes` (look at Allocated resources).
Add nodes or enable the cluster autoscaler.
Evict/scale down lower-priority workloads to free `{2}`.

patterns.title: Pod unschedulable — node taints
patterns.diagnosis: All {1} nodes carry taints the pod doesn't tolerate, so the scheduler rejects it. Common with control-plane or dedicated GPU nodes.
fixes: Add a matching `tolerations` block to the pod spec.
Inspect taints: `kubectl describe node <node> | grep Taints`.
If a taint shouldn't be there, remove it: `kubectl taint nodes <node> <key>-`.
For control-plane scheduling, tolerate `node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane`.

patterns.match: 0/(\d+) nodes are available:.*node\(s\) didn't (?:match|find available) (?:Pod's node affinity|persistent volume)
patterns.title: Pod unschedulable — affinity / volume mismatch
patterns.diagnosis: The scheduler couldn't place the pod on any of {1} nodes because node-affinity rules or a required PersistentVolume's topology don't match.
fixes: Check the pod's `nodeAffinity`/`nodeSelector` against actual node labels: `kubectl get nodes --show-labels`.
Relax overly strict `requiredDuringScheduling...` to `preferred...` if appropriate.
For PVs, ensure a PV in the same zone/StorageClass exists for the PVC.
Loosen or correct the `nodeSelector` keys to ones the nodes actually have.

patterns.title: Container OOMKilled
patterns.diagnosis: The kernel killed a container in pod `{1}` for exceeding its memory limit. Kubernetes reports it as OOMKilled (exit code 137).
fixes: Raise `resources.limits.memory` if the app legitimately needs more.
Find the real usage: `kubectl top pod {1}` and inspect for leaks.
Lower the app's heap/cache settings to fit under the limit.
Set requests close to actual usage so the scheduler reserves enough.

patterns.match: The connection to the server ([^\s]+) was refused - did you specify the right host or port\?
patterns.title: kubectl can't reach the API server
patterns.diagnosis: kubectl tried to contact the API server at `{1}` and the connection was refused. The cluster is down, the context is wrong, or kubeconfig points at a dead endpoint.
fixes: Check your context: `kubectl config current-context` and `kubectl config get-contexts`.
If it's a local cluster (minikube/kind/k3d), is it started? e.g. `minikube status`.
Verify the server URL in `~/.kube/config` matches the running control plane.
Network/VPN required for a remote cluster at `{1}`? Connect first.

patterns.match: error: unable to recognize "([^"]+)": no matches for kind "([\w]+)" in version "([^"]+)"
patterns.title: Unknown kind / apiVersion in manifest
patterns.diagnosis: `kubectl apply` couldn't process `{1}` because the cluster has no `{2}` registered under `{3}`. The apiVersion is outdated or a CRD isn't installed.
fixes: Check supported versions: `kubectl api-resources | grep {2}` and `kubectl api-versions`.
Update `apiVersion` to a version this cluster serves (APIs graduate, e.g. `networking.k8s.io/v1`).
If `{2}` is a CRD, install the CRD/operator first.
Match manifests to your cluster version — old tutorials use removed beta APIs.

patterns.title: Unknown field in manifest
patterns.diagnosis: The manifest has field `{2}` under `{1}` that the schema doesn't recognize — usually a typo, wrong nesting, or an indentation error in the YAML.
fixes: Check spelling and case of `{2}` (fields are camelCase: `containerPort`, not `container_port`).
Verify indentation — a misplaced key lands under the wrong parent.
See the real schema: `kubectl explain {1}`.
Dry-run to validate before applying: `kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f file.yaml`.

patterns.title: Container config error — missing ConfigMap/Secret
patterns.diagnosis: Pod `{1}` can't build its container config, almost always because it references a ConfigMap or Secret key that doesn't exist.
fixes: See exactly what's missing: `kubectl describe pod {1}` (Events name the resource/key).
Confirm the ConfigMap/Secret exists in the same namespace: `kubectl get configmap,secret`.
Check `valueFrom.configMapKeyRef`/`secretKeyRef` keys match real keys.
Create the missing resource before (re)deploying the pod.

patterns.title: Volume failed to mount
patterns.diagnosis: Pod `{1}` couldn't mount volume `{2}`. The PVC may be unbound, the underlying disk unavailable, or a referenced Secret/ConfigMap is missing.
fixes: Check the PVC bound: `kubectl get pvc` (status should be `Bound`, not `Pending`).
For cloud disks, confirm the volume is in the same zone as the node.
`kubectl describe pod {1}` shows the specific mount failure for `{2}`.
If it's a secret/configmap volume, make sure that resource exists.

patterns.match: (?:persistentvolumeclaim\/)?([\w-]+)\s+Pending.*no persistent volumes available|waiting for a volume to be created
patterns.title: PVC stuck Pending
patterns.diagnosis: PVC `{1}` can't bind — no matching PersistentVolume exists and no provisioner is creating one. Usually a missing/incorrect StorageClass.
fixes: Check StorageClasses: `kubectl get storageclass` (is there a default?).
Set the PVC's `storageClassName` to an existing class, or mark one default.
For static PVs, ensure a PV matches the PVC's size, accessModes, and class.
`kubectl describe pvc {1}` reports why the bind/provision failed.
patterns.example_fix:
kubectl get storageclass
kubectl describe pvc {1}

patterns.match: (?:pod\/)?([\w-]+).*Liveness probe failed: (?:HTTP probe failed with statuscode: (\d+)|.*connection refused)
patterns.title: Liveness probe failing
patterns.diagnosis: The liveness probe for pod `{1}` failed, so the kubelet restarts the container. The endpoint returned a bad status or wasn't listening yet.
fixes: Verify the probe path/port match what the app actually serves.
If the app starts slowly, increase `initialDelaySeconds` or add a `startupProbe`.
Test the endpoint from inside: `kubectl exec {1} -- curl -s localhost:<port>/<path>`.
Don't point the probe at a dependency (DB) — it should reflect the app's own health.

patterns.match: error: error parsing ([^:]+): error converting YAML to JSON: yaml: line (\d+): (.+)
patterns.title: Invalid YAML in manifest
patterns.diagnosis: `{1}` isn't valid YAML — at line {2}: {3}. Most often tabs used for indentation, misaligned keys, or an unquoted special character.
fixes: YAML forbids tabs for indentation — use spaces only.
Check alignment around line {2} of `{1}`; list items (`-`) and map keys must line up consistently.
Quote values containing `:`, `#`, `{`, or leading symbols.
Lint it: `yamllint {1}` or `kubectl apply --dry-run=client -f {1}`.

patterns.title: Cannot find module
patterns.diagnosis: Node can't resolve `{1}`. Either it isn't installed, the path is wrong, or `node_modules` is stale/missing.
fixes: If it's a dependency, install it: `npm install {1}`.
If it's a local file, check the relative path and extension — `require('./utils')` needs `./` and the file to actually exist.
Blow away and reinstall: `rm -rf node_modules package-lock.json && npm install`.
Confirm you're running from the project root where `node_modules` lives.

patterns.match: Error \[ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND\]: Cannot find module '([^']+)' imported from ([^\s]+)
patterns.title: ESM module not found
patterns.diagnosis: An ES-module `import` from `{2}` couldn't resolve `{1}`. In ESM, relative imports must include the file extension.
fixes: Add the explicit extension: `import x from './thing.js'` (not `./thing`).
If `{1}` is a package, install it: `npm install {1}`.
Check the path is relative (`./` or `../`) for local files — bare specifiers are treated as packages.
Verify `"type": "module"` in package.json matches how you're importing.

patterns.match: ReferenceError: require is not defined( in ES module scope)?
patterns.title: require not available in ESM
patterns.diagnosis: You called `require()` in an ES module. `require` doesn't exist in ESM scope (it's a CommonJS-only function).
fixes: Use `import` instead: `import x from 'x'`.
If you need `require` in ESM, recreate it: `import { createRequire } from 'module'; const require = createRequire(import.meta.url);`.
Or remove `"type": "module"` from package.json to go back to CommonJS.
Rename the file to `.cjs` if just this one file should be CommonJS.
patterns.example_fix:
import { createRequire } from 'module';
const require = createRequire(import.meta.url);

patterns.match: ReferenceError: (__dirname|__filename) is not defined( in ES module scope)?
patterns.title: {1} not available in ESM
patterns.diagnosis: `{1}` is a CommonJS global and doesn't exist in ES modules. ESM uses `import.meta.url` instead.
fixes: Recreate it: `import { fileURLToPath } from 'url'; const __dirname = path.dirname(fileURLToPath(import.meta.url));`.
For the file path: `const __filename = fileURLToPath(import.meta.url);`.
Or convert the file back to CommonJS (`.cjs`) if you rely on these globals heavily.

patterns.title: Tried to require() an ES module
patterns.diagnosis: You called `require()` on `{1}`, but it's an ES module (ESM). CommonJS `require` can't load pure ESM packages synchronously.
fixes: Use dynamic import: `const mod = await import('{1}')`.
Convert your file to ESM (`"type": "module"` or `.mjs`) and use `import`.
Check if the package ships a CommonJS build or an older version that does.
Pin to an older CJS-compatible version if upgrading isn't an option.

patterns.title: Reading a property of undefined/null
patterns.diagnosis: You accessed a property on something that was `undefined` or `null`. The object you expected wasn't there.
fixes: Use optional chaining: `obj?.{1}`.
Guard first: `if (obj) { ... }` before accessing.
Trace back — find which variable is empty by logging it one step earlier.
If it comes from an async call, make sure you `await`ed it before reading.

patterns.match: Error: listen EADDRINUSE:? address already in use :::?(\d+)
patterns.title: Port {1} already in use
patterns.diagnosis: Another process is already listening on port {1}, so your server can't bind to it.
fixes: Find and kill it: `lsof -ti:{1} | xargs kill -9`.
Use a different port: `PORT=3001 node server.js`.
If it's a leftover dev server, kill stray node processes: `pkill -f node`.
Make sure you only call `app.listen({1})` once.

patterns.title: Connection refused to {1}:{2}
patterns.diagnosis: Nothing is accepting connections at {1}:{2}. The target service is down, not started yet, or you've got the wrong host/port.
fixes: Confirm the service (DB, API, etc.) is actually running on port {2}.
Check the host — `127.0.0.1` vs `localhost` vs a container name can differ.
If in Docker, the service may need its container name instead of localhost.
Add a startup wait/retry if your app races the dependency.

patterns.match: Error: ENOENT: no such file or directory, (?:open|stat|scandir) '([^']+)'
patterns.title: File or directory not found
patterns.diagnosis: Node tried to access `{1}` but it doesn't exist. Often a wrong relative path — paths resolve from the current working directory, not the script's folder.
fixes: Build an absolute path from the script location: `path.join(__dirname, 'file')`.
Check `process.cwd()` — relative `fs` paths are relative to it, not your file.
Verify the file exists and spelling/case is exact (case matters on Linux).
Create the directory first with `fs.mkdirSync(dir, { recursive: true })` if writing.

patterns.title: Permission denied on {1}
patterns.diagnosis: The Node process lacks permission to access `{1}`. The file is owned by another user or the directory isn't writable.
fixes: Fix ownership: `sudo chown -R $(whoami) {1}`.
Don't run npm/node with `sudo` — it creates root-owned files that break later.
Pick a writable location (e.g. inside the project, not a system dir).
Check the file mode with `ls -l {1}` and adjust with `chmod` if needed.

patterns.title: Unhandled promise rejection
patterns.diagnosis: A promise rejected with `{1}` and nothing caught it. In modern Node this also crashes the process.
fixes: Add a `.catch()` to the promise, or wrap the `await` in `try/catch`.
Make sure async functions that can throw are awaited inside a try block.
Add a global net: `process.on('unhandledRejection', err => { ... })` for logging.
Trace the rejecting call — the message `{1}` tells you what threw.

patterns.match: FATAL ERROR: .*(?:Allocation failed|Reached heap limit).*JavaScript heap out of memory
patterns.title: Out of memory — heap exhausted
patterns.diagnosis: Node hit V8's heap limit. Usually a runaway data structure, a leak, or processing more data than fits in the default heap.
fixes: Raise the limit: `node --max-old-space-size=4096 app.js` (4 GB).
Stream large files/data instead of loading them all into memory.
Look for unbounded growth — arrays/maps that only ever grow, listeners never removed.
Profile with `node --inspect` and take a heap snapshot to find the leak.

patterns.title: MODULE_NOT_FOUND for {1}
patterns.diagnosis: Node's resolver couldn't locate `{1}` anywhere in the module path. It's not installed or the local file path is wrong.
fixes: Install it if it's a package: `npm install {1}`.
For a local module, double-check the relative path and that the file exists.
Delete `node_modules` and reinstall to fix a corrupt install.
Run from the directory that has the right `node_modules`.

patterns.title: Deprecation warning
patterns.diagnosis: Node is warning that you (or a dependency) used something deprecated: `{1}`. It still works now but may be removed in a future version.
fixes: Read the message — it usually names the replacement API to use.
If it's from a dependency, update it: `npm update <pkg>`.
Run `node --trace-deprecation app.js` to find exactly where it's triggered.
Suppress only as a last resort: `node --no-deprecation` (hides real warnings too).

patterns.match: Error \[ERR_UNSUPPORTED_DIR_IMPORT\]: Directory import ([^\s]+) is not supported
patterns.title: Directory import not supported in ESM
patterns.diagnosis: You imported a directory (`{1}`) in ESM. Unlike CommonJS, ESM won't auto-resolve `index.js` inside a folder.
fixes: Import the file explicitly: `import x from './dir/index.js'`.
Add an `exports` map in that package's package.json pointing to the entry.
Always include the file and extension in ESM relative imports.
Or switch the importing file to CommonJS if you rely on directory resolution.

patterns.title: Connection reset (ECONNRESET)
patterns.diagnosis: The remote end closed the TCP connection abruptly while Node was reading. Often a timeout, a server restart, or a dropped keep-alive socket.
fixes: Add retry-with-backoff around the request — transient resets are common.
If it's an HTTP client, set sane timeouts and handle the `'error'` event.
Check the server logs — it may be crashing or closing idle connections.
For pooled connections, lower keep-alive timeouts or recreate stale sockets.

patterns.title: DNS lookup failed for {1}
patterns.diagnosis: Node couldn't resolve the hostname `{1}` to an IP. The name is wrong, DNS is unreachable, or you're offline.
fixes: Check `{1}` for typos and that it's a real, reachable host.
Test resolution outside Node: `ping {1}` or `nslookup {1}`.
If behind a proxy/VPN/container, verify DNS is configured there.
For localhost services use `127.0.0.1` to bypass DNS entirely.

patterns.title: Self-signed TLS certificate rejected
patterns.diagnosis: Node refused a TLS connection because the server's certificate is self-signed (or signed by an untrusted CA).
fixes: Add the CA cert properly: `NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS=/path/to/ca.pem node app.js`.
For a known-internal host, pass the CA in the request's `ca` option.
Only for local dev, never prod: `NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED=0` (insecure).
Get a properly-signed certificate for production endpoints.

patterns.match: (?:Error|throw) .*The engine "node" is incompatible with this module\. Expected version "([^"]+)"
patterns.title: Node version incompatible (need {1})
patterns.diagnosis: A package's `engines` field requires Node `{1}`, but your installed Node doesn't satisfy it.
fixes: Check your version: `node -v`, then install a matching one with `nvm install` / `nvm use`.
Use a version manager (nvm, fnm, volta) to switch easily per project.
If you must proceed anyway: `npm install --engine-strict=false` (may break at runtime).
Pin the project's Node version in `.nvmrc` so the whole team aligns.

patterns.title: Invalid JSON
patterns.diagnosis: `JSON.parse` got malformed JSON. Common: trailing commas, single quotes, an HTML error page returned instead of JSON, or an empty string.
fixes: Log the raw text before parsing — you may be getting HTML or an empty body.
JSON requires double quotes and no trailing commas.
Wrap the parse in try/catch and handle the bad-data case.
If from `fetch`, check `res.ok` and content-type before calling `res.json()`.
patterns.example_fix:
if (!res.ok) throw new Error(res.status);
const data = await res.json();

patterns.title: Callback called more than once
patterns.diagnosis: An async callback (often via the `async` library or a custom one) was invoked twice. Usually a missing `return` after calling it on an error path.
fixes: Add `return` after every callback call: `return cb(err)`.
Make sure error and success paths are mutually exclusive (no fall-through).
Check loops that call `cb` per item but should call it once at the end.
Consider migrating to promises/async-await to avoid double-call hazards.

patterns.match: npm ERR! code ENOENT[\s\S]*?npm ERR! enoent ENOENT: no such file or directory, open '([^']*package\.json)'
patterns.title: npm: no package.json here
patterns.diagnosis: npm couldn't find `{1}` in the current directory. You're running npm somewhere without a project manifest.
fixes: `cd` into the actual project folder that contains package.json.
If starting fresh, create one: `npm init -y`.
Check you didn't run the command one directory too high or too low.
Confirm with `ls package.json` before running npm scripts.

patterns.match: npm ERR! code ERESOLVE[\s\S]*?(?:could not resolve|unable to resolve dependency tree)
patterns.title: npm ERESOLVE — dependency conflict
patterns.diagnosis: npm 7+ found conflicting peer-dependency requirements it can't satisfy with one version tree.
fixes: Read the conflict block — it names the package and the incompatible peers.
Bring deps into alignment by upgrading/downgrading the offending package.
Force it (accepts a possibly-broken tree): `npm install --legacy-peer-deps`.
As a last resort: `npm install --force` (more aggressive, riskier).

patterns.match: npm ERR! code E404[\s\S]*?'([^']+)' is not in (?:this registry|the npm registry)
patterns.title: npm 404 — package {1} not found
patterns.diagnosis: The registry has no package named `{1}` at the requested version. Likely a typo, a private/scoped package, or a version that doesn't exist.
fixes: Check the exact spelling on npmjs.com.
If it's scoped/private, configure the registry/auth: `npm config set @scope:registry ...`.
Verify the version exists: `npm view {1} versions`.
If you renamed a local dep, fix the name/path in package.json.

patterns.title: npm EACCES — permission denied at {1}
patterns.diagnosis: npm can't write to `{1}`, usually a global install directory owned by root because of an earlier `sudo npm`.
fixes: Never use `sudo npm` — fix the prefix instead: set npm's global dir to your home.
Reclaim ownership: `sudo chown -R $(whoami) ~/.npm` and the global prefix.
Better: use a version manager (nvm) so global installs go in your home dir.
For project installs, run from a folder you own (not a system path).

patterns.match: npm ERR! code ELIFECYCLE[\s\S]*?npm ERR! .* (\w[\w:-]*) script
patterns.title: npm script '{1}' failed
patterns.diagnosis: The `{1}` script exited with a non-zero code. The real failure is in the output above this npm summary — npm just reports the script died.
fixes: Scroll up: the actual error/stack from your code is printed before this line.
Run the script's command directly to see clearer output.
Reproduce with verbose logs: `npm run {1} --loglevel verbose`.
If install-related, clear cache and reinstall: `npm cache clean --force && rm -rf node_modules && npm install`.

patterns.title: npm: missing script "{1}"
patterns.diagnosis: There's no `"{1}"` entry under `scripts` in package.json, so `npm run {1}` has nothing to run.
fixes: List what's available: `npm run`.
Add the script under `"scripts"` in package.json.
Check for a typo — script names are case-sensitive.
Make sure you're in the right project (the script may live in a subpackage).

patterns.title: npm: package.json is invalid JSON
patterns.diagnosis: npm couldn't parse `{1}`. There's a JSON syntax error — usually a trailing comma, a missing quote, or a stray comment.
fixes: JSON has no trailing commas and no comments — remove them.
All keys and string values need double quotes.
Validate it: `node -e "require('./package.json')"` or paste into a JSON linter.
Check the line/column npm points to in the error.

patterns.title: npm EBADENGINE — Node {1} required
patterns.diagnosis: A package declares it needs Node `{1}`, but your Node version doesn't match. It's a warning, so install proceeded, but runtime may break.
fixes: Switch Node versions: `nvm install {1} && nvm use {1}`.
Add `.nvmrc` / `engines` to your project to keep versions consistent.
If the warning is harmless for your use, you can ignore it — but test thoroughly.
Check `node -v` to see what you're actually running.

patterns.match: npm ERR! .*Cannot read propert(?:y|ies) .* of (?:null|undefined)[\s\S]*?npm ERR! .*(?:lock|package-lock)
patterns.title: Corrupt npm lockfile / node_modules
patterns.diagnosis: npm crashed reading internal state, typically a corrupt `package-lock.json` or a half-finished `node_modules`.
fixes: Nuke and reinstall: `rm -rf node_modules package-lock.json && npm install`.
Clear the cache if it persists: `npm cache clean --force`.
Make sure no other npm/install process is running concurrently.
Update npm itself: `npm install -g npm@latest`.

patterns.match: npm ERR! code ETIMEDOUT[\s\S]*?npm ERR! .*(?:network|request to ([^\s]+))
patterns.title: npm network timeout
patterns.diagnosis: npm couldn't reach the registry within the timeout. Network is slow/down, a proxy is blocking, or the registry is unreachable.
fixes: Check connectivity: `ping registry.npmjs.org`.
If behind a corporate proxy, set it: `npm config set proxy ...` / `https-proxy ...`.
Bump the timeout: `npm config set fetch-timeout 60000`.
Retry — registry hiccups are often transient.

patterns.title: npm: install already running / stale lock
patterns.diagnosis: npm thinks another install is in progress. Either one really is, or a previous run died and left a stale internal lock.
fixes: Wait for / stop any other npm process, then retry.
If none is running, clear the cache lock: `rm -rf ~/.npm/_locks` (or `npm cache clean --force`).
Delete `node_modules` and `package-lock.json`, then reinstall.
Update npm if this recurs: `npm install -g npm@latest`.

patterns.title: node-gyp native build failed
patterns.diagnosis: A package with native (C/C++) code failed to compile via node-gyp — typically missing build tools, a Python mismatch, or a Node version the addon doesn't support.
fixes: Install build tooling: macOS `xcode-select --install`; Debian `apt install build-essential`; Windows `npm install -g windows-build-tools`.
node-gyp needs Python 3 on PATH — verify `python3 --version`.
Match the package to a supported Node version (prebuilt binaries may not exist for newer Node).
Clean and rebuild: `rm -rf node_modules && npm install`.

patterns.match: Parse error: syntax error, unexpected (?:token )?'([^']+)'(?:, expecting '([^']+)')?
patterns.title: PHP parse error — unexpected token
patterns.diagnosis: PHP's parser hit `{1}` where it didn't belong{2:, while expecting `{2}`}. This is almost always a missing semicolon, comma, brace, or parenthesis on the line *before* the one reported.
fixes: Check the line above the reported one for a missing `;` at the end of a statement.
Count your brackets — an unclosed `{`, `(`, or `[` makes the parser blame the next token `{1}`.
If `{1}` is `}`, you likely have an extra closing brace or a missing one earlier.
Make sure every `case`/statement inside a block ends correctly and arrays use commas between elements.

patterns.match: Fatal error: Uncaught Error: Call to undefined function ([\w\\]+)\(\)
patterns.title: PHP — undefined function
patterns.diagnosis: PHP can't find a function named `{1}()`. It's misspelled, lives in a namespace you didn't qualify, or comes from an extension/file that isn't loaded.
fixes: Check spelling and case (function names are case-insensitive, but typos still bite).
If `{1}` is from a library, make sure you `require`/`include` the file or it's autoloaded via Composer.
If it's namespaced, call it as `\Vendor\{1}()` or add a `use` statement.
If it's an extension function (e.g. `mb_*`, `gd_*`), confirm the extension is enabled in php.ini.

patterns.match: Fatal error: Uncaught Error: Call to undefined method ([\w\\]+)::(\w+)\(\)
patterns.title: PHP — undefined method
patterns.diagnosis: The class `{1}` has no method called `{2}()`. Either it's misspelled, defined on a different class, or `$this` isn't the object you think it is.
fixes: Check the method name spelling and case against the class `{1}` definition.
Confirm the object is actually an instance of `{1}` (var_dump it).
If `{2}` is inherited, make sure `{1}` extends the right parent class.
For magic calls, implement `__call()` on `{1}` if you intended dynamic dispatch.

patterns.match: Fatal error: Uncaught Error: Class "([\w\\]+)" not found
patterns.title: PHP — class not found
patterns.diagnosis: PHP couldn't locate the class `{1}`. Usually a missing autoload entry, a wrong namespace, or a forgotten `require`.
fixes: Run `composer dump-autoload` if you added the class recently.
Check the namespace at the top of the file matches the PSR-4 path in composer.json.
If not using Composer, `require_once` the file that defines `{1}`.
Qualify the class: leading `\` for global, or add `use {1};` at the top.

patterns.title: PHP — undefined variable or array key
patterns.diagnosis: You read `{1}` before it was ever set. In PHP 8 this is a Warning (was a Notice in PHP 7) and yields `null`.
fixes: Initialize the variable before use: `${1} = '';`.
For array keys, guard with `isset($arr['{1}'])` or `array_key_exists()`.
Use the null-coalescing operator: `$value = $arr['{1}'] ?? 'default';`.
Check spelling — `$userName` and `$username` are different variables.

patterns.match: Fatal error: Uncaught Error: Attempt to (?:read|assign) propert(?:y|ies) "(\w+)" on (\w+)
patterns.title: PHP — property access on non-object
patterns.diagnosis: You tried `->{1}` but the thing on the left is a `{2}` (often `null`), not an object. A query or function returned nothing and you chained off it.
fixes: Check that the value isn't `null` before the arrow: `if ($obj !== null) { $obj->{1}; }`.
Use nullsafe chaining (PHP 8): `$obj?->{1}`.
Trace back where the `{2}` came from — a failed `find()`/`fetch()` often returns null/false.
If it should be an array, use `['{1}']` instead of `->{1}`.

patterns.match: Fatal error: Uncaught TypeError: ([\w\\:]+)\(\): Argument #(\d+) \(\$(\w+)\) must be of type (\w+), (\w+) given
patterns.title: PHP — argument type mismatch
patterns.diagnosis: `{1}()` expects argument #{2} (`${3}`) to be `{4}`, but you passed a `{5}`. PHP's type declarations are being enforced (strict or coercive mode).
fixes: Cast or convert the value to `{4}` before passing it (e.g. `(int)`, `(string)`).
Check upstream — a `{5}` here often means a function returned the wrong thing or null slipped in.
If `{4}` should accept `{5}`, widen the param to a union type like `{4}|{5}` or make it nullable `?{4}`.
Remove `declare(strict_types=1)` only if you truly want coercion (not recommended).

patterns.match: Fatal error: Uncaught ArgumentCountError: Too few arguments to function ([\w\\:]+)\(\), (\d+) passed .* and (?:exactly|at least) (\d+) expected
patterns.title: PHP — too few arguments
patterns.diagnosis: `{1}()` needs at least {3} argument(s) but you only passed {2}. A required parameter has no default.
fixes: Pass the missing argument(s) at the call site.
Give the parameter a default value in the signature: `function f($x = null)`.
Check you didn't shift arguments by leaving a comma or value out.
Make the trailing parameter optional or accept variadics with `...$args`.

patterns.match: Fatal error: Allowed memory size of (\d+) bytes exhausted \(tried to allocate (\d+) bytes\)
patterns.title: PHP — memory exhausted
patterns.diagnosis: The script blew past the {1}-byte `memory_limit` while trying to grab {2} more bytes. Usually a runaway loop, loading a huge result set, or recursion that never ends.
fixes: Don't load everything into memory — stream rows/lines instead of building one giant array.
Process large datasets in chunks (paginate DB queries, `fgets` line-by-line).
Look for unbounded recursion or an array that keeps growing inside a loop.
As a last resort raise the limit: `ini_set('memory_limit', '256M');` — but fix the real cause.

patterns.match: Fatal error: Maximum execution time of (\d+) seconds exceeded
patterns.title: PHP — max execution time exceeded
patterns.diagnosis: The script ran longer than the {1}-second `max_execution_time`. Likely an infinite loop, a slow external call, or processing too much data per request.
fixes: Find the slow spot — log timestamps or use a profiler (Xdebug, Blackfire).
Move long-running work to a background queue/cron instead of a web request.
Add timeouts to external HTTP/DB calls so they fail fast.
For legit long CLI jobs: `set_time_limit(0);` (CLI ignores the limit by default).

patterns.match: Warning: (?:require|include)(?:_once)?\(([^)]+)\): [Ff]ailed to open stream: No such file or directory
patterns.title: PHP — include/require file not found
patterns.diagnosis: PHP couldn't open `{1}`. The path is wrong, relative to the wrong directory, or the file isn't there.
fixes: Use an absolute path: `require __DIR__ . '/{1}';` so it's relative to the current file.
Check the filename spelling and case (case matters on Linux).
Verify the file actually exists at that path and is readable.
If it's a Composer dependency, `require __DIR__ . '/vendor/autoload.php';` instead.

patterns.match: Warning: foreach\(\) argument must be of type array\|object, (\w+) given
patterns.title: PHP — foreach on non-iterable
patterns.diagnosis: You passed a `{1}` to `foreach`, but it only iterates arrays and objects. Often a function returned `null`/`false` instead of an array.
fixes: Guard before looping: `if (is_array($x)) { foreach ($x as $v) {...} }`.
Default to an empty array: `foreach (($x ?? []) as $v)`.
Trace why `{1}` came back — a failed query or JSON decode returns null/false.
Cast a single value to array if appropriate: `foreach ((array)$x as $v)`.

patterns.title: PHP — database (PDO/mysqli) error
patterns.diagnosis: The database driver threw SQLSTATE `{1}` (code {2}): {3}. The query failed — bad SQL, a missing column/table, a constraint, or a connection issue.
fixes: Echo/log the exact SQL and the error message `{3}` to see what the DB rejected.
For syntax errors, check quoting, reserved words, and placeholder counts.
Use prepared statements with bound params to avoid quoting/injection bugs.
For connection refusals, verify host, port, credentials, and that the DB is running.

patterns.match: Deprecated: ([\w\\:]+)\(\): Passing null to parameter #(\d+) \(\$(\w+)\) of type (\w+) is deprecated
patterns.title: PHP 8.1 — passing null to non-nullable param
patterns.diagnosis: In PHP 8.1+, passing `null` to the `{4}` parameter `${3}` (#{2}) of `{1}()` is deprecated and will error in PHP 9. A value upstream is null when it shouldn't be.
fixes: Coalesce before the call: `{1}($value ?? '')`.
Fix the source so `${3}` is never null at this point.
If null is legitimately allowed, this is a built-in function — guard the call with an `if`.
Update the call to pass an empty string/array/default matching `{4}`.

patterns.match: Fatal error: Uncaught Error: Cannot use object of type (\w+) as array
patterns.title: PHP — object used as array
patterns.diagnosis: You indexed `{1}` with `[]` but it's an object, not an array. Common when JSON was decoded to objects (default `json_decode`) but you treated it like an associative array.
fixes: Use property syntax: `$obj->key` instead of `$obj['key']`.
Decode JSON as arrays: `json_decode($json, true)`.
Cast the object to an array: `(array)$obj`.
If you control the class, implement `ArrayAccess` to allow `[]`.

patterns.match: Warning: Trying to access array offset on value of type (\w+)
patterns.title: PHP — array offset on non-array
patterns.diagnosis: You used `[...]` on a `{1}` value (often `null`). The variable isn't the array you expected.
fixes: Check the variable is an array before indexing: `is_array($x)`.
Use null-coalescing on the access: `$x['key'] ?? null`.
Trace back — a failed lookup or function frequently returns `null`/`false`.
Initialize the array earlier so it's never `{1}`.

patterns.match: Fatal error: Uncaught Error: Using \$this when not in object context
patterns.title: PHP — $this outside object context
patterns.diagnosis: `$this` was used in a static method or a plain function. `$this` only exists inside a non-static instance method.
fixes: Make the method non-static (remove `static`) and call it on an instance.
Inside a static method, use `self::` / `static::` instead of `$this->`.
Pass the object in as a parameter if you need it in a standalone function.
Check you didn't call an instance method statically with `::`.

patterns.title: PHP — headers already sent
patterns.diagnosis: Something already produced output (started at {1}:{2}) before your `header()`/`setcookie()`/`session_start()` call. Once any byte is sent, headers can't change.
fixes: Move all `header()`/`session_start()` calls before any `echo`/HTML/whitespace.
Check for whitespace or a BOM before the opening `<?php` or after a closing `?>`.
Remove the closing `?>` tag at the end of pure-PHP files to avoid stray output.
Use output buffering (`ob_start()`) as a workaround if you can't reorder.

patterns.title: Ruby — undefined method on nil (NoMethodError)
patterns.diagnosis: You called `.{1}` on `nil`. Something earlier returned `nil` (a missing hash key, an empty `find`, an unassigned attribute) and you chained a method off it.
fixes: Use the safe-navigation operator: `obj&.{1}`.
Guard with a conditional: `obj.{1} if obj`.
Trace where the `nil` came from — `Hash#[]` and `Array#find` return nil on miss.
Provide a default: `(value || default).{1}`.

patterns.title: Ruby — undefined method (NoMethodError)
patterns.diagnosis: Objects of type `{2}` don't respond to `.{1}`. The method is misspelled, defined on another class, or you have the wrong object type.
fixes: Check the method name spelling — Ruby is case-sensitive.
Confirm the receiver is really a `{2}`: `p obj.class`.
If `{1}` lives in a module, make sure it's `include`d into `{2}`.
If you expected a different class, fix where the `{2}` was produced.

patterns.match: undefined local variable or method `([^']+)' for
patterns.title: Ruby — undefined local variable or method
patterns.diagnosis: Ruby can't find a local variable or method named `{1}` in scope. It's misspelled, not yet defined, or you meant an instance variable (`@{1}`).
fixes: Check spelling and that `{1}` is assigned before this line.
Did you mean an instance variable? Use `@{1}` inside the class.
If `{1}` is a method, confirm it's defined and reachable (right class/module).
Inside a block, remember variables defined outside are visible but block-locals aren't visible outside.

patterns.title: Ruby — wrong number of arguments (ArgumentError)
patterns.diagnosis: You called a method with {1} argument(s) but it expects {2}. The signature doesn't match the call.
fixes: Match the call to the method definition — count required params.
Give parameters defaults to make them optional: `def f(x, y = nil)`.
If passing a hash of options, wrap it in braces or use keyword args.
For splat collection use `def f(*args)` to accept any count.

patterns.title: Ruby — uninitialized constant (NameError)
patterns.diagnosis: Ruby can't find the constant/class/module `{1}`. It's not loaded, misspelled, or in a different namespace than where you referenced it.
fixes: `require` (or `require_relative`) the file that defines `{1}`.
Check the spelling and namespace — use `Foo::{1}` or a leading `::` for top-level.
In Rails, confirm the file name matches the constant (autoloading is name-based).
If it's a gem, add it to the Gemfile and `bundle install`, then `require` it.

patterns.title: Ruby — no implicit conversion (TypeError)
patterns.diagnosis: Ruby refused to auto-convert a `{1}` where a `{2}` was required — typically interpolating or concatenating mismatched types, like `"x" + 5` or `arr[some_string]`.
fixes: Convert explicitly: `.to_s`, `.to_i`, `.to_a` as appropriate.
For string building, use interpolation `"#{value}"` instead of `+`.
Check array/hash indexing — an Array needs an Integer index, not a `{1}`.
Trace the `{1}` value; it may be the wrong variable entirely.

patterns.title: Ruby — can't convert types (TypeError)
patterns.diagnosis: An operation needed a `{2}` but got a `{1}` and couldn't coerce it. Common with arithmetic or concatenation mixing strings and numbers.
fixes: Call the right conversion: `{1}` → `{2}` via `.to_s`/`.to_i`/`.to_f`.
Ensure both operands of `+`/`*` are the same kind (both numbers or both strings).
Validate input from params/JSON — it often arrives as a String.
Use `Integer(x)`/`Float(x)` for strict numeric parsing that errors on junk.

patterns.title: Ruby — NameError
patterns.diagnosis: At line {1} in `{2}`, Ruby couldn't resolve a name: {3}. A variable, method, or constant referenced there doesn't exist in scope.
fixes: Read the message `{3}` — it names exactly what's missing.
Check spelling and that the name is defined before line {1}.
For constants, `require` the defining file or fix the namespace.
For instance variables, prefix with `@`; they default to `nil`, not a NameError, so a NameError means a bare local.

patterns.title: Ruby — division by zero
patterns.diagnosis: Integer division (or `%`) by zero. Note: float division by `0.0` returns `Infinity`, but integer `/ 0` raises this.
fixes: Guard the divisor: `n / d unless d.zero?`.
Provide a fallback: `d.zero? ? 0 : n / d`.
Convert to float if you actually want `Infinity`/`NaN`: `n.to_f / d`.
Validate the denominator's source — it may be an unset/`0` default.

patterns.title: Ruby — KeyError from Hash#fetch
patterns.diagnosis: `Hash#fetch` was asked for key `{1}` but the hash has no such key. `fetch` raises (unlike `[]`, which returns nil).
fixes: Provide a default: `hash.fetch('{1}', default_value)`.
Use a block default: `hash.fetch('{1}') { compute_it }`.
Check the key spelling and whether it should be a Symbol vs String.
If a nil result is acceptable, use `hash['{1}']` instead of `fetch`.

patterns.title: Ruby — array index out of bounds
patterns.diagnosis: You used `Array#fetch` (or insert) with index {1}, but the valid range is {2}...{3}. `fetch` raises on out-of-range; `[]` would have returned nil.
fixes: Check the index is within `0...array.size`.
Use `array[{1}]` (returns nil) instead of `fetch` if out-of-range is acceptable.
Provide a fetch default: `array.fetch({1}, nil)`.
Negative indices count from the end — verify {1} is what you intend.

patterns.title: Ruby — syntax error
patterns.diagnosis: At {1}:{2}, Ruby hit `{3}` unexpectedly{4:, while expecting `{4}`}. Usually a missing `end`, an unbalanced `do`/`{`, or a stray keyword.
fixes: Check that every `def`/`do`/`if`/`class`/`module` has a matching `end`.
Look just above line {2} — the real mistake is often on the preceding line.
Balance brackets and string quotes; an unterminated string swallows code.
Run `ruby -c file.rb` to syntax-check without executing.

patterns.title: Ruby — cannot load file (LoadError)
patterns.diagnosis: `require`/`require_relative` couldn't find `{1}`. The gem isn't installed, the path is wrong, or it's not on the load path.
fixes: If it's a gem, add it to the Gemfile and run `bundle install` (then `bundle exec`).
Install directly: `gem install {1}`.
For local files use `require_relative './{1}'` with the correct relative path.
Check the file/gem name spelling and that it's on `$LOAD_PATH`.

patterns.title: Ruby — comparison failed
patterns.diagnosis: Tried to compare/sort a `{1}` against a `{2}` and they aren't comparable (no shared `<=>`). Common when sorting a mixed array or comparing `nil` with a number.
fixes: Make the collection homogeneous before sorting (all numbers or all strings).
Strip or coerce `nil`s: `array.compact.sort` or map to a comparable key.
Use `sort_by { |x| x.to_s }` (or `.to_i`) to force a consistent comparison key.
Define `<=>` on your class if comparing custom objects.

patterns.title: Ruby — stack level too deep
patterns.diagnosis: Infinite (or far too deep) recursion blew the call stack. A method keeps calling itself or two methods call each other without a base case.
fixes: Add a base case that returns without recursing.
Check for an accidental self-call — e.g. a getter `def name; name; end` (should be `@name`).
Watch for `method_missing`/`super` loops and alias-method cycles.
Convert deep recursion to an iterative loop for large inputs.

patterns.title: Ruby — can't modify frozen object (FrozenError)
patterns.diagnosis: You tried to mutate a frozen `{1}`. In Ruby 3.x string literals may be frozen (especially with `# frozen_string_literal: true`), and some constants/objects are frozen on purpose.
fixes: Work on a copy: `value.dup` then mutate the dup.
Build a new object instead of mutating in place (e.g. `str + x` not `str << x`).
Remove or account for the `# frozen_string_literal: true` magic comment.
Don't mutate shared constants — `FOO.dup` first.

patterns.title: Ruby — undefined method on a class
patterns.diagnosis: The class object `{2}` has no class/singleton method `{1}`. You likely called an instance method on the class itself, or the method is misnamed.
fixes: Instantiate first if `{1}` is an instance method: `{2}.new.{1}`.
Define it as a class method (`def self.{1}`) if it should be callable on `{2}`.
Check spelling and the right class — class vs instance method confusion is common.
If from a mixin, `extend` the module (class methods) vs `include` (instance methods).

patterns.match: deadlock detected \(fatal\)|No live threads left\. Deadlock\?
patterns.title: Ruby — deadlock detected
patterns.diagnosis: All threads are blocked waiting on each other (or on a queue/mutex that will never be signaled). Ruby aborts rather than hang forever.
fixes: Make sure every `Mutex#lock` has a matching `unlock` — prefer `mutex.synchronize { }`.
Don't have a thread wait on a queue/condition that nothing else will ever push to.
Acquire multiple locks in a consistent global order across all threads.
Add timeouts to blocking waits so a stuck thread fails instead of deadlocking.

patterns.match: TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined \(reading '([^']+)'\)
patterns.title: Reading a property off undefined
patterns.diagnosis: Something evaluated to `undefined`, and then you tried to read `.{1}` off it. The object you expected was never assigned, a function returned nothing, or a key/index that doesn't exist gave back `undefined`.
fixes: Use optional chaining: `obj?.{1}` so it short-circuits to `undefined` instead of throwing.
Guard first: `if (obj) { obj.{1} }` or `const x = obj || {{}}`.
Log the parent value right before this line — find which step produced `undefined`.
