patterns.match: (?:\.go:\d+:\d+: )?multiple-value ([\w.]+)\([^)]*\) (?:in single-value context|\(value of type [^)]+\) in single-value context)
patterns.title: Multi-value call in single-value context
patterns.diagnosis: `{1}` returns more than one value, but you used it where only one value fits (e.g. as a single argument or in a single assignment).
fixes: Assign all returns first, then use them: `v, err := {1}(...)`.
Handle the error return instead of ignoring it.
You can't inline a multi-return call as one argument — capture it in variables first.

patterns.match: go: (?:cannot find main module|go\.mod file not found in current directory or any parent directory)
patterns.title: No go.mod found
patterns.diagnosis: You're outside a module — there's no go.mod in this directory or any parent, so module-aware commands fail.
fixes: Initialize a module: `go mod init <module-path>` (e.g. `go mod init example.com/myapp`).
Run the command from inside your module's directory tree.
If you cloned a repo, make sure you're at or below the directory containing go.mod.

patterns.match: (?:go: )?missing go\.sum entry for module providing package ([\w./-]+)
patterns.title: Missing go.sum entry
patterns.diagnosis: The package `{1}` is required but has no checksum recorded in go.sum, so the build can't verify it.
fixes: Run `go mod tidy` to add the missing require and go.sum entries.
Or `go mod download` to populate go.sum for existing requirements.
Run `go get {1}` to add the dependency explicitly.

patterns.match: (?:go: )?(?:no required module provides package|cannot find package) ([\w./-]+)
patterns.title: No module provides this package
patterns.diagnosis: Nothing in your module graph provides `{1}`. The dependency isn't required, or the import path is wrong.
fixes: Add it: `go get {1}` then `go mod tidy`.
Double-check the import path for typos — it must match the module's real path.
If it's a local package, ensure the path matches your module prefix in go.mod.

patterns.title: Module version resolution failed
patterns.diagnosis: Go couldn't resolve or read `{1}` — the version tag may not exist, the proxy is unreachable, or the path is wrong.
fixes: Verify the version exists: `go list -m -versions <module>`.
Use a valid semver tag or a pseudo-version, or pin with `@latest`.
Check network/proxy: try `GOPROXY=direct go get ...` or set GOPROXY appropriately.
Run `go mod tidy` to let Go pick a consistent version.

patterns.match: (?:\.go:\d+:\d+: )?([\w.]+) \(variable of type [^)]+\) is not (?:a type|an interface)
patterns.title: Used a value where a type was expected
patterns.diagnosis: `{1}` is a variable, but the syntax here (a type assertion, conversion, or generic constraint) needs a type name.
fixes: Pass the type itself, not a value: e.g. `x.(MyType)`, not `x.(myVar)`.
Check for a name collision between a variable and a type.
In a type switch use `x.(type)`; in an assertion use a concrete type name.

patterns.title: Cannot range over this value
patterns.diagnosis: `{1}` has type `{2}`, which isn't rangeable. `range` works over arrays, slices, strings, maps, channels, and (Go 1.22+) integers/functions.
fixes: If `{2}` is a pointer to a slice/array, dereference first: `for i := range *{1}`.
Make sure you're ranging the collection, not a scalar.
For maps/channels confirm the value is actually that type with `fmt.Printf("%T", {1})`.

patterns.title: Mismatched types in operation
patterns.diagnosis: You applied an operator between `{1}` (type `{3}`) and `{2}` (type `{4}`). Go won't auto-convert between distinct types.
fixes: Convert one operand so both sides share a type: `{3}({2})` or `{4}({1})`.
Untyped constants adapt automatically, but two different named/numeric types do not.
If these are custom types over the same base, convert explicitly before comparing/combining.

patterns.title: Cannot assign to map element field
patterns.diagnosis: You tried to assign to a field of a struct stored by value in a map (`m[k].Field = x`). Map values aren't addressable, so you can't mutate them in place.
fixes: Read out, modify, write back: `v := m[k]; v.Field = x; m[k] = v`.
Store pointers in the map instead: `map[K]*T`, then `m[k].Field = x` works.
For whole-value replacement just assign a new value: `m[k] = T{...}`.
patterns.example_fix:
v := m[k]
v.Field = x
m[k] = v

patterns.title: Label problem
patterns.diagnosis: The label `{1}` is either declared but never targeted by a break/continue/goto, or referenced without being defined.
fixes: Remove the unused label `{1}`, or actually `break {1}` / `continue {1}` to it.
If referenced, make sure the label is declared in the same function before/above its use.
Labels only attach to `for`, `switch`, and `select` statements.

patterns.match: panic: runtime error: comparing uncomparable type ([\w.\[\]]+)
patterns.title: Comparing uncomparable type
patterns.diagnosis: A comparison (often via `==`, map key, or interface compare) involved `{1}`, which is uncomparable — slices, maps, and functions can't be compared with `==`.
fixes: Don't use slices/maps/funcs as map keys or in `==`; compare with reflect.DeepEqual or element-wise instead.
If it's an interface holding a slice/map, switch on the concrete type and compare its parts.
Use a comparable key (string, struct of comparables) for the map.

patterns.title: Constant overflows type
patterns.diagnosis: The constant `{1}` doesn't fit in a `{2}`. Its value exceeds that type's range.
fixes: Use a wider type (e.g. `int64`, `uint64`, `float64`) for `{2}`.
Double-check the literal — a typo may have added digits.
For bit patterns near the limit, an explicit conversion may be needed: `uint32(0xFFFFFFFF)`.

patterns.title: Invalid conversion
patterns.diagnosis: Go won't convert `{1}` to `{2}` — the types aren't convertible (e.g. string to int directly, or unrelated struct types).
fixes: String↔number needs the strconv package: `strconv.Atoi`, `strconv.Itoa`, `strconv.ParseFloat`.
`[]byte`↔`string` conversions are allowed; arbitrary structs are not.
Confirm the underlying types are compatible before converting.

patterns.match: (?:\.go:\d+:\d+: )?([\w.]+)\.([\w]+) undefined \(type ([\w.*\[\]]+) has no field or method ([\w]+)\)
patterns.title: No such field or method
patterns.diagnosis: `{1}` is a `{3}`, which has no field or method named `{2}`. It's misspelled, unexported, or on a different type.
fixes: Check spelling and exported-name casing — `{4}` must match exactly.
If it's a method with a pointer receiver, call it on a pointer (`(&v).{2}()` or use a `*{3}`).
Make sure you're using the right type; print `fmt.Printf("%T\n", {1})` to confirm.

patterns.match: (?:\.go:\d+:\d+: )?fmt\.(?:Printf|Sprintf|Errorf) format %([\w])(?: has arg [\w]+ of wrong type ([\w.*\[\]]+)| reads arg #\d+, but call has \d+ args)?
patterns.title: Printf format verb mismatch (vet)
patterns.diagnosis: `go vet` flagged a format directive %{1} that doesn't match the argument {2} or the number of args supplied.
fixes: Match the verb to the type: %d for ints, %s for strings, %v for anything, %f for floats.
Use %v or %+v when unsure of the type.
Check that the count of % verbs equals the count of trailing arguments.

patterns.title: Assignment count mismatch
patterns.diagnosis: The left side has {1} variables but the right side produces {2} values. The counts must match exactly.
fixes: Add or remove variables on the left so the count equals {2}.
Use the blank identifier `_` for values you want to discard.
If a function returns (value, error), capture both: `v, err := f()`.
patterns.example_fix: v, _ := lookup(key) // discard the second return

patterns.title: E0382 — use of moved value
patterns.diagnosis: `{1}` was moved (ownership transferred) into another binding, function call, or closure, so it can no longer be used here. Non-Copy types like `String`, `Vec`, and `Box` move instead of copy.
fixes: Borrow instead of moving: pass `&{1}` and have the callee take `&T`.
Clone if you genuinely need a second owned copy: `{1}.clone()`.
Restructure so the value is used only once, or return it back from the function that consumed it.
If the type is cheap and logically copyable, `#[derive(Clone, Copy)]` on it.

patterns.match: error\[E0502\]: cannot borrow `([^`]+)` as mutable because it is also borrowed as immutable
patterns.title: E0502 — mutable + immutable borrow at once
patterns.diagnosis: You're trying to borrow `{1}` mutably while an immutable borrow of it is still alive. Rust forbids a `&mut` and `&` to the same value overlapping.
fixes: End the immutable borrow before the mutable one — let the earlier reference go out of scope or stop using it.
Copy the value you read out (e.g. `let x = {1}[0];`) so you no longer hold a reference while mutating.
Split the work into two non-overlapping scopes using `{ ... }` blocks.
For collections, fetch the index/length first, then mutate.
patterns.example_fix:
let len = {1}.len(); // read first
{1}.push(len);     // then mutate

patterns.match: error\[E0499\]: cannot borrow `([^`]+)` as mutable more than once at a time
patterns.title: E0499 — two mutable borrows at once
patterns.diagnosis: `{1}` is borrowed mutably (`&mut`) twice with both borrows live simultaneously. Rust allows only one `&mut` at a time.
fixes: Use one mutable borrow, finish with it, then take the next.
Scope the first borrow in a `{ ... }` block so it drops before the second.
If you need disjoint pieces of a struct/slice, use `split_at_mut` or destructure fields separately.
Consider `RefCell`/`Cell` only if you truly need interior mutability.

patterns.match: error\[E0759\]: `([^`]+)` has lifetime `'_` but it needs to satisfy a `'static` lifetime requirement
patterns.title: E0759 — argument needs 'static
patterns.diagnosis: `{1}` carries a non-`'static` lifetime, but it's used where `'static` is required (commonly `impl Trait + 'static` returns or trait objects sent across threads).
fixes: Take the argument by owned value or add a `+ 'static` bound on it.
Replace borrowed references inside with owned data.
Change the return type to borrow the input: `-> impl Trait + '_`.

patterns.match: error\[E0700\]: hidden type for `impl Trait` captures lifetime that does not appear in bounds
patterns.title: E0700 — impl Trait captures hidden lifetime
patterns.diagnosis: The concrete type behind an `impl Trait` return borrows from a lifetime that isn't mentioned in the return type's bounds.
fixes: Add the lifetime to the return: `-> impl Trait + 'a`.
Use `'_` to capture the elided input lifetime: `-> impl Trait + '_`.
Return owned data so no input lifetime is captured.
patterns.example_fix: fn f(s: &str) -> impl Iterator<Item = char> + '_ { s.chars() }

patterns.match: error\[E0772\]: `([^`]+)` has lifetime `'([^`']+)` but it needs to satisfy a `'static`
patterns.title: E0772 — trait object needs 'static
patterns.diagnosis: `{1}` is being coerced into a trait object that requires `'static`, but its lifetime `'{2}` is shorter.
fixes: Add a `'static` bound or use owned data inside `{1}`.
Annotate the trait object with the borrowed lifetime: `Box<dyn Trait + 'a>`.
Avoid sending borrowed data across an API that demands `'static`.

patterns.title: E0308 — mismatched types
patterns.diagnosis: An expression has a different type than the context expects. The compiler shows `expected X, found Y` just below this line.
fixes: Read the `expected`/`found` lines and convert: e.g. `.to_string()`, `as i64`, `&x`, or `*x`.
For `Result`/`Option`, you may need `?`, `.unwrap()`, `Ok(...)`, or `Some(...)`.
Check `&T` vs `T` — add or remove a borrow/deref.
Numeric literals may need a suffix or cast (`1u32`, `n as usize`).

patterns.match: error\[E0277\]: the trait bound `([^`]+): ([^`]+)` is not satisfied
patterns.title: E0277 — trait bound not satisfied
patterns.diagnosis: Type `{1}` doesn't implement the trait `{2}` that this operation requires.
fixes: Add `#[derive({2})]` to your type if it's derivable (Debug, Clone, PartialEq, etc.).
Add a bound on a generic: `where T: {2}`.
Implement `{2}` for `{1}` manually with an `impl {2} for {1}` block.
Use a different type that already implements `{2}`.

patterns.match: error\[E0599\]: no method named `([^`]+)` found for (?:type|struct|enum|reference|.*) `([^`]+)`
patterns.title: E0599 — no such method
patterns.diagnosis: There's no method `{1}` on `{2}`. Either it's misspelled, defined on a trait you haven't imported, or it's actually a free function.
fixes: Check spelling and the receiver type — autocomplete the available methods.
If the method comes from a trait, bring it into scope: `use the_trait::Trait;`.
Maybe you need `&` / `*` to match the method's `self` type.
Confirm the method exists for that exact type, not a similar one.

patterns.title: E0609 — no such field
patterns.diagnosis: Type `{2}` has no field named `{1}`. It may be misspelled, private, or you may be on a tuple struct (use `.0`, `.1`).
fixes: Check the field name and the struct definition.
For tuple structs, use numeric fields: `x.0`, `x.1`.
If the field is private, add a getter method or make it `pub`.
Make sure the variable is the struct itself, not a wrapper like `Option`/`Box`.

patterns.match: error\[E0610\]: `([^`]+)` is a primitive type and therefore doesn't have fields
patterns.title: E0610 — field access on primitive
patterns.diagnosis: You tried to access a field on a primitive `{1}` (like `i32` or `f64`), which has no fields.
fixes: Remove the `.field` access, or call a method instead (`x.abs()`, `x.to_string()`).
If you meant a tuple, build one and index it with `.0`/`.1`.
Check the variable's real type — it may not be the struct you think.

patterns.title: E0614 — cannot dereference
patterns.diagnosis: You used `*` on `{1}`, but that type doesn't implement `Deref`, so there's nothing to dereference.
fixes: Drop the `*` if `{1}` isn't a reference or smart pointer.
Only dereference `&T`, `Box<T>`, `Rc<T>`, etc.
Check whether you meant to call a method rather than deref.

patterns.match: error\[E0599\]: the method `([^`]+)` exists for .* but its trait bounds were not satisfied
patterns.title: E0599 — method exists but bounds unmet
patterns.diagnosis: Method `{1}` would exist, but the receiver type doesn't satisfy the trait bounds that method requires (e.g. `T: Ord` for `.sort()`).
fixes: Add the missing trait bound or `#[derive(...)]` so the type qualifies.
Use a concrete type that meets the bounds.
Read the note lines — they list exactly which bound is missing.

patterns.title: E0282 — type annotations needed
patterns.diagnosis: The compiler can't infer the type of a value and needs you to spell it out.
fixes: Annotate the variable: `let v: Vec<i32> = ...;`.
Add a turbofish: `"42".parse::<i32>()` or `collect::<Vec<_>>()`.
Give an explicit return type to the function in question.

patterns.match: error\[E0283\]: type annotations needed: cannot satisfy `([^`]+)`
patterns.title: E0283 — ambiguous type, can't satisfy bound
patterns.diagnosis: Multiple types could satisfy `{1}`, so inference is ambiguous and the compiler can't pick one.
fixes: Use a turbofish or explicit type to disambiguate.
Specify the concrete type on the binding or function call.
Reduce the candidate set by adding more specific bounds.

patterns.match: error\[E0284\]: type annotations needed: cannot satisfy `([^`]+)`
patterns.title: E0284 — can't infer associated type
patterns.diagnosis: Inference failed because an associated type from `{1}` can't be determined here.
fixes: Annotate the result type explicitly.
Use a turbofish on the call producing the associated type.
Add a where-clause pinning the associated type: `where I: Iterator<Item = u8>`.

patterns.match: error\[E0034\]: multiple applicable items in scope
patterns.title: E0034 — ambiguous method/item
patterns.diagnosis: More than one trait in scope provides an item with the same name, so the compiler can't decide which to call.
fixes: Use fully-qualified syntax: `Trait::method(&value)` or `<Type as Trait>::method(...)`.
Bring only the trait you want into scope.
Rename or scope the conflicting imports.

patterns.title: E0277 — can't add these types
patterns.diagnosis: There's no `Add` impl letting you add `{1}` to `{2}` — the types or reference forms don't line up.
fixes: Convert one operand so both sides are the same numeric type (`as`, `.into()`).
Deref references: `*a + *b`, or borrow as needed.
Implement `std::ops::Add` for your custom type if you want `+` on it.

patterns.match: error\[E0369\]: binary operation `([^`]+)` cannot be applied to type `([^`]+)`
patterns.title: E0369 — operator not supported for type
patterns.diagnosis: The `{1}` operator isn't defined for `{2}`. Operators map to traits (`+`→`Add`, `==`→`PartialEq`, `<`→`PartialOrd`).
fixes: Derive or implement the matching trait for `{2}` (`#[derive(PartialEq, PartialOrd)]`).
Compare/operate on a field or value that does support the operator.
Convert `{2}` to a primitive before using the operator.

patterns.match: error\[E0600\]: cannot apply unary operator `([^`]+)` to type `([^`]+)`
patterns.title: E0600 — unary operator not supported
patterns.diagnosis: The unary `{1}` operator (like `!` or `-`) isn't defined for `{2}`.
fixes: For `-`, the type must implement `Neg`; for `!`, `Not`. Derive/implement it.
Use a signed/boolean type that supports the operator.
Replace with an explicit method call if one exists.

patterns.match: error\[E0204\]: the trait `Copy` cannot be implemented for this type
patterns.title: E0204 — type can't be Copy
patterns.diagnosis: You tried to derive/implement `Copy`, but the type contains a field that isn't `Copy` (like `String` or `Vec`).
fixes: Derive only `Clone`, not `Copy`, for types holding heap data.
Replace non-Copy fields with Copy ones if Copy semantics are required.
Use `.clone()` explicitly instead of relying on implicit copies.

patterns.match: error\[E0277\]: `([^`]+)` cannot be sent between threads safely
patterns.title: E0277 — type is not Send
patterns.diagnosis: `{1}` isn't `Send`, so it can't be moved to another thread. Types like `Rc`, raw pointers, and some cells are not `Send`.
fixes: Use `Arc` instead of `Rc` for shared ownership across threads.
Wrap mutable shared state in `Arc<Mutex<...>>` rather than `Rc<RefCell<...>>`.
Keep the non-Send value on one thread and send owned, Send-safe data instead.

patterns.match: error\[E0277\]: `([^`]+)` cannot be shared between threads safely
patterns.title: E0277 — type is not Sync
patterns.diagnosis: `{1}` isn't `Sync`, so a shared reference to it can't be accessed from multiple threads at once.
fixes: Use `Mutex`/`RwLock` (with `Arc`) instead of `Cell`/`RefCell` for cross-thread sharing.
Use atomic types (`AtomicUsize`, etc.) for simple shared counters.
Confine the non-Sync value to one thread.

patterns.match: error\[E0594\]: cannot assign to `([^`]+)`, as it is not declared as mutable
patterns.title: E0594 — assign to immutable binding
patterns.diagnosis: `{1}` is an immutable binding, so you can't assign to it after initialization.
fixes: Declare it mutable: `let mut {1} = ...;`.
If you only need a new value, shadow it: `let {1} = new_value;`.
For struct fields, the whole binding holding the struct must be `mut`.

patterns.match: error\[E0596\]: cannot borrow `([^`]+)` as mutable, as it is not declared as mutable
patterns.title: E0596 — mutable borrow of immutable binding
patterns.diagnosis: You're taking `&mut {1}`, but `{1}` was declared without `mut`, so a mutable borrow isn't allowed.
fixes: Add `mut`: `let mut {1} = ...;`.
If `{1}` is a function parameter, declare it `mut {1}: T` (or take `&mut T`).
For shared mutability without `mut`, consider `Cell`/`RefCell`.

patterns.match: error\[E0384\]: cannot assign twice to immutable variable `([^`]+)`
patterns.title: E0384 — assigned twice to immutable
patterns.diagnosis: `{1}` is immutable and already initialized, so a second assignment is rejected.
fixes: Make it mutable: `let mut {1} = ...;` then reassign.
Or shadow with a fresh `let {1} = ...;` if you want a new binding.
If it's a constant value, compute it once and don't reassign.

patterns.match: error\[E0386\]: cannot assign to data in (?:a `&` reference|an immutable static item)
patterns.title: E0386 — assign through immutable reference
patterns.diagnosis: You're assigning through a shared `&` reference (or to an immutable static), which doesn't allow mutation.
fixes: Take a `&mut` reference instead, and ensure the source is `mut`.
For shared mutation, use `Cell`/`RefCell`/atomics.
Make a static `static mut` only with great care, or use a `Mutex`/`OnceLock`.

patterns.match: error\[E0017\]: references in (?:statics|constants) may only refer to immutable values
patterns.title: E0017 — mutable ref in const/static
patterns.diagnosis: A `const` or `static` can't hold a `&mut` reference; their values must be immutable at compile time.
fixes: Use a shared `&` reference in the constant.
Move the mutable state into runtime code (a `Mutex`/`OnceLock`).
Compute the constant as an owned, immutable value.

patterns.match: error\[E0382\]: borrow of partially moved value: `([^`]+)`
patterns.title: E0382 — partially moved value
patterns.diagnosis: Part of `{1}` was moved out (e.g. one field or tuple element), so the whole value can no longer be borrowed or used.
fixes: Borrow the fields you need instead of moving them out.
Clone the moved-out part so the original stays intact.
Destructure with `ref`/`ref mut` to borrow rather than move during a match.
patterns.example_fix: let Foo { ref name, .. } = foo; // borrow, don't move

patterns.match: error\[E0508\]: cannot move out of type `([^`]+)`, a non-copy fixed-size array
patterns.title: E0508 — move out of fixed array
patterns.diagnosis: You're moving one element out of the fixed-size array `{1}`, but non-Copy array elements can't be individually moved.
fixes: Use `&arr[i]` to borrow, or `arr[i].clone()`.
Swap it out with `std::mem::replace(&mut arr[i], default)`.
Use a `Vec` and `.remove(i)`/`.swap_remove(i)` if you need ownership.

patterns.match: error\[E0512\]: cannot transmute between types of different sizes
patterns.title: E0512 — transmute size mismatch
patterns.diagnosis: `std::mem::transmute` requires source and destination types to have identical sizes; here they differ.
fixes: Avoid `transmute` — use safe conversions (`as`, `.to_le_bytes()`, `From`/`Into`).
If you must transmute, ensure both types have the exact same size and layout.
Use a `#[repr(C)]` struct or `bytemuck` for safe reinterpretation.

patterns.match: error\[E0161\]: cannot move a value of type `([^`]+)`: the size of `[^`]+` cannot be statically determined
patterns.title: E0161 — move of unsized value
patterns.diagnosis: `{1}` is unsized (`?Sized`, like `[T]` or `str` or `dyn Trait`), so it can't be moved by value.
fixes: Put it behind a pointer: `Box<{1}>`, `&{1}`, or `Rc<{1}>`.
Work with slices/`&str` rather than owned unsized values.
Box trait objects: `Box<dyn Trait>` instead of `dyn Trait`.

patterns.title: E0533 — bad value in pattern/const context
patterns.diagnosis: An identifier used where a unit struct, unit variant, or constant was expected doesn't actually name one.
fixes: Use the full path to the variant: `Enum::Variant`.
Make sure the constant is in scope and spelled correctly.
If you meant a binding, it must be lowercase or shadow won't apply in patterns.

patterns.match: error\[E0277\]: the size for values of type `([^`]+)` cannot be known at compilation time
patterns.title: E0277 — type is not Sized
patterns.diagnosis: `{1}` is dynamically sized (a slice, `str`, or `dyn Trait`), so it can't be used directly by value where a `Sized` type is required.
fixes: Put it behind a pointer: `&{1}`, `Box<{1}>`, or `Rc<{1}>`.
Add `?Sized` to a generic bound if the function should accept unsized types: `fn f<T: ?Sized>(x: &T)`.
Box trait objects: `Box<dyn Trait>`.

patterns.match: error\[E0746\]: return type cannot have an unboxed trait object
patterns.title: E0746 — unboxed trait object return
patterns.diagnosis: A function tries to return `dyn Trait` by value, which is unsized and not allowed.
fixes: Return `Box<dyn Trait>` for dynamic dispatch.
Return `impl Trait` if there's a single concrete type.
Use an enum if you return one of a few known types.

patterns.match: error\[E0038\]: the trait `([^`]+)` cannot be made into an object
patterns.title: E0038 — trait is not object-safe
patterns.diagnosis: `{1}` can't be used as `dyn {1}` because it isn't object-safe (e.g. it has generic methods, `Self` returns, or associated constants).
fixes: Use generics with a bound (`fn f<T: {1}>`) instead of `dyn {1}`.
Split out the non-object-safe methods into a separate trait.
Add `where Self: Sized` to methods that should be excluded from the object.

patterns.title: E0432 — unresolved import
patterns.diagnosis: Rust can't find `{1}` to import — the path is wrong, the crate isn't a dependency, or the item is private.
fixes: Check the path segments and spelling against the crate's modules.
Add the crate to `Cargo.toml` if it's an external dependency.
Make the target item `pub`, or use `crate::`/`super::`/`self::` correctly.
Run `cargo build` after editing `Cargo.toml` to fetch the crate.

patterns.match: error\[E0433\]: failed to resolve: (?:use of undeclared|could not find) .* `([^`]+)`
patterns.title: E0433 — failed to resolve path
patterns.diagnosis: The path component `{1}` couldn't be resolved — it's an undeclared crate, module, or type.
fixes: `use` the item or write the full path: `crate::module::{1}`.
Add the crate to `Cargo.toml` if it's external.
Check that the module is declared with `mod {1};` and the file exists.

patterns.match: error\[E0412\]: cannot find type `([^`]+)` in this scope
patterns.title: E0412 — type not found
patterns.diagnosis: There's no type named `{1}` in scope. It may be misspelled or need importing.
fixes: `use` the type: `use crate::module::{1};`.
Check spelling and capitalization.
Add `<T>` if you meant a generic parameter you forgot to declare.

patterns.match: error\[E0425\]: cannot find value `([^`]+)` in this scope
patterns.title: E0425 — value not found
patterns.diagnosis: No variable, constant, or function named `{1}` is visible here.
fixes: Check spelling and that `{1}` is defined before use.
Import it if it lives in another module: `use path::{1};`.
If it's a method/field, you may need `self.{1}` or the right receiver.

patterns.title: E0423 — used a type where a value was expected
patterns.diagnosis: You used `{1}` (a struct/enum/module name) where a value or function call belongs.
fixes: Construct it: `{1} { field: ... }` or `{1}(args)` for a tuple struct.
Reference an associated function: `{1}::new(...)`.
Use an enum variant rather than the enum name.

patterns.title: E0603 — item is private
patterns.diagnosis: `{1}` exists but isn't `pub`, so it can't be accessed from outside its module.
fixes: Add `pub` (or `pub(crate)`) to `{1}`'s definition.
Re-export it: `pub use module::{1};`.
Access it only from within the module where it's defined.

patterns.match: error\[E0428\]: the name `([^`]+)` is defined multiple times
patterns.title: E0428 — duplicate definition
patterns.diagnosis: `{1}` is defined more than once in the same scope/module.
fixes: Rename one of the definitions.
Remove the duplicate `fn`/`struct`/`use`.
If both are imports, alias one: `use a::{1} as Other;`.

patterns.match: error\[E0252\]: the name `([^`]+)` is defined multiple times
patterns.title: E0252 — duplicate import
patterns.diagnosis: Two imports both bring `{1}` into scope, which clashes.
fixes: Alias one: `use foo::{1} as Foo1;`.
Remove the redundant `use`.
Import the parent module and qualify the name at the call site.

patterns.match: error\[E0255\]: the name `([^`]+)` is defined multiple times
patterns.title: E0255 — import collides with definition
patterns.diagnosis: An imported name `{1}` collides with a local item of the same name.
fixes: Alias the import: `use path::{1} as Imported;`.
Rename the local item.
Drop the import and use the full path where needed.

patterns.title: E0004 — non-exhaustive match
patterns.diagnosis: A `match` doesn't cover the pattern `{1}`. Every possible value must be handled.
fixes: Add an arm for `{1}`.
Add a catch-all `_ => { ... }` arm.
For `Option`/`Result`, handle both `Some`/`None` or `Ok`/`Err`.

patterns.match: error\[E0005\]: refutable pattern in (?:local binding|function argument)
patterns.title: E0005 — refutable pattern in let
patterns.diagnosis: A `let` (or function argument) used a pattern that can fail to match, but those positions require an always-matching (irrefutable) pattern.
fixes: Use `if let` or `let ... else` to handle the failing case.
Match exhaustively with a full `match`.
Only destructure structs/tuples (always match) directly in `let`.

patterns.match: error\[E0008\]: cannot bind by-move into a pattern guard
patterns.title: E0008 — move binding in match guard
patterns.diagnosis: A pattern with a `if` guard tried to bind a value by move, which isn't allowed because the guard might not match.
fixes: Bind by reference in the pattern (`ref x`) and clone/move inside the arm if needed.
Move the condition check into the arm body instead of the guard.
Restructure so the guard only reads borrowed data.

patterns.match: error\[E0009\]: cannot bind by-move and by-ref in the same pattern
patterns.title: E0009 — mixed move/ref binding
patterns.diagnosis: One pattern mixes a by-move binding with a by-reference binding, which is contradictory.
fixes: Make all bindings consistent — all `ref` or all by-value.
Use `.clone()` to get an owned copy where you need by-value alongside refs.
Split into separate destructuring steps.

patterns.title: E0381 — use of uninitialized variable
patterns.diagnosis: `{1}` was declared but never assigned a value before being used.
fixes: Initialize it at declaration: `let {1} = ...;`.
Ensure every branch assigns `{1}` before it's read.
Give it a default value up front.

patterns.match: error\[E0080\]: (?:evaluation of constant value failed|.* overflow)
patterns.title: E0080 — const evaluation failed
patterns.diagnosis: Evaluating a constant expression failed at compile time (e.g. arithmetic overflow, divide by zero, or out-of-bounds index in a const).
fixes: Fix the const arithmetic so it can't overflow or divide by zero.
Use a wider integer type for the constant.
Move the computation to runtime if it can't be a constant.

patterns.title: E0658 — unstable feature used
patterns.diagnosis: You used a feature that's only available on the nightly compiler behind a feature gate.
fixes: Switch to a stable alternative if one exists.
Use the nightly toolchain (`rustup default nightly`) and add `#![feature(...)]`.
Check the docs for when the feature stabilizes.

patterns.match: error\[E0117\]: only traits defined in the current crate can be implemented for (?:types defined outside of the crate|arbitrary types)
patterns.title: E0117 — orphan rule violation
patterns.diagnosis: You're implementing a foreign trait for a foreign type. The orphan rule requires either the trait or the type to be local to your crate.
fixes: Wrap the foreign type in your own newtype struct and impl on that.
Define your own trait and implement it instead.
Submit the impl upstream to the crate that owns the type or trait.
patterns.example_fix:
struct MyVec(Vec<i32>);
impl SomeTrait for MyVec { /* ... */ }

patterns.title: E0119 — conflicting trait impls
patterns.diagnosis: Two `impl` blocks both apply for trait `{1}` to overlapping types, so the compiler can't choose.
fixes: Remove one of the overlapping impls.
Make the impls disjoint with more specific types or bounds.
If a blanket impl already covers your type, delete the redundant specific one.

patterns.match: error\[E0210\]: type parameter `([^`]+)` must be (?:used as the type parameter for some local type|covered by another type)
patterns.title: E0210 — uncovered type param in impl
patterns.diagnosis: A generic type parameter `{1}` in your trait impl isn't constrained by a local type, which the orphan rule disallows.
fixes: Ensure a local type appears before the uncovered parameter in the impl.
Use a newtype wrapper that's local to your crate.
Constrain `{1}` so it's covered by a local type.

patterns.title: E0201 — duplicate impl item
patterns.diagnosis: An `impl` block defines `{1}` more than once (two methods or associated items with the same name).
fixes: Rename or remove the duplicate definition.
Merge the two definitions if they were meant to be one.
Check for an accidental copy-paste in the impl.

patterns.match: error\[E0046\]: not all trait items implemented, missing: `([^`]+)`
patterns.title: E0046 — missing trait method
patterns.diagnosis: Your `impl` of a trait doesn't define the required item `{1}`.
fixes: Implement `{1}` in the impl block.
If the trait provides a default, make sure your signature matches it exactly.
Copy the method signature from the trait definition and fill in the body.

patterns.match: error\[E0050\]: method `([^`]+)` has (\d+) parameters but the declaration .* has
patterns.title: E0050 — wrong parameter count in impl
patterns.diagnosis: Your impl of method `{1}` has {2} parameters, which doesn't match the trait's declaration.
fixes: Match the trait's exact signature, including `&self`/`&mut self`/`self`.
Add or remove parameters to align with the trait.
Copy the signature straight from the trait.

patterns.match: error\[E0053\]: method `([^`]+)` has an incompatible type for trait
patterns.title: E0053 — incompatible method type
patterns.diagnosis: Your impl of `{1}` has a type that doesn't match the trait's declared signature (parameter or return type differs).
fixes: Make the parameter and return types exactly match the trait.
Watch reference/ownership differences (`&T` vs `T`).
Check associated types are used consistently.

patterns.match: error\[E0407\]: method `([^`]+)` is not a member of trait `([^`]+)`
patterns.title: E0407 — extra method in impl
patterns.diagnosis: Your `impl` of trait `{2}` defines `{1}`, but the trait has no such method.
fixes: Remove `{1}` from the trait impl, or move it to an inherent `impl` block.
Add `{1}` to the trait definition if it belongs there.
Check for a typo in the method name.

patterns.match: error\[E0220\]: associated type `([^`]+)` not found for `([^`]+)`
patterns.title: E0220 — unknown associated type
patterns.diagnosis: `{1}` isn't an associated type of `{2}`.
fixes: Use the correct associated type name (check the trait).
Define `type {1};` in the trait if it should exist.
Drop the `Trait<{1} = ...>` constraint if it's not valid.

patterns.match: error\[E0191\]: the value of the associated type `([^`]+)` .* must be specified
patterns.title: E0191 — associated type not specified
patterns.diagnosis: When using a trait object/bound, the associated type `{1}` must be given concretely.
fixes: Specify it: `dyn Iterator<Item = u8>` or `impl Iterator<Item = u8>`.
Add it to the where-clause: `where I: Iterator<Item = u8>`.
Use a concrete type instead of the bare trait.

patterns.title: E0107 — wrong number of generic args
patterns.diagnosis: The number of generic arguments (type or lifetime) supplied for `{1}` doesn't match its definition.
fixes: Provide exactly as many `<...>` arguments as the definition declares.
Use `_` to let the compiler infer a type argument.
Check whether a lifetime parameter is missing or extra.

patterns.match: error\[E0393\]: the type parameter `([^`]+)` must be explicitly specified
patterns.title: E0393 — default type param must be specified
patterns.diagnosis: `{1}` has a default but the compiler still needs it spelled out in this context.
fixes: Provide the type explicitly: `Trait<{1} = ConcreteType>`.
Avoid relying on the default in a position where inference can't apply it.
Use a fully-qualified path with the type argument.

patterns.title: E0392 — unused type parameter
patterns.diagnosis: The generic parameter `{1}` is declared on a type but never used in any field, so Rust can't determine its variance.
fixes: Use `{1}` in a field, or add `PhantomData<{1}>`.
Remove `{1}` if it's truly unneeded.
Add `std::marker::PhantomData<{1}>` to mark intended ownership/variance.
patterns.example_fix:
use std::marker::PhantomData;
struct Tagged<T> { value: u32, _marker: PhantomData<T> }

patterns.match: error\[E0207\]: the type parameter `([^`]+)` is not constrained by the impl trait, self type, or predicates
patterns.title: E0207 — unconstrained impl type param
patterns.diagnosis: Generic parameter `{1}` on an `impl` isn't used in the trait, the self type, or any bound, so it's unconstrained.
fixes: Use `{1}` in the implemented type or the trait reference.
Move `{1}` onto a method instead of the impl if only a method needs it.
Constrain it with an associated type or where-clause.

patterns.title: E0275 — recursive trait bound overflow
patterns.diagnosis: Resolving the bound `{1}` recurses without end (often a type that references itself through a trait).
fixes: Break the recursion by boxing: `Box<dyn Trait>` or `Box<T>`.
Add an explicit, simpler bound to stop the recursion.
Restructure recursive types so they terminate.

patterns.match: error\[E0276\]: impl has stricter requirements than trait
patterns.title: E0276 — impl bound stricter than trait
patterns.diagnosis: Your trait impl adds a where-clause the trait didn't declare, which isn't allowed.
fixes: Remove the extra bound from the impl.
Add the bound to the trait definition if every impl needs it.
Make the trait method itself carry the bound (`where Self: ...`).

patterns.title: E0271 — associated type mismatch
patterns.diagnosis: An associated type didn't resolve to the expected type while satisfying `{1}` (e.g. `Iterator::Item` is the wrong type).
fixes: Adjust the iterator/closure so the associated type matches (map/convert items).
Pin the associated type explicitly: `Iterator<Item = ExpectedType>`.
Convert values with `.map(|x| x.into())` to align item types.

patterns.title: E0599 — not an iterator
patterns.diagnosis: You called an iterator method on `{1}`, but it doesn't implement `Iterator` (or `IntoIterator`).
fixes: Call `.iter()` / `.into_iter()` / `.chars()` first to get an iterator.
For a `HashMap`, iterate with `.iter()` or `.values()`.
Implement `Iterator` for `{1}` if it should be iterable.

patterns.title: E0013 — const refers to static
patterns.diagnosis: A `const` can't reference a `static`, because constants are inlined and statics have a fixed memory location.
fixes: Make both `const`, or both `static`, as appropriate.
Read the static at runtime instead of in a constant.
Use a `const fn` or literal value for the constant.

patterns.match: error\[E0015\]: cannot call non-const (?:fn|function) `([^`]+)` in (?:constants|statics|constant functions)
patterns.title: E0015 — non-const fn in const context
patterns.diagnosis: `{1}` isn't a `const fn`, so it can't be called while evaluating a constant.
fixes: Compute the value at runtime instead of in a `const`/`static`.
Use a `const fn` alternative if one exists.
Initialize lazily with `OnceLock`/`LazyLock` at first use.

patterns.match: error\[E0493\]: destructor of `([^`]+)` cannot be evaluated at compile-time
patterns.title: E0493 — Drop type in const
patterns.diagnosis: A constant holds `{1}`, which has a destructor (`Drop`), and destructors can't run during const evaluation.
fixes: Don't store `Drop` types in `const`; use a runtime binding.
Use a type without a custom `Drop` for the constant.
Initialize lazily at runtime.

patterns.match: error\[E0010\]: allocations are not allowed in (?:constants|statics)
patterns.title: E0010 — allocation in const
patterns.diagnosis: Heap allocation (e.g. building a `Vec` or `Box`) isn't permitted inside a `const`/`static` initializer.
fixes: Use a fixed-size array or `&'static [T]` literal instead of `Vec`.
Move the allocation to runtime.
Use `LazyLock`/`OnceLock` to build the heap value on first access.

patterns.match: error\[E0525\]: expected a closure that implements the `([^`]+)` trait
patterns.title: E0525 — closure doesn't meet Fn bound
patterns.diagnosis: The closure captures its environment in a way that only satisfies a weaker trait than `{1}` (e.g. it's `FnMut`/`FnOnce` where `Fn` is needed).
fixes: Avoid mutating or moving captures if `Fn` is required — read by shared reference.
Change the bound to `FnMut`/`FnOnce` if mutation/consumption is intended.
Clone captured values inside the closure instead of mutating outer state.

patterns.match: error\[E0373\]: closure may outlive the current function, but it borrows `([^`]+)`
patterns.title: E0373 — closure outlives borrowed capture
patterns.diagnosis: A closure borrows `{1}` from the enclosing function but may outlive it (returned or sent to a thread), which would dangle.
fixes: Add `move` so the closure takes ownership of `{1}`.
Clone `{1}` and move the clone in.
Ensure the closure doesn't escape the function's scope.

patterns.match: error\[E0524\]: two closures require unique access to `([^`]+)` at the same time
patterns.title: E0524 — two closures need same capture
patterns.diagnosis: Two closures each need unique (mutable) access to `{1}`, but both are alive at once.
fixes: Use the closures one at a time so their captures don't overlap.
Capture by shared reference if reading is enough.
Use a `RefCell`/`Cell` for controlled interior mutability.

patterns.match: error\[E0434\]: can't capture dynamic environment in a fn item
patterns.title: E0434 — fn item can't capture
patterns.diagnosis: A regular `fn` (defined with `fn name`) tried to use an outer variable. Only closures can capture environment.
fixes: Turn the `fn` into a closure: `let f = |x| outer + x;`.
Pass the needed value in as a parameter.
Make the value a `const`/`static` if it's compile-time constant.

patterns.match: error\[E0626\]: borrow may still be in use when (?:generator|coroutine) yields
patterns.title: E0626 — borrow across yield
patterns.diagnosis: A borrow is held across a `yield`/await point in a generator/async block, which isn't allowed because the reference might not survive the suspension.
fixes: Limit the borrow's scope so it ends before the yield/await.
Copy/clone the needed value before yielding.
Restructure so borrows don't span suspension points.

patterns.match: error\[E0728\]: `await` is only allowed inside `async` functions and blocks
patterns.title: E0728 — await outside async
patterns.diagnosis: You used `.await` in a non-async context. `await` only works inside `async fn` or an `async {}` block.
fixes: Make the enclosing function `async fn`.
Wrap the code in an `async { ... }` block.
Block on the future with an executor (`block_on`) if you're in sync code.

patterns.match: error\[E0733\]: recursion in an `async fn` requires boxing
patterns.title: E0733 — recursive async fn
patterns.diagnosis: An `async fn` calls itself, producing an infinitely-sized future. Recursion needs an indirection.
fixes: Return `Pin<Box<dyn Future<Output = T>>>` and box the recursive call.
Use the `async-recursion` crate's `#[async_recursion]` attribute.
Rewrite the recursion as a loop if possible.

patterns.match: error: future cannot be sent between threads safely
patterns.title: Async future is not Send
patterns.diagnosis: A future holds a non-`Send` value (often across an await point, like a `Rc` or `MutexGuard`), so it can't run on a multi-threaded executor.
fixes: Drop non-Send values before the next `.await`.
Use `Arc`/`tokio::sync::Mutex` instead of `Rc`/`std::sync::MutexGuard` across awaits.
Scope the guard in a block that ends before awaiting.

patterns.title: E0277 — value is not a Future
patterns.diagnosis: You `.await`ed `{1}`, but it doesn't implement `Future`.
fixes: Only `.await` values returned by `async fn`/`async {}` or futures.
If it returns a `Result<Future>`, await after unwrapping.
Remove `.await` from a plain (non-future) value.

patterns.match: error\[E0072\]: recursive type `([^`]+)` has infinite size
patterns.title: E0072 — infinitely sized type
patterns.diagnosis: `{1}` contains itself directly, so its size would be infinite.
fixes: Box the recursive field: `Box<{1}>` (or `Rc`/`Vec`).
Use indirection for linked structures (`Option<Box<Node>>`).
Store children in a `Vec<{1}>` instead of an inline field.
patterns.example_fix: struct Node { value: i32, next: Option<Box<Node>> }

patterns.match: error\[E0133\]: (?:call to unsafe function|use of .*) (?:is|requires) unsafe
patterns.title: E0133 — unsafe operation outside unsafe
patterns.diagnosis: You performed an `unsafe` operation (raw pointer deref, unsafe fn call, etc.) outside an `unsafe` block.
fixes: Wrap it in `unsafe { ... }` only after verifying the safety invariants.
Prefer a safe API if one exists.
Mark the enclosing function `unsafe fn` if it must expose unsafe behavior.

patterns.match: error\[E0408\]: variable `([^`]+)` is not bound in all patterns
patterns.title: E0408 — binding missing in or-pattern
patterns.diagnosis: In an or-pattern (`A | B`), `{1}` is bound in some alternatives but not all. Every alternative must bind the same names.
fixes: Bind `{1}` in every alternative of the or-pattern.
Split into separate match arms if the alternatives differ.
Remove `{1}` from the arm body if it isn't always available.

patterns.match: error\[E0411\]: cannot find type `Self`|the `Self` (?:type|constructor) is only allowed in
patterns.title: Self used outside impl/trait
patterns.diagnosis: `Self` was used outside an `impl` block or trait, where it has no meaning.
fixes: Use the concrete type name instead of `Self`.
Move the code into an `impl` block if it's meant to be a method.
Inside trait definitions, `Self` is fine — check you're actually there.

patterns.title: E0463 — crate not found
patterns.diagnosis: The compiler can't find the crate `{1}` — it's not declared as a dependency or not installed.
fixes: Add `{1}` to `[dependencies]` in `Cargo.toml` and run `cargo build`.
Check the crate name spelling (hyphens vs underscores).
For workspace crates, ensure the path/member is configured.

patterns.match: error\[E0405\]: cannot find trait `([^`]+)` in this scope
patterns.title: E0405 — trait not found
patterns.diagnosis: No trait named `{1}` is in scope.
fixes: `use` the trait: `use path::{1};`.
Check spelling and that the trait is `pub`.
Add the defining crate to `Cargo.toml` if external.

patterns.title: E0573 — expected a type
patterns.diagnosis: `{1}` is a value/variant/method, but a type was expected here.
fixes: Use the enclosing type name, not a variant: `MyEnum`, not `MyEnum::Variant`.
Check you didn't put a value where a type annotation goes.
For associated types, write the full `<Type as Trait>::Assoc` path.

patterns.match: error\[E0061\]: this function takes (\d+) arguments? but (\d+) arguments? (?:was|were) supplied
patterns.title: E0061 — wrong number of arguments
patterns.diagnosis: The function expects {1} arguments but you passed {2}.
fixes: Pass exactly {1} arguments in the right order.
Check whether a `self`/receiver is being counted.
Look at the function signature for defaults or tuples you may have collapsed.

patterns.match: error\[E0026\]: (?:struct|variant) `([^`]+)` does not have (?:a field|fields) named `([^`]+)`
patterns.title: E0026 — unknown field in pattern
patterns.diagnosis: While destructuring `{1}`, you referenced field `{2}`, which doesn't exist.
fixes: Check the field name against the struct definition.
Use `..` to ignore the rest of the fields.
Fix the typo or remove the nonexistent field.

patterns.match: error\[E0027\]: pattern does not mention field `([^`]+)`
patterns.title: E0027 — pattern missing field
patterns.diagnosis: A struct pattern didn't mention field `{1}`. Struct patterns must cover all fields unless you use `..`.
fixes: Add `{1}` to the pattern, or `{1}: _` to ignore it.
End the pattern with `..` to ignore remaining fields.
Match all fields explicitly.

patterns.match: error\[E0063\]: missing field `([^`]+)` in initializer of `([^`]+)`
patterns.title: E0063 — missing field in struct literal
patterns.diagnosis: Constructing `{2}` left out the required field `{1}`.
fixes: Provide a value for `{1}` in the struct literal.
Use `..Default::default()` to fill the rest if the type derives `Default`.
Add a constructor (`{2}::new`) that sets all fields.

patterns.title: E0560 — unknown field in struct literal
patterns.diagnosis: When building `{1}`, you set field `{2}`, which the struct doesn't have.
fixes: Check the field name against the definition.
Remove or rename `{2}`.
Make sure you're constructing the right struct.

patterns.match: error\[E0759\]: cannot return value referencing (?:local variable|temporary value) `([^`]+)`
patterns.title: E0759 — return references local
patterns.diagnosis: The returned value borrows `{1}`, a local that's dropped when the function ends, so the reference would dangle.
fixes: Return an owned value (e.g. `String` instead of `&str`).
Take the data as a parameter so its lifetime extends past the function.
Move ownership out instead of returning a reference.

patterns.match: error\[E0515\]: cannot return (?:value|reference) referencing (?:local variable|temporary value) `([^`]+)`
patterns.title: E0515 — return reference to local
patterns.diagnosis: You're returning a reference tied to local `{1}`, which is destroyed at function exit — the reference would dangle.
fixes: Return owned data instead of a reference.
Borrow from an input parameter (whose lifetime outlives the call).
Allocate the data on the heap and return ownership (`Box`/`String`/`Vec`).
patterns.example_fix: fn first(v: &Vec<i32>) -> &i32 { &v[0] } // borrows the param, not a local

patterns.match: error\[E0716\]: temporary value dropped while borrowed
patterns.title: E0716 — temporary dropped while borrowed
patterns.diagnosis: You borrowed a temporary value, but the temporary is freed at the end of the statement while the borrow tries to live on.
fixes: Bind the temporary to a `let` so it lives long enough: `let tmp = make(); let r = &tmp;`.
Avoid taking a reference to the result of a chained expression that produces a temporary.
Return/store owned data instead of a borrow of a temporary.
patterns.example_fix:
let s = format!("{}", n);
let r = &s; // s lives long enough now

patterns.match: error\[E0597\]: `([^`]+)` does not live long enough
patterns.title: E0597 — value doesn't live long enough
patterns.diagnosis: `{1}` is dropped while a reference to it is still needed — the borrow outlives the data.
fixes: Move `{1}`'s declaration to an outer scope so it outlives the borrow.
Store owned data instead of borrowing `{1}`.
Shorten the lifetime of the borrow so it ends before `{1}` is dropped.

patterns.match: error\[E0712\]: thread-local variable borrowed past end of function
patterns.title: E0712 — thread-local borrow escapes
patterns.diagnosis: A reference to a thread-local was returned or kept past the function, but thread-locals can't be borrowed beyond the access scope.
fixes: Copy/clone the value out of the thread-local instead of borrowing it.
Do all work with the thread-local inside the `with` closure.
Return owned data, not a reference into the thread-local.

patterns.title: E0767 — unreachable loop label
patterns.diagnosis: The label `{1}` referenced by `break`/`continue` isn't on an enclosing loop in scope.
fixes: Make sure the label is declared on a loop that encloses the `break`/`continue`.
Check label spelling (`'outer:`).
Move the labeled loop so it contains the jump.

patterns.match: error\[E0571\]: `break` with value from a `([^`]+)` loop
patterns.title: E0571 — break with value from while/for
patterns.diagnosis: You used `break value`, but only `loop` can produce a value with `break`; `{1}` loops cannot.
fixes: Use `loop { ... break value; }` if you need a value.
Set an outer variable inside the loop and use it afterward.
Restructure to return from a function instead of breaking with a value.

patterns.title: E0267 — break outside a loop
patterns.diagnosis: `break` was used where there's no loop to break out of (e.g. inside a closure or const).
fixes: Only use `break` inside `loop`/`while`/`for`.
From a closure, use `return` instead of `break`.
Restructure the control flow.

patterns.title: E0268 — continue outside a loop
patterns.diagnosis: `continue` was used where there's no enclosing loop.
fixes: Only use `continue` inside a loop body.
Inside closures, restructure to skip iterations differently.
Check you didn't put it in a const/static context.

patterns.match: error\[E0070\]: invalid left-hand side of assignment
patterns.title: E0070 — invalid assignment target
patterns.diagnosis: The left side of `=` isn't a place you can assign to (it's an expression, function call, or literal).
fixes: Assign to a variable, field, or index — not a function result or literal.
Did you mean `==` for comparison?
Bind the value first, then assign to that binding.

patterns.title: E0308 — if/else type mismatch
patterns.diagnosis: The `if` and `else` branches of an expression produce different types, so the overall `if` has no single type.
fixes: Make both branches return the same type.
Convert one branch (`.to_string()`, `as`, etc.) to match the other.
If one branch shouldn't yield a value, end it with `;` or use a statement `if`.

patterns.title: E0308 — match arms type mismatch
patterns.diagnosis: Different arms of a `match` produce different types, so the `match` expression has no consistent type.
fixes: Make every arm return the same type.
Convert arm results so they unify (e.g. all `String`).
Use the match as a statement (with `;`) if the value isn't needed.

patterns.match: error\[E0658\]: let expressions in this position are unstable
patterns.title: E0658 — let-chains unstable
patterns.diagnosis: `if let ... && ...` chains (let-chains) aren't stable on the current toolchain.
fixes: Nest the conditions: `if let Some(x) = a { if cond { ... } }`.
Use a `match` to combine the bindings.
Switch to nightly with the feature gate if you must use let-chains.

patterns.match: error\[E0759\]: cannot infer an appropriate lifetime
patterns.title: Cannot infer lifetime
patterns.diagnosis: The compiler couldn't work out the lifetime relationship for a reference and needs guidance.
fixes: Add explicit lifetime parameters tying inputs to outputs.
Return owned data to avoid lifetime inference.
Use `'_` to capture an elided lifetime where appropriate.

patterns.match: error\[E0277\]: a value of type `([^`]+)` cannot be built from an iterator over elements of type `([^`]+)`
patterns.title: E0277 — collect target mismatch
patterns.diagnosis: `.collect()` can't build `{1}` from items of type `{2}`.
fixes: Use a turbofish matching the item type: `.collect::<Vec<{2}>>()`.
For `Result`/`Option`, collect into `Result<Vec<_>, _>` to short-circuit.
Map items into the element type the target collection expects first.

patterns.match: error\[E0599\]: no function or associated item named `([^`]+)` found for (?:type|struct|enum) `([^`]+)`
patterns.title: E0599 — no such associated function
patterns.diagnosis: There's no associated function/constructor `{1}` on `{2}` (e.g. you called `{2}::{1}()` and it doesn't exist).
fixes: Check the constructor name (often `new`, `from`, `with_capacity`).
If it comes from a trait, import the trait into scope.
Verify the type actually defines `{1}`.

patterns.title: E0223 — ambiguous associated type
patterns.diagnosis: An associated type path is ambiguous because the compiler can't tell which trait it belongs to.
fixes: Use fully-qualified syntax: `<Type as Trait>::Assoc`.
Bring only one defining trait into scope.
Annotate the type more specifically.

patterns.title: E0277 — type doesn't implement Display
patterns.diagnosis: `{1}` can't be printed with `{}` because it doesn't implement `Display`.
fixes: Use `{:?}` with `#[derive(Debug)]` for debugging output.
Implement `std::fmt::Display` for `{1}` for user-facing output.
Print a field that is `Display`able instead of the whole value.

patterns.title: E0277 — type doesn't implement Debug
patterns.diagnosis: `{1}` can't be formatted with `{:?}` because it doesn't implement `Debug`.
fixes: Add `#[derive(Debug)]` to `{1}`.
Ensure all fields of `{1}` are also `Debug`.
Implement `std::fmt::Debug` manually if deriving isn't possible.
patterns.example_fix:
#[derive(Debug)]
struct Point { x: i32, y: i32 }

patterns.match: error\[E0599\]: the method `clone` exists .* but .* `([^`]+)` .* does not implement `Clone`
patterns.title: E0599 — type doesn't implement Clone
patterns.diagnosis: `.clone()` was called but `{1}` (or a field of it) doesn't implement `Clone`.
fixes: Add `#[derive(Clone)]` to the type.
Make sure every field is also `Clone`.
Wrap shared data in `Rc`/`Arc` to make cloning cheap and possible.

patterns.match: error\[E0689\]: can't call method `([^`]+)` on ambiguous numeric type `([^`]+)`
patterns.title: E0689 — ambiguous numeric type
patterns.diagnosis: Calling `{1}` on `{2}` is ambiguous because the exact numeric type isn't pinned down yet.
fixes: Annotate the literal/type: `let x: f64 = 2.0; x.{1}()`.
Add a suffix to the literal: `2.0f64`, `5i32`.
Use a turbofish or explicit cast to fix the type.

patterns.match: error\[E0658\]: `impl Trait` in (?:type aliases|associated types) is unstable
patterns.title: E0658 — impl Trait in alias unstable
patterns.diagnosis: Using `impl Trait` in a type alias or associated type isn't stable yet.
fixes: Name the concrete type instead of `impl Trait` in the alias.
Box the value: `Box<dyn Trait>`.
Use nightly with the `type_alias_impl_trait` feature if you must.

patterns.title: E0594 — assign to field of immutable value
patterns.diagnosis: You're assigning to field `{1}` of `{2}`, but `{2}` isn't mutable, so its fields can't change.
fixes: Declare the owner mutable: `let mut {2} = ...;`.
If `{2}` is behind `&`, take `&mut` instead.
Use `Cell`/`RefCell` for interior mutability if you can't add `mut`.

patterns.match: error\[E0512\]: cannot transmute_copy between types of different sizes
patterns.title: E0512 — transmute_copy size mismatch
patterns.diagnosis: `transmute_copy` between differently-sized types is rejected because it would read uninitialized or out-of-bounds memory.
fixes: Use safe conversions instead of `transmute_copy`.
Match the sizes exactly, or read only the bytes you need.
Reach for `bytemuck`/`zerocopy` for safe reinterpretation.

patterns.match: error\[E0277\]: the trait bound `([^`]+): Sized` is not satisfied
patterns.title: E0277 — type not Sized for this use
patterns.diagnosis: `{1}` is unsized but used in a position that requires a known size.
fixes: Add `?Sized` to the generic bound if accepting unsized types: `T: ?Sized`.
Box or reference the value: `Box<{1}>`, `&{1}`.
Use a slice or trait object behind a pointer.

patterns.match: error\[E0793\]: reference to packed field is unaligned
patterns.title: E0793 — reference to packed field
patterns.diagnosis: Taking a reference into a `#[repr(packed)]` struct can produce an unaligned pointer, which is undefined behavior.
fixes: Copy the field into a local first, then reference the local.
Use `std::ptr::addr_of!` to get a raw pointer without an intermediate reference.
Avoid `repr(packed)` if you need ordinary references to fields.
patterns.example_fix: let v = packed.field; // copy out, then use v

patterns.match: error\[E0512\]: lang item required, but not found: `([^`]+)`
patterns.title: Missing lang item
patterns.diagnosis: A core language item `{1}` is missing — common in `#![no_std]` builds without the right setup.
fixes: Provide the required lang item or include the crate that defines it.
Link `alloc`/`std` if you didn't mean to be `no_std`.
Check your `no_std` boilerplate (panic handler, allocator).

patterns.title: E0152 — duplicate lang item
patterns.diagnosis: Two definitions of the lang item `{1}` exist — usually `std` is linked alongside a `no_std` crate that also defines it.
fixes: Make the build consistently `no_std` or consistently use `std`.
Remove the duplicate lang-item definition.
Check for conflicting versions of `core`/`alloc` in the dependency tree.

patterns.match: error\[E0521\]: borrowed data escapes outside of (?:closure|method|function)
patterns.title: E0521 — borrowed data escapes
patterns.diagnosis: A reference is being moved somewhere (a closure, thread, or returned value) that outlives the data it borrows.
fixes: Use `move` and pass owned/cloned data instead of a borrow.
Ensure the borrowed data outlives where the reference ends up.
Restructure so the reference doesn't escape its valid scope.

patterns.match: error\[E0712\]: thread-local variable `([^`]+)` accessed during(?: or after)? destruction
patterns.title: Thread-local accessed during shutdown
patterns.diagnosis: Thread-local `{1}` was accessed while it was being destroyed at thread exit.
fixes: Use `try_with` and handle the `AccessError`.
Avoid touching thread-locals from `Drop` impls.
Cache the value earlier in the thread's life.

patterns.match: error\[E0382\]: use of moved value: `([^`]+)`(?:.*in (?:previous|each) iteration of loop)
patterns.title: E0382 — value moved in a loop
patterns.diagnosis: `{1}` is moved inside a loop body, so the second iteration finds it already gone.
fixes: Clone `{1}` inside the loop if each iteration needs its own copy.
Borrow `{1}` instead of moving it.
Move ownership creation inside the loop so a fresh value exists each pass.

patterns.match: error\[E0277\]: `\?` couldn't convert the error to `([^`]+)`
patterns.title: E0277 — ? can't convert error type
patterns.diagnosis: The `?` operator tried to convert the inner error into `{1}`, but no `From` impl exists for that conversion.
fixes: Add a `From<InnerError> for {1}` impl.
Use `.map_err(|e| ...)` to convert the error before `?`.
Use `Box<dyn std::error::Error>` or `anyhow::Error` as a catch-all error type.

patterns.match: error\[E0277\]: the `\?` operator can only be used (?:on|in) (?:a function|.*) that returns `Result` or `Option`
patterns.title: E0277 — ? in wrong return type
patterns.diagnosis: `?` was used in a function whose return type isn't `Result`, `Option`, or another `Try` type.
fixes: Change the function to return `Result<T, E>` or `Option<T>`.
In `main`, use `fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>>`.
Handle the value with `match`/`if let` instead of `?`.
patterns.example_fix: fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> { /* ... ? ... */ Ok(()) }

patterns.match: error\[E0759\]?: returns a value referencing data owned by the current function
patterns.title: Returns reference to function-local data
patterns.diagnosis: The returned value borrows data created inside the function, which is freed when the function returns.
fixes: Return owned data (`String`, `Vec`, `Box`) instead of a reference.
Borrow from a parameter so the data outlives the call.
Use an out-parameter or pass a buffer in.

patterns.match: error\[E0308\]: arguments to this (?:function|method) are incorrect
patterns.title: E0308 — wrong argument types
patterns.diagnosis: One or more arguments don't match the function's expected parameter types. The notes point at which argument.
fixes: Convert the offending argument (`&x`, `x.into()`, `x as T`).
Match reference vs value (`&T` vs `T`).
Check argument order — types may be swapped.

patterns.match: error\[E0533\]: expected value, found struct variant `([^`]+)`
patterns.title: E0533 — struct variant used as value
patterns.diagnosis: `{1}` is a struct-style enum variant, so it can't be used as a bare value; it needs its fields.
fixes: Construct it with fields: `Enum::{1} { field: ... }`.
Match it in a pattern with braces: `Enum::{1} { field } => ...`.
Use a unit or tuple variant if you wanted a value-like form.

patterns.match: error\[E0506\]: cannot assign to `\*([^`]+)` because it is borrowed
patterns.title: E0506 — assign through borrowed pointer
patterns.diagnosis: Assigning through `*{1}` is blocked because `{1}` (or its target) is borrowed elsewhere.
fixes: End the conflicting borrow before assigning.
Read what you need first, then mutate.
Use `RefCell` if you need controlled aliasing with mutation.

patterns.match: error\[E0617\]: can't pass `([^`]+)` to variadic function
patterns.title: E0617 — bad type for variadic (FFI)
patterns.diagnosis: Passing `{1}` to a C variadic function (`...`) isn't allowed; only specific C-compatible types are permitted.
fixes: Cast to a C-compatible type (`c_int`, `c_double`, pointers).
Promote small integers to `c_int` and `f32` to `f64`.
Pass a pointer for strings: `c_str.as_ptr()`.

patterns.match: error\[E0445\]: (?:private trait|crate-private trait) `([^`]+)` in public interface
patterns.title: E0445 — private trait in public API
patterns.diagnosis: A public item exposes the private trait `{1}` in its signature, leaking a private type into the public API.
fixes: Make `{1}` `pub` (or `pub(crate)` matching the item's visibility).
Reduce the item's visibility to match the trait.
Hide the trait behind a public wrapper.

patterns.match: error\[E0446\]: private type `([^`]+)` in public interface
patterns.title: E0446 — private type in public API
patterns.diagnosis: A public function/struct exposes the private type `{1}`, which would leak it to callers who can't name it.
fixes: Make `{1}` `pub`.
Lower the visibility of the exposing item.
Return a public type or a boxed trait object instead.

patterns.title: E0451 — private field in struct literal
patterns.diagnosis: You tried to set the private field `{1}` of `{2}` from outside its module.
fixes: Use a public constructor like `{2}::new(...)`.
Make `{1}` `pub` if it should be settable directly.
Provide a builder or setter method.

patterns.title: Unused variable
patterns.diagnosis: Go refuses to build because the variable {1} was created but never read anywhere. Go treats unused locals as errors, not warnings.
fixes: Use {1} somewhere, or delete the line that declares it
If you need the value but not the name, assign to the blank identifier: _ = {1}
Comment out the declaration while you figure out the rest

patterns.title: Unused import
patterns.diagnosis: You imported the package {1} but never used anything from it. Go won't compile with dangling imports.
fixes: Remove the import line for {1}
If you imported it only for side effects, use a blank import: import _ "{1}"
Run `goimports` to clean imports automatically

patterns.title: Undefined name
patterns.diagnosis: The compiler can't find anything named {1} in scope. It may be misspelled, unexported, or its package isn't imported.
fixes: Check the spelling and capitalization of {1}
If {1} lives in another package, import that package and qualify it
If {1} is from the same package, make sure that file is in the build

patterns.match: missing return(?: at end of function)?
patterns.title: Missing return
patterns.diagnosis: A function that promises to return a value has a path that falls off the end without returning anything.
fixes: Add a return statement at the end of the function
Make sure every if/else branch returns or that there's a final fallthrough return
If a loop is meant to always return, add a return or panic after it

patterns.title: Type mismatch
patterns.diagnosis: You passed a value of type {2} where Go expected {3}. Go does not auto-convert between these types.
fixes: Convert explicitly: {3}(yourValue) if the conversion is allowed
Fix the variable so it's already the right type
Check that you didn't swap two arguments
patterns.example_fix:
var n int = 5
var f float64 = float64(n)

patterns.match: too many arguments(?: in call)? to (\w+)
patterns.title: Too many arguments
patterns.diagnosis: You gave the function {1} more arguments than its signature accepts.
fixes: Check {1}'s definition and remove the extra argument
Make sure you didn't accidentally pass the same thing twice
If {1} takes a slice, pass one slice instead of many values
patterns.example_fix:
// def: func greet(name string)
greet("Sam") // not greet("Sam", "extra")

patterns.match: not enough arguments(?: in call)? to (\w+)
patterns.title: Not enough arguments
patterns.diagnosis: The function {1} needs more arguments than you provided.
fixes: Look at {1}'s signature and supply every required parameter
If the last param is variadic, you can pass zero, but earlier params are required
Pass zero values explicitly if you don't have real ones yet
patterns.example_fix:
// def: func add(a, b int) int
sum := add(2, 3)

patterns.title: Code outside a function
patterns.diagnosis: You put a statement (like an assignment or a function call) at the top level of the file, where only declarations are allowed.
fixes: Move the statement inside func main() or another function
At package level you can only use var, const, type, func, and import
Use var x = ... at package level instead of x := ...
patterns.example_fix:
var greeting = "hi" // ok at top level
func main() { fmt.Println(greeting) }

patterns.title: Unexpected token
patterns.diagnosis: The parser found {1} but expected {2}. Usually a typo, a missing brace, or a stray symbol nearby.
fixes: Look just before the reported spot for a missing comma, brace, or paren
Check that every { has a matching }
Run `gofmt` — it often points to the real spot

patterns.title: Expected a declaration
patterns.diagnosis: At the top of the file Go expected a declaration but saw {1}. Often a function or variable written outside any function.
fixes: Wrap loose statements in a func
Make sure the file starts with `package name`
Check for a missing closing brace above that leaked top-level code
patterns.example_fix:
package main
func main() { /* code here */ }

patterns.title: Missing semicolon/newline
patterns.diagnosis: Go auto-inserts semicolons at line ends, and it expected one before {1}. Usually two statements share a line, or a brace is misplaced.
fixes: Put each statement on its own line
Don't put an opening brace on its own line in Go (it must follow the statement)
Check for a missing operator between two tokens

patterns.title: Mismatched types in operation
patterns.diagnosis: You tried to combine a {2} and a {3} in one operation, but Go won't mix these types.
fixes: Convert one side so both are the same type
For numbers, wrap one in float64(...) or int(...)
Check you didn't compare a string to a number

patterns.title: Illegal conversion
patterns.diagnosis: Go can't convert a {2} into a {3}; these types aren't convertible to each other.
fixes: For numbers and strings of runes, conversion works; for unrelated types it doesn't
To turn a number into text use strconv.Itoa or fmt.Sprintf, not a cast
To parse text into a number use strconv.Atoi

patterns.title: Variable redeclared
patterns.diagnosis: You declared {1} twice in the same block. Go allows := to reuse a name only if at least one new variable joins it.
fixes: Use = instead of := for the second assignment
Rename one of the two {1} variables
Combine the two declarations into one

patterns.match: no new variables on left side of :=
patterns.title: No new variables with :=
patterns.diagnosis: Every name on the left of := already exists, so := has nothing new to declare.
fixes: Switch := to = for a plain assignment
Introduce at least one genuinely new variable on the left
Check you didn't repeat a := that was meant once

patterns.match: assignment mismatch: (\d+) variables? but .*? returns (\d+) values?
patterns.title: Assignment count mismatch
patterns.diagnosis: You tried to assign to {1} variables, but the right side gives {2} values. The counts must match.
fixes: Add or remove variables on the left to match {2}
Use the blank identifier _ to drop values you don't need
Many Go funcs return (value, error) — capture both
patterns.example_fix:
v, err := strconv.Atoi(s)
if err != nil { /* handle */ }

patterns.title: Multi-value in single-value spot
patterns.diagnosis: The call {1} returns more than one value, but you used it where only one fits.
fixes: Assign all results: a, b := {1}
Use the blank identifier for the ones you ignore
Don't nest a multi-return call inside another call argument

patterns.match: (\w+)\.(\w+) undefined \(type (\S+) has no field or method (\w+)\)
patterns.title: No such field or method
patterns.diagnosis: You accessed {1}.{2}, but type {3} has no field or method named {4}. Maybe a typo or an unexported member.
fixes: Check the spelling and capitalization of {4}
Confirm {4} is exported (capitalized) if it's in another package
Look at the struct/interface definition to see what's actually there

patterns.title: Can't range over this
patterns.diagnosis: You used `for range` on a {2}, but range only works over arrays, slices, maps, strings, channels, and (in Go 1.22+) ints/functions.
fixes: Make sure the value is a slice, map, string, array, or channel
If it's a pointer to an array, dereference it first
If it's a struct, range over one of its slice/map fields
patterns.example_fix: for i, v := range mySlice { _ = i; _ = v }

patterns.title: Assigning to map value field
patterns.diagnosis: You tried to modify a field of a struct stored directly in a map ({1}). Map values aren't addressable, so you can't change part of one in place.
fixes: Pull the value out, change it, then put it back
Store pointers in the map instead of structs
m[k] = newWholeStruct{...}

patterns.title: Can't take address
patterns.diagnosis: You used & on {1}, which isn't addressable — like a map element, a literal, or a function result.
fixes: Store the value in a variable first, then take that variable's address
Don't take the address of map[key]; copy it out first
Constants and literals can't be addressed directly

patterns.match: index out of range \[(-?\d+)\] with length (\d+)
patterns.title: Index out of range
patterns.diagnosis: You read or wrote index {1} of a slice/array whose length is {2}. Valid indexes are 0 through {2}-1.
fixes: Check the index is >= 0 and < len(slice)
Use len() in your loop condition: for i < len(s)
If the slice might be empty, guard with if len(s) > 0

patterns.match: slice bounds out of range \[:?(\d+):?\] with (?:capacity|length) (\d+)
patterns.title: Slice bounds out of range
patterns.diagnosis: A slice expression asked for index {1}, past the slice's size {2}. Low and high bounds must stay within len/cap.
fixes: Make sure high bound <= len(slice) (or cap for three-index slices)
Clamp the bound: end := min(want, len(s))
Check off-by-one math in your slicing

patterns.match: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference
patterns.title: Nil pointer dereference
patterns.diagnosis: Your program followed a pointer that was nil — reading or writing through a value that was never set.
fixes: Check the pointer/struct isn't nil before using it
Initialize the value before dereferencing: x := &T{} or make(...)
If a function returns (ptr, err), check err before using ptr

patterns.match: assignment to entry in nil map
patterns.title: Write to nil map
patterns.diagnosis: You tried to add a key to a map that was declared but never made, so it's nil. Reading a nil map is fine; writing panics.
fixes: Create the map with make before writing: m := make(map[K]V)
Use a map literal: m := map[K]V{}
If it's a struct field, initialize it in the constructor

patterns.title: Bad type assertion
patterns.diagnosis: You asserted an interface value held a {2}, but it actually held a {1}, so the assertion panicked.
fixes: Use the two-result form to check first: v, ok := x.({2})
Switch on the real type with a type switch
Assert to the type the value actually is ({1})
patterns.example_fix: if v, ok := x.(string); ok { use(v) }

patterns.match: interface conversion: (\S+) is not (\S+): missing method (\w+)
patterns.title: Type doesn't satisfy interface
patterns.diagnosis: A value of type {1} was asserted to interface {2}, but {1} doesn't implement {3}, so it doesn't satisfy {2}.
fixes: Add a {3} method to {1} matching the interface signature
Check whether the method should be on {1} or on *{1}
Assert to an interface the value actually implements
patterns.example_fix: func (t T) Method() {} // implement the missing method

patterns.title: Missing interface method
patterns.diagnosis: You used {1} where a {2} is required, but {1} lacks the {3} method the interface demands.
fixes: Implement {3} on {1} with the exact signature the interface specifies
Make sure the method name's capitalization matches
Check the receiver type — value vs pointer receiver matters

patterns.match: (\S+) does not implement (\S+) \((\w+) method has pointer receiver\)
patterns.title: Pointer receiver needed
patterns.diagnosis: {1} almost satisfies {2}, but {3} is defined on a pointer receiver, so only *{1} satisfies the interface — not {1} itself.
fixes: Pass a pointer: var i {2} = &myValue
Change the method to a value receiver if that's appropriate
Store *{1} where the interface is expected

patterns.title: Goroutine panic stack
patterns.diagnosis: A goroutine panicked and dumped its stack trace. The actual cause is on the panic line just above this trace.
fixes: Read the panic message above the stack, not the trace itself
Add recover() in a deferred function to handle panics gracefully
Trace the top frame to the line that crashed
patterns.example_fix: defer func() { if r := recover(); r != nil { log.Println(r) } }()

patterns.title: Deadlock
patterns.diagnosis: Every goroutine is blocked waiting on something that will never happen — usually a channel send/receive with no partner.
fixes: Make sure a channel has both a sender and a receiver
Don't receive from a channel nothing ever sends to
Close channels when done, or buffer them if appropriate

patterns.title: Send on closed channel
patterns.diagnosis: You wrote to a channel that was already closed, which always panics. Only senders should close, and only once.
fixes: Close a channel only after all sends are finished
Let the sender (not a receiver) own closing
Use a sync.Once or a done signal to coordinate who closes

patterns.title: Double close
patterns.diagnosis: You called close() on a channel that was already closed. A channel may only be closed once.
fixes: Ensure only one place closes the channel
Guard with sync.Once so close runs at most once
Don't close in multiple goroutines

patterns.title: Close nil channel
patterns.diagnosis: You called close() on a channel that was never made (it's nil). Closing a nil channel panics.
fixes: Create the channel with make before closing it
Check the channel isn't nil before close
A struct's channel field defaults to nil — initialize it

patterns.title: Package not found
patterns.diagnosis: Go can't locate the package {1}. It's not in the standard library and isn't a dependency in your module.
fixes: Run `go get {1}` to add it as a dependency
Check the import path is spelled exactly right
Run `go mod tidy` to sync go.mod

patterns.title: No module for package
patterns.diagnosis: Go modules can't find any module that provides {1}, so it can't be imported.
fixes: Run `go get {1}` to fetch it
Run `go mod tidy` to resolve and record dependencies
Verify the import path matches the real module path

patterns.match: go: go\.mod file not found in current directory or any parent
patterns.title: No go.mod
patterns.diagnosis: You're running a Go module command but there's no go.mod anywhere up the tree, so Go has no module context.
fixes: Run `go mod init <modulepath>` to create one
cd into the directory that contains go.mod
Check you're not outside your project folder

patterns.match: missing go\.sum entry for module providing package (\S+)
patterns.title: Missing go.sum entry
patterns.diagnosis: go.sum has no checksum for the module that provides {1}, so Go won't trust it.
fixes: Run `go mod download` to populate go.sum
Run `go mod tidy` to add the missing entry
Commit go.sum so teammates get the checksums too

patterns.match: go\.mod file indicates go (\S+), but maximum version supported by tidy is (\S+)
patterns.title: Go version too new in go.mod
