patterns.diagnosis: go.mod requires Go {1} but your toolchain only supports up to {2}. The module wants a newer Go than you have.
fixes: Upgrade your Go toolchain to {1} or later
Lower the go directive in go.mod to {2} if the code allows it
Use a `toolchain` line or GOTOOLCHAIN to fetch the right version

patterns.match: build constraints exclude all Go files in (\S+)
patterns.title: Build constraints exclude all files
patterns.diagnosis: Every Go file in {1} is filtered out by build tags or by GOOS/GOARCH name suffixes, so there's nothing left to build.
fixes: Check //go:build tags at the top of the files
Make sure a file matches your target GOOS/GOARCH
Remove an over-restrictive build tag or add a matching file

patterns.title: main declared twice
patterns.diagnosis: The package has more than one func main, or main is declared alongside another main symbol in the same package.
fixes: Keep exactly one func main in package main
Check you didn't paste main twice across files
Make sure no other file in the package also defines main

patterns.match: function main is undeclared in the main package
patterns.title: No main function
patterns.diagnosis: Package main needs a func main as the program's entry point, but none was found.
fixes: Add func main() { ... } to a file in package main
Make sure the file's package line says `package main`
Check the function isn't accidentally named Main or main2

patterns.match: can't load package: package (\S+): cannot find package
patterns.title: Can't load package
patterns.diagnosis: The build tool couldn't load package {1} — the path doesn't resolve to source files.
fixes: Verify the import path points to a real package
Run `go mod tidy` and `go build ./...`
Check the directory actually contains .go files

patterns.title: Two packages in one dir
patterns.diagnosis: A single directory has files declaring two different packages, {1} and {2}. Each directory holds exactly one package (plus its _test).
fixes: Make every .go file in the dir use the same package name
Move one package's files into their own directory
The only allowed second name is yourpkg_test for external tests

patterns.title: Missing package clause
patterns.diagnosis: Every Go file must start with a package clause, but the first thing the compiler saw was {1}.
fixes: Add `package name` as the first line (after any build tags)
Build tags and comments may precede it, but code may not
Check the file isn't missing its top line

patterns.title: Import cycle
patterns.diagnosis: Two or more packages import each other in a loop. Go forbids circular imports.
fixes: Move the shared types into a third, lower-level package
Invert one dependency using an interface
Merge the two packages if they're really one concept

patterns.title: Unused label
patterns.diagnosis: You wrote the label {1}: but no break, continue, or goto ever targets it.
fixes: Reference {1} from a break/continue/goto, or remove it
Check you didn't misspell the label in the break statement
Delete leftover labels from refactoring

patterns.title: Undefined label
patterns.diagnosis: A goto, break, or continue refers to label {1}, but no such label exists in scope.
fixes: Define the label: {1}: before the statement you want
Check the label's spelling matches the jump
Labels are function-scoped — make sure it's in the same function

patterns.title: Goto jumps over declaration
patterns.diagnosis: A `goto {1}` would skip past where {2} is declared, leaving {2} in scope but uninitialized. Go forbids this.
fixes: Move the declaration of {2} above the goto
Put {2} inside a block { } that the goto doesn't enter
Restructure the code to avoid jumping over declarations

patterns.match: const initializer .+ is not a constant
patterns.title: Non-constant const
patterns.diagnosis: A const must be set from a compile-time constant, but you assigned a value computed at runtime.
fixes: Use a var instead of const for runtime values
Only literals and constant expressions can be const
Function calls (except some builtins) aren't allowed in const
patterns.example_fix: var x = compute() // use var, not const

patterns.title: Constant overflow
patterns.diagnosis: The constant {1} is too big (or too negative) to fit in the type {2} it's being assigned to.
fixes: Use a wider type like int64 or uint64
Check the literal isn't larger than the type allows
For unsigned types, don't assign negative constants

patterns.title: Divide by zero (constant)
patterns.diagnosis: A constant expression divides by zero, which the compiler rejects outright.
fixes: Don't divide by a literal 0
Guard runtime division: if d != 0 { q := n / d }
Check the divisor constant isn't accidentally 0

patterns.title: Integer divide by zero (runtime)
patterns.diagnosis: At runtime an integer was divided by zero, which panics in Go (unlike floats, which give Inf).
fixes: Check the divisor isn't zero before dividing
Guard: if d != 0 { use(n / d) }
Validate user input that becomes a divisor

patterns.title: Blank identifier used as value
patterns.diagnosis: You tried to read the blank identifier _, but it's write-only — it discards values and can never be read.
fixes: Assign to a real variable if you need the value
Use _ only on the left side of assignments
Don't print or compare _
patterns.example_fix: x := someValue // not _ if you need x

patterns.title: Too many return values
patterns.diagnosis: Your return gives values ({1}) but the function signature wants ({2}). The counts or types don't line up.
fixes: Return exactly the values the signature lists
Drop extra values or add the missing return types to the signature
Match the order and types of the declared returns

patterns.title: Not enough return values
patterns.diagnosis: Your return gives ({1}) but the function must return ({2}). You're returning too few values.
fixes: Return every value the signature requires
Add the missing value, often a nil error: return result, nil
Use zero values if you don't have real ones yet

patterns.match: naked return in function with named results .+ not allowed
patterns.title: Bad naked return
patterns.diagnosis: A bare `return` is used but the function's named results aren't fully set in this context.
fixes: Return values explicitly: return a, b
Set all named results before the naked return
Avoid naked returns in long functions for clarity

patterns.title: Variadic not last
patterns.diagnosis: The variadic parameter (...) must be the final parameter of a function, but you put another parameter after it.
fixes: Move the ...T parameter to the end of the parameter list
A function may have only one variadic parameter, and it must be last
Reorder so fixed params come first

patterns.match: cannot use \.\.\. in call to non-variadic (\w+)
patterns.title: Spread on non-variadic
patterns.diagnosis: You used slice... to spread arguments into {1}, but {1} doesn't take a variadic parameter.
fixes: Remove the ... if {1} expects fixed arguments
Only spread into functions whose last param is ...T
Pass the slice as a single argument if that's what {1} wants
patterns.example_fix: f(nums...) // only if f is variadic

patterns.match: first argument to append must be a slice; have (\S+)
patterns.title: append needs a slice
patterns.diagnosis: append's first argument must be a slice, but you passed a {1}.
fixes: Pass a slice as the first argument to append
If you have an array, slice it first: arr[:]
Initialize the variable as a slice, not a single value

patterns.match: too few arguments to conversion to (\S+)
patterns.title: Conversion needs an argument
patterns.diagnosis: You wrote {1}() with no value inside. A type conversion needs exactly one argument to convert.
fixes: Put a value inside the parentheses: {1}(value)
If you meant a function call, that function isn't {1}
Check you didn't confuse a type name with a function

patterns.title: Non-constant array size
patterns.diagnosis: An array's length must be a constant known at compile time, but {1} is a variable.
fixes: Use a slice instead: make([]T, n) for dynamic length
Declare the size as a const if it's truly fixed
Arrays need literal or const sizes; slices handle runtime sizes

patterns.title: Invalid array length
patterns.diagnosis: You declared an array with length {1}, but array lengths must be non-negative constants.
fixes: Use a length >= 0
Don't compute array sizes from negative expressions
Switch to a slice if the length comes from runtime data

patterns.title: Mixed named/unnamed params
patterns.diagnosis: A parameter or result list mixes named entries with unnamed ones. It must be all-named or all-unnamed.
fixes: Give every parameter a name, or none of them
func f(a int, b int) — name all
func f(int, int) — name none
patterns.example_fix: func f(a, b int) int { return a + b }

patterns.title: Duplicate field or method
patterns.diagnosis: The type defines {1} more than once. Each field and method name must be unique within a type.
fixes: Rename or remove the duplicate {1}
Check for an embedded type that also provides {1}
Merge the two definitions if they were meant to be one

patterns.title: Unknown struct field
patterns.diagnosis: In a struct literal you set a field {1} that the struct type doesn't have.
fixes: Check the field name's spelling and capitalization
Look at the struct definition for the real field names
Remove {1} if it doesn't belong to this struct

patterns.title: Too few values in struct literal
patterns.diagnosis: A positional struct literal lists fewer values than the struct has fields. Positional literals must set every field.
fixes: Provide a value for every field, in order
Better: use named fields {Name: x} so order and count don't matter
Switch to keyed literal to set only some fields

patterns.title: Too many values in struct literal
patterns.diagnosis: A positional struct literal lists more values than the struct has fields.
fixes: Remove the extra value
Use named fields so you can't over- or under-fill
Check the struct definition for the real field count

patterns.match: mixture of field:value and value initializers
patterns.title: Mixed struct literal styles
patterns.diagnosis: A struct literal mixes keyed (Field: value) and positional (value) initializers. Pick one style for the whole literal.
fixes: Use named fields throughout: {A: 1, B: 2}
Or use positional throughout: {1, 2}
Don't combine the two in the same literal

patterns.match: cannot use promoted field (\S+) in struct literal
patterns.title: Promoted field in literal
patterns.diagnosis: You set {1} in a struct literal, but it's promoted from an embedded struct, not a direct field. Embedded fields can't be set by their promoted name in a literal.
fixes: Set it through the embedded struct: Outer{Inner: Inner{Field: x}}
Initialize the embedded struct explicitly
Promoted fields are only for access, not literal init

patterns.title: Recursive type without indirection
patterns.diagnosis: Type {1} contains itself directly, so its size would be infinite. You need a pointer, slice, or map to break the cycle.
fixes: Use a pointer to the type: Next *{1}
Use a slice of the type: Children []{1}

patterns.title: Missing type in composite literal

patterns.diagnosis: sed tried to open `{1}` but it isn't there. Either the filename is wrong or you meant to pipe input in.
fixes: Check the filename with `ls`.
To read from a pipe instead of a file, drop the filename: `echo hi | sed 's/h/H/'`.
Mind quoting — `sed 's/a/b/' *.txt` needs at least one matching file.

patterns.title: sed — nothing to edit
patterns.diagnosis: sed got a script but no file and no piped input, so it has nothing to work on.
fixes: Give it a file: `sed 's/a/b/' file.txt`.
Or pipe text in: `echo hello | sed 's/l/L/g'`.
With `-i` you must name the file to edit in place.

patterns.match: sed: -i may not be used with stdin
patterns.title: sed -i needs a real file
patterns.diagnosis: The in-place edit flag `-i` rewrites a file on disk, so it can't work with piped input (there's no file to rewrite).
fixes: Use `-i` only with named files: `sed -i 's/a/b/' file.txt`.
For pipes, drop `-i` and just let the output flow.
To capture pipe output to a file, redirect: `... | sed 's/a/b/' > out.txt`.

patterns.title: awk — program syntax error
patterns.diagnosis: awk couldn't parse your program near `{1}`. Usually a missing brace, quote, or stray character.
fixes: Wrap the whole program in single quotes: `awk '{print $1}'`.
Each rule body goes in `{ }` braces.
Check that `{` and `}` are balanced.

patterns.match: awk: fatal: cannot open file `([^`']+)' for reading
patterns.title: awk — can't open input file
patterns.diagnosis: awk tried to read `{1}` and failed — wrong path or no read permission.
fixes: Confirm the file exists with `ls {1}`.
Check read permission: `ls -l {1}`.
If you meant to pipe, don't pass a filename — `cmd | awk ...`.

patterns.match: awk: fatal: division by zero attempted
patterns.title: awk — divide by zero
patterns.diagnosis: Your awk program divided by a value that was zero (often an empty or missing field treated as 0).
fixes: Guard the divisor: `$2 != 0 ? $1/$2 : 0`.
Empty fields read as 0 in numeric context — check the column number.
Print the row to see what `$2` actually holds.

patterns.match: awk: warning: escape sequence `\\([^`']*)' treated as plain
patterns.title: awk — unknown escape sequence
patterns.diagnosis: awk saw `\{1}` which isn't a real escape, so it dropped the backslash. Often a regex slash that needed double-escaping.
fixes: In a dynamic regex string, double the backslash: `\\.` for a literal dot.
Use a regex literal `/.../ ` instead of a string when you can.
Known escapes: `\n \t \\ \/`.

patterns.title: awk — file not found (mawk)
patterns.diagnosis: mawk (Debian/Ubuntu's awk) can't open `{1}`. Path is wrong, or it's actually program text mistaken for a filename.
fixes: Quote your program so it isn't read as a filename.
Verify the path with `ls`.
mawk differs slightly from gawk — try `gawk` if a feature is missing.

patterns.match: grep: ([^:]+): No such file or directory
patterns.title: grep — file not found
patterns.diagnosis: grep tried to search inside `{1}` but it doesn't exist. Typo, or the glob matched nothing.
fixes: Check the path: `ls {1}`.
To search a folder, add `-r`: `grep -r 'word' dir/`.
If a `*.log` glob matched nothing, the literal `*.log` got passed — that's why it's missing.

patterns.title: grep — unknown flag
patterns.diagnosis: grep doesn't recognize the `-{1}` flag. It may belong to another tool, or your search term started with `-`.
fixes: If your pattern starts with a dash, use `grep -e '-pattern'` or `grep -- '-pattern'`.
Common flags: `-i` (ignore case), `-r` (recursive), `-n` (line numbers), `-v` (invert).
Check `grep --help` for valid options.

patterns.title: grep — dangling backslash
patterns.diagnosis: Your grep pattern ends with a lone `\`, which escapes nothing. Often a shell-eaten backslash.
fixes: Wrap the pattern in single quotes so the shell keeps your backslashes.
To match a literal backslash, use `'\\'` inside single quotes.
Remove the trailing `\` if it was a typo.

patterns.title: grep — broken regex
patterns.diagnosis: The pattern you gave grep isn't a valid regular expression — usually unbalanced `[ ]`, `( )`, or `{ }`.
fixes: Close your brackets: `[abc]` not `[abc`.
For literal special characters, use `grep -F 'fixed text'`.
With `-E` (extended regex) the grouping/quantifier syntax changes — match the flag to your pattern.

patterns.title: grep — pointed at a folder
patterns.diagnosis: You asked grep to search `{1}` but it's a directory, not a file. grep skips directories unless told to recurse.
fixes: Add `-r` to search recursively: `grep -r 'word' {1}`.
Or name a specific file inside it.
`grep -d skip` quietly ignores directories.

patterns.match: tar: ([^:]+): Cannot open: No such file or directory
patterns.title: tar — file/path not found
patterns.diagnosis: tar couldn't find `{1}` to add to or extract from the archive.
fixes: Check the path with `ls`.
Order matters: `tar -czf out.tar.gz files` — the `-f` filename comes right after the flags.
When extracting, `-f archive.tar` must point at a real archive.

patterns.match: tar: Refusing to read archive contents from terminal
patterns.title: tar — no archive given
patterns.diagnosis: tar would read the archive from your keyboard because you didn't give `-f filename`. It's stopping to protect you.
fixes: Always include `-f` with the archive name: `tar -xf thing.tar`.
To read from a pipe on purpose, use `-f -`.
Check the flag order — `f` should be the last flag before the filename.

patterns.match: tar: Error is not recoverable: exiting now
patterns.title: tar — fatal archive error
patterns.diagnosis: tar hit an error it can't continue past — often a truncated, corrupt, or wrong-format archive.
fixes: Check the file type: `file thing.tar.gz`.
If it's gzip, you need `-z`; for bzip2 `-j`; for xz `-J`.
Re-download or re-create the archive if it's truncated.

patterns.title: tar — member not in archive
patterns.diagnosis: You asked tar to extract `{1}` but no such entry exists in the archive (maybe a path-prefix difference).
fixes: List the contents first: `tar -tf archive.tar`.
Match the exact stored path — often archives store `./name` or `dir/name`.
Extract everything (drop the member name) if unsure.

patterns.match: tar: Removing leading `/' from member names
patterns.title: tar — absolute paths stripped
patterns.diagnosis: tar removed the leading `/` so the archive stays relative (safer to extract). This is a warning, not an error.
fixes: This is normal and usually fine — extraction happens relative to the current folder.
Use `-P` to keep absolute paths if you really need them (risky).
Better: `cd` into the parent and archive relative paths.

patterns.title: rsync — connection dropped
patterns.diagnosis: The rsync session ended early — usually SSH login failed or rsync isn't installed on the remote.
fixes: Test the SSH login by itself first: `ssh user@host`.
Make sure rsync is installed on BOTH ends.
Check the remote path and that you have permission there.

patterns.match: rsync: link_stat "([^"]+)" failed: No such file or directory
patterns.title: rsync — source missing
patterns.diagnosis: rsync can't find the source `{1}` to copy from.
fixes: Check the source path with `ls {1}`.
A trailing slash matters: `src/` copies contents, `src` copies the folder.
Quote paths with spaces.

patterns.match: rsync: failed to set permissions on "([^"]+)"
patterns.title: rsync — can't set permissions
patterns.diagnosis: rsync copied `{1}` but couldn't apply its permissions on the destination (common on FAT/exFAT or NFS).
fixes: Add `--no-perms --no-owner --no-group` for filesystems that don't track them.
Use `-rt` instead of `-a` to skip perms/owner.
Run as a user that can chmod on the destination.

patterns.match: rsync error: some files\/attrs were not transferred \(see previous errors\) \(code 23\)
patterns.title: rsync — code 23 partial transfer
patterns.diagnosis: rsync finished but couldn't transfer every file or attribute. Code 23 means partial success — check earlier lines for the real cause.
fixes: Scroll up: the actual error (permission, vanished file) is printed first.
Use `--no-perms` if it's an attribute problem on the target filesystem.
If files vanished mid-transfer, that's often harmless on a live system.

patterns.title: rsync — not installed
patterns.diagnosis: rsync isn't installed on this machine (or the remote one).
fixes: Install it: `sudo apt install rsync` or `brew install rsync`.
On the remote side too — rsync must exist on both ends.
As a fallback, `scp -r` copies recursively without rsync.

patterns.match: scp: ([^:]+): No such file or directory
patterns.title: scp — path missing
patterns.diagnosis: scp couldn't find `{1}` — either the local source or the remote destination folder doesn't exist.
fixes: Verify the local file exists.
The remote target folder must already exist — scp won't create parent dirs.
Remote syntax is `user@host:/path`, with the colon.

patterns.match: scp: warning: Using SFTP protocol because a \(-O\) flag was not provided
patterns.title: scp — now uses SFTP
patterns.diagnosis: Newer OpenSSH scp uses SFTP under the hood. This is just a heads-up, not an error.
fixes: Usually safe to ignore.
If a server only speaks legacy scp, add `-O` to force the old protocol.
Consider switching to `sftp` or `rsync` for big transfers.

patterns.title: ssh — can't resolve host
patterns.diagnosis: SSH couldn't turn the name `{1}` into an IP address. DNS failure or a typo in the hostname.
fixes: Check the spelling of `{1}`.
Try pinging it or `nslookup {1}`.
If it's a private name, add it to `~/.ssh/config` or `/etc/hosts`.

patterns.title: ssh — key file too readable
patterns.diagnosis: Your private key `{1}` is readable by others, so SSH refuses to use it for safety.
fixes: Lock it down: `chmod 600 {1}`.
The `.ssh` folder should be `chmod 700`.
Never share or world-read a private key.

patterns.title: ssh — key signing failed
patterns.diagnosis: SSH found your `{2}` key but the agent couldn't sign with it — often a key removed from the agent or a hardware-key (FIDO) not present.
fixes: Re-add the key: `ssh-add {2}`.
Check the agent is running: `ssh-add -l`.
For FIDO/sk keys, make sure the security device is plugged in.

patterns.match: ssh: connect to host ([^ ]+) port [0-9]+: Connection timed out
patterns.title: ssh — connection timed out
patterns.diagnosis: SSH never got a reply from `{1}` — the host is down, firewalled, or the wrong address.
fixes: Check the host is up and reachable: `ping {1}`.
Confirm the port (default 22) isn't blocked by a firewall.
Verify the address and try `-p PORT` if SSH runs on a custom port.

patterns.match: ssh: connect to host ([^ ]+) port [0-9]+: No route to host
patterns.title: ssh — no route to host
patterns.diagnosis: The network can't find a path to `{1}` — wrong subnet, host offline, or a firewall dropping packets.
fixes: Check you're on the right network (VPN up?).
Confirm the IP is correct and the machine is on.
Look for a firewall blocking the route.

patterns.match: Pseudo-terminal will not be allocated because stdin is not a terminal
patterns.title: ssh — no TTY for piped input
patterns.diagnosis: You ran ssh with piped input, so it can't grab an interactive terminal. Usually harmless.
fixes: Add `-T` to disable TTY allocation cleanly.
Use `-t` to force a TTY if you really need interactivity.
For one-off commands, just `ssh host 'command'`.

patterns.match: Received disconnect from ([^ ]+) port [0-9]+:[0-9]+: Too many authentication failures
patterns.title: ssh — too many auth attempts
patterns.diagnosis: SSH offered too many keys to `{1}` and the server cut the session. The agent likely has many keys it tries in turn.
fixes: Point at one key explicitly: `ssh -i ~/.ssh/thekey -o IdentitiesOnly=yes host`.
Trim keys in the agent: `ssh-add -D` then add just the one.
Set `IdentitiesOnly yes` for that host in `~/.ssh/config`.

patterns.match: kex_exchange_identification: Connection closed by remote host
patterns.title: ssh — closed during handshake
patterns.diagnosis: The server hung up before SSH could agree on a connection. Often rate-limiting (fail2ban), a wrong port, or a non-SSH service on that port.
fixes: Wait a minute if you've retried a lot — you may be temporarily blocked.
Confirm SSH actually runs on that port.
Check the server's `/var/log/auth.log` if you control it.

patterns.title: jq — filter syntax error
patterns.diagnosis: jq couldn't parse your filter near `{1}`. Often a missing `.`, quote, or pipe.
fixes: Field access needs a leading dot: `.name`, `.items[0]`.
Quote the whole filter in single quotes so the shell leaves it alone.
Pipe stages with `|`: `.items[] | .name`.

patterns.title: jq — wrong type for index
patterns.diagnosis: You tried to read field `{2}` but the value there is a `{1}`, not an object. The JSON shape isn't what you expected.
fixes: Inspect the shape first: `jq '.' file.json`.
If it's an array, index it: `.[0].field`.
Use `?` to skip mismatches: `.field?`.

patterns.match: jq: error: Could not open file ([^:]+): No such file or directory
patterns.title: jq — input file missing
patterns.diagnosis: jq couldn't open `{1}`. Wrong path, or you put the filename where the filter goes.
fixes: Filter comes first, file second: `jq '.x' file.json`.
Check the path with `ls`.
To read piped JSON, drop the filename: `curl ... | jq '.x'`.

patterns.match: parse error: Invalid numeric literal at line [0-9]+, column [0-9]+
patterns.title: jq — invalid JSON input
patterns.diagnosis: The data you fed jq isn't valid JSON — often it's HTML, an error page, or has trailing junk.
fixes: Print the raw input first to see what it really is.
APIs sometimes return HTML errors — check the HTTP status.
For JSON-lines (one object per line) use `jq -c` or `--stream`.
patterns.example_fix: curl -s url | head; curl -s url | jq .

patterns.match: cut: you must specify a list of bytes, characters, or fields
patterns.title: cut — missing field spec
patterns.diagnosis: `cut` needs to know WHAT to cut: bytes (`-b`), characters (`-c`), or fields (`-f`).
fixes: Pick fields with `-f`: `cut -d, -f1 file.csv`.
Set the delimiter with `-d` (default is TAB).
Characters: `cut -c1-5` for the first five chars.

patterns.match: cut: invalid byte, character or field list
patterns.title: cut — bad field range
patterns.diagnosis: The range you gave `-f`/`-c` isn't valid — fields start at 1 and ranges look like `1-3` or `1,4`.
fixes: Use `-f1`, `-f1,3`, or `-f2-` (field 2 to end).
Fields are 1-based, not 0-based.
No spaces inside the list: `-f 1,2` not `-f 1, 2`.

patterns.match: sort: cannot read: ([^:]+): No such file or directory
patterns.title: sort — input file missing
patterns.diagnosis: sort couldn't open `{1}`. Wrong path, or a glob that matched nothing.
fixes: Check the path with `ls`.
To sort piped data, drop the filename.
`sort -k2` sorts by the second column — make sure the column exists.

patterns.match: sort: ([^:]+): No such file or directory
patterns.title: sort — file not found
patterns.diagnosis: sort was given `{1}` but it isn't there.
fixes: Verify with `ls {1}`.
Numeric sort needs `-n`; otherwise 10 sorts before 2.
Combine with `uniq` only on already-sorted input.

patterns.title: sort -c — not sorted
patterns.diagnosis: You ran `sort -c` to CHECK ordering and `{1}` is the first out-of-order line.
fixes: Drop `-c` to actually sort instead of just checking.
Match the check flags to the sort flags (`-n`, `-k`).
`sort -c` exits non-zero when input isn't sorted — that's expected.

patterns.title: tr — too many arguments
patterns.diagnosis: tr translates from stdin, so it takes only the SET strings — `{1}` looks like a filename it didn't expect.
fixes: tr reads piped input, not files: `cat file | tr a-z A-Z`.
It takes one or two SET arguments, nothing else.
To edit a file, redirect: `tr a-z A-Z < in > out`.

patterns.title: tr — needs a second set
patterns.diagnosis: For translation, tr needs two character sets but you only gave `{1}`.
fixes: Translate: `tr 'abc' 'xyz'`.
Delete instead: `tr -d 'abc'` takes just one set.
Squeeze repeats: `tr -s ' '`.

patterns.match: paste: ([^:]+): No such file or directory
patterns.title: paste — file missing
patterns.diagnosis: paste couldn't open `{1}` to merge columns.
fixes: Check each filename you pass.
Use `-` for stdin: `paste - - <file` pairs lines.
Set a delimiter with `-d`.

patterns.title: xargs — unbalanced quote in input
patterns.diagnosis: xargs tries to honor quotes in its input, and one line had a stray `'`. Filenames with quotes confuse it.
fixes: Use `-0` with `find -print0` so names are split on NUL, not whitespace/quotes.
`xargs -0` ignores quoting entirely — much safer.
Avoid xargs parsing surprises for weird filenames.

patterns.match: xargs: ([^:]+): No such file or directory
patterns.title: xargs — command not found
patterns.diagnosis: xargs tried to run `{1}` as the command but couldn't find it.
fixes: Check the command name xargs is invoking.
The command goes after the options: `xargs -n1 echo`.
If no command is given, xargs defaults to `echo`.

patterns.title: chmod — bad mode
patterns.diagnosis: `{1}` isn't a valid permission mode. Use octal (`755`) or symbolic (`u+x`).
fixes: Octal: `chmod 644 file` (owner rw, others r).
Symbolic: `chmod +x script.sh` to make it runnable.
Don't mix — `chmod 7+x` is invalid.

patterns.match: chmod: cannot access '([^']+)': No such file or directory
patterns.title: chmod — target missing
patterns.diagnosis: chmod can't change `{1}` because that file or folder isn't there.
fixes: Check the path with `ls {1}`.
Mind the order: `chmod 755 path`, not the path first.
Use `-R` to recurse into a directory.

patterns.title: chown — no such user
patterns.diagnosis: There's no user named `{1}` on this system, so chown can't set them as owner.
fixes: List users: `cut -d: -f1 /etc/passwd`.
Use a numeric UID if the name isn't known: `chown 1000 file`.
Format is `user:group` — check the colon.

patterns.match: chown: changing ownership of '([^']+)': Operation not permitted
patterns.title: chown — needs root
patterns.diagnosis: Only root can change a file's owner. You don't have permission on `{1}`.
fixes: Prefix with `sudo`: `sudo chown user file`.
Regular users can't give away their files.
To change just the group you own, use `chgrp`.

patterns.match: ln: failed to create symbolic link '([^']+)': File exists
patterns.title: ln — link target exists
patterns.diagnosis: There's already a file or link at `{1}`, so `ln -s` won't overwrite it by default.
fixes: Force replace: `ln -sf target {1}`.
Or remove the old one first: `rm {1}`.
Double-check you're not about to clobber a real file.

patterns.match: ln: failed to create hard link '([^']+)' => '([^']+)': Invalid cross-device link
patterns.title: ln — hard link across filesystems
patterns.diagnosis: Hard links can't cross filesystems. `{1}` and `{2}` live on different disks/mounts.
fixes: Use a symbolic link instead: `ln -s {2} {1}`.
Symlinks work across devices; hard links don't.
Or copy the file if you need a real duplicate.

patterns.title: cp — directory needs -r
patterns.diagnosis: `{1}` is a folder, but `cp` only copies folders when you add `-r`.
fixes: Add `-r`: `cp -r {1} dest/`.
Use `-a` to also preserve permissions/timestamps.
For files only, leave off `-r`.

patterns.match: cp: cannot stat '([^']+)': No such file or directory
patterns.title: cp — source missing
patterns.diagnosis: cp can't find the source `{1}` to copy.
fixes: Check the path with `ls {1}`.
A glob like `*.txt` that matches nothing passes literally.
Quote names with spaces.

patterns.match: cp: target '([^']+)' is not a directory
patterns.title: cp — multiple sources need a dir
patterns.diagnosis: When copying several files, the last argument `{1}` must be a directory, but it's a file.
fixes: Make sure the destination is a folder: `cp a b c destdir/`.
Create it first: `mkdir destdir`.
To copy ONE file to a new name, give exactly two arguments.
patterns.example_fix: mkdir out && cp a.txt b.txt out/

patterns.match: mv: cannot move '([^']+)' to '([^']+)': Directory not empty
patterns.title: mv — destination dir has files
patterns.diagnosis: mv tried to replace the folder `{2}` with `{1}`, but `{2}` already has stuff in it.
fixes: Merge contents instead: `mv {1}/* {2}/`.
Or empty/remove the target first if it's safe.
mv won't overwrite a non-empty directory.

patterns.match: mv: cannot stat '([^']+)': No such file or directory
patterns.title: mv — source missing
patterns.diagnosis: mv can't find `{1}` to move.
fixes: Verify with `ls {1}`.
Watch for typos and case.
A non-matching glob is passed literally.

patterns.match: rm: cannot remove '([^']+)': Is a directory
patterns.title: rm — needs -r for folders
patterns.diagnosis: `{1}` is a directory; plain `rm` only deletes files.
fixes: Recurse: `rm -r {1}` (careful!).
For an empty folder, `rmdir {1}` is safer.
Always double-check the path before `rm -r`.

patterns.match: rm: cannot remove '([^']+)': No such file or directory
patterns.title: rm — nothing to delete
patterns.diagnosis: `{1}` isn't there — already gone, wrong path, or a glob matched nothing.
fixes: It may already be deleted — usually safe to ignore.
Use `rm -f` to silence missing-file complaints.
Check the path before assuming.

patterns.match: rmdir: failed to remove '([^']+)': Directory not empty
patterns.title: rmdir — folder not empty
patterns.diagnosis: rmdir only deletes EMPTY folders, and `{1}` still has things inside.
fixes: List what's left: `ls -A {1}`.
To delete it and its contents, use `rm -r {1}` (carefully).
Empty it first, then rmdir.

patterns.match: mkdir: cannot create directory '([^']+)': File exists
patterns.title: mkdir — already exists
patterns.diagnosis: Something already lives at `{1}` (a file or folder), so mkdir won't make it.
fixes: If you just want it to exist, use `mkdir -p {1}` (no error if present).
If a FILE is in the way, rename or remove it.
`-p` also creates missing parent folders.

patterns.match: mkdir: cannot create directory '([^']+)': No such file or directory
patterns.title: mkdir — missing parent
patterns.diagnosis: The parent folder of `{1}` doesn't exist, so mkdir can't make the child.
fixes: Create the whole chain at once: `mkdir -p {1}`.
Or make the parent first.
`-p` is almost always what you want for nested paths.

patterns.title: kill — process already gone
patterns.diagnosis: There's no process with PID {1} — it already exited, or the PID was wrong.
fixes: List current processes: `ps aux | grep name`.
Find the right PID with `pgrep name`.
The job may have finished on its own.

patterns.title: kill — not your process
patterns.diagnosis: PID {1} belongs to another user (often root), so you can't signal it.
fixes: Use `sudo kill {1}` if you have rights.
You can only kill your own processes otherwise.
Double-check the PID is the one you meant.

patterns.title: kill — bad arguments
patterns.diagnosis: kill got arguments it didn't understand — usually a missing PID or a malformed signal.
fixes: Give a PID: `kill 1234`.
Force-kill: `kill -9 1234` (last resort).
List signals with `kill -l`.

patterns.title: kill — unknown signal
patterns.diagnosis: `{1}` isn't a real signal name or number.
fixes: Common signals: `TERM` (default), `KILL` (9), `HUP` (1), `INT` (2).
Use the number or the name without `SIG`: `-9` or `-KILL`.
List all: `kill -l`.

patterns.title: job control — no such job
patterns.diagnosis: You referenced job `{1}` (like `%2`) but there's no background job with that number.
fixes: List jobs: `jobs`.
Use `%1`, `%2` for job numbers from that list.
`fg`/`bg` with no argument uses the most recent job.

patterns.title: no job control in this shell
patterns.diagnosis: This shell can't manage background jobs — common in non-interactive scripts or some `sh` modes.
fixes: Job control (`fg`/`bg`/`%n`) only works in interactive shells.
In scripts, use `&` plus `wait $!` to manage background processes.
Run interactively (a real terminal) if you need `fg`.

patterns.match: bash: warning: run_pending_traps: bad value in trap_list
patterns.title: bash — corrupt trap list
patterns.diagnosis: Bash's internal trap table got into a bad state — usually a buggy or recursive trap handler.
fixes: Avoid resetting traps inside the trap handler itself.
Keep trap handlers short and simple.
Update bash if it's very old — this was a known bug in some versions.

patterns.match: bash: read: `([^`']+)': not a valid identifier
patterns.title: read — bad variable name
patterns.diagnosis: `{1}` can't be used as a variable for `read` — names must start with a letter/underscore and contain no dashes or spaces.
fixes: Use names like `line`, `my_var`, `x1`.
No hyphens: `my-var` is invalid, `my_var` is fine.
Don't put `$` before the name when reading: `read x` not `read $x`.

patterns.title: printf — bad format spec
patterns.diagnosis: `{1}` isn't a valid printf conversion. printf reads `%` directives like `%s`, `%d`, `%f`.
fixes: Strings use `%s`, integers `%d`, floats `%.2f`.
To print a literal `%`, write `%%`.
Mind the order: format string first, then arguments.

patterns.title: mapfile — bad option
patterns.diagnosis: `mapfile`/`readarray` doesn't accept `-{1}`.
fixes: `-t` strips trailing newlines (most common).
`-d` sets a custom delimiter (bash 4.4+).
Read lines into an array: `mapfile -t arr < file`.

patterns.title: mapfile — needs bash 4+
patterns.diagnosis: `mapfile` doesn't exist in old bash or in plain `sh`.
fixes: Check your version: `bash --version` (need 4.0+).
On macOS, the system bash is old — install a newer one via Homebrew.
Fallback: loop with `while read -r line; do arr+=("$line"); done < file`.
patterns.example_fix: while read -r l; do a+=("$l"); done < f

patterns.match: bash: declare: `([^`']+)': not a valid identifier
patterns.title: declare — invalid name
patterns.diagnosis: `{1}` isn't a legal variable name for `declare` (bad characters, or a value where a name belongs).
fixes: Names: letters, digits, underscores; can't start with a digit.
For an assignment use `declare x=5`, not `declare 5`.
Array: `declare -a arr` then `arr[0]=x`.

patterns.match: bash: local: can only be used in a function
patterns.title: local — outside a function
patterns.diagnosis: `local` declares function-scoped variables, so it's meaningless at the top level of a script.
fixes: Only use `local` inside a function body.
At script level, just assign normally: `x=5`.
Wrap the code in a function if you want local scope.

patterns.match: bash: export: `([^`']+)': not a valid identifier
patterns.title: export — bad name
patterns.diagnosis: `export` got `{1}`, which isn't a valid variable name. Often a stray space around `=`.
fixes: No spaces around `=`: `export PATH=/x` not `export PATH = /x`.
Export an existing var by name: `export MYVAR`.
Names can't contain dashes or start with digits.

patterns.match: bash: unset: `([^`']+)': not a valid identifier
patterns.title: unset — bad name
patterns.diagnosis: `{1}` can't be unset because it isn't a valid identifier.
fixes: Unset by bare name: `unset MYVAR` (no `$`).
For an array element: `unset 'arr[2]'` (quote it).
Names follow the usual letter/underscore rules.

patterns.title: shell ran a number as a command
patterns.diagnosis: The shell tried to execute `{1}` as a program. Usually you meant arithmetic but used the wrong syntax.
fixes: For math use `$(( ))`: `result=$(( 2 + 2 ))`.
Don't put a number alone on a line expecting a calculation.
`let 'x = 2 + 2'` also works.

patterns.match: bash: ([^:]+): syntax error: operand expected \(error token is "([^"]+)"\)
patterns.title: arithmetic — missing operand
patterns.diagnosis: Inside `(( ))`, the expression `{1}` is missing a value near `{2}` — often an empty/unset variable used as a number.
fixes: Empty variables become nothing in arithmetic — default them: `${x:-0}`.
Check the variable holds a number, not text.
Initialize counters before incrementing: `count=0`.

patterns.title: arithmetic — divide by zero
patterns.diagnosis: An arithmetic expression divided by zero near `{2}`. The divisor was 0 (maybe an unset variable).
fixes: Guard the divisor: `(( b != 0 )) && r=$(( a / b ))`.
Unset variables read as 0 — set them first.
Print the values just before the division.

patterns.match: bash: let: ([^:]+): syntax error in expression
patterns.title: let — bad expression
patterns.diagnosis: `let` couldn't evaluate the expression `{1}`. Spaces or special characters often need quoting.
fixes: Quote the whole expression: `let 'x = a * b'`.
Or use `(( ))` which is cleaner: `(( x = a * b ))`.
Make sure operands are numeric.

patterns.match: bash: ([^:]+): value too great for base \(error token is "([^"]+)"\)
patterns.title: arithmetic — bad number base
patterns.diagnosis: A leading zero made bash treat `{2}` as octal, but it has digits 8 or 9 which octal can't have.
fixes: Force base 10: `$(( 10#$num ))`.
Strip leading zeros before doing math.
This bites time strings like `09` — always use `10#`.

patterns.title: test — expected a number
patterns.diagnosis: A numeric test like `-eq`/`-lt` got `{1}`, which isn't an integer.
fixes: Use string tests (`=`, `!=`) for text, number tests (`-eq`, `-lt`) for numbers.
Empty variables fail numeric tests — default them: `${x:-0}`.
Quote the variable: `[ "$x" -eq 5 ]`.

patterns.match: bash: \[\[: ([^:]+): syntax error in conditional expression
patterns.title: [[ ]] — bad condition
patterns.diagnosis: The conditional `{1}` inside `[[ ]]` is malformed — often a missing operator or stray bracket.
fixes: String compare: `[[ $a == $b ]]`.
Use `&&`/`||` between conditions, not inside the brackets oddly.

patterns.match: bash: syntax error in conditional expression: unexpected token `([^`']+)'
patterns.title: [[ ]] — unexpected token
patterns.diagnosis: `{1}` showed up where `[[ ]]` didn't expect it — commonly an unquoted glob or a missing operator.
fixes: Quote the right side or use `==` for pattern matching deliberately.
For regex use `=~` with the pattern UNquoted.
Balance your brackets and parentheses.

patterns.title: case — stray ;;
patterns.diagnosis: A `;;` appeared outside a `case` statement, or your case structure is malformed.
fixes: `;;` ends each branch inside `case ... esac` only.
Each pattern looks like `pattern) commands ;;`.
Close the whole thing with `esac`.
patterns.example_fix: case $x in a) echo A;; esac

patterns.match: bash: syntax error near unexpected token `esac'
patterns.title: case — esac without case
patterns.diagnosis: Bash hit `esac` but the `case` block above it is broken or missing.
fixes: Every `case word in` must close with `esac`.
Each branch needs `pattern) ... ;;`.
Check for a missing `in` after the word.

patterns.title: glob matched nothing (nullglob/zsh)
patterns.diagnosis: The pattern `{1}` didn't match any files, and the shell is set to error on that (zsh default, or bash `failglob`).
fixes: In zsh, prefix with `noglob` or quote the pattern if you want it literal.
Set `setopt nullglob` to let unmatched globs vanish.
Confirm files matching the pattern actually exist.

patterns.title: parameter substitution failed
patterns.diagnosis: A `${...}` expansion on `{1}` couldn't complete — often a bad pattern in `${var/.../...}` replacement.
fixes: Check the replace syntax: `${var/old/new}`.
Escape special characters in the pattern part.
Print `$var` to confirm it holds what you expect.

patterns.title: bad ${ } substitution
patterns.diagnosis: The expansion `${{1}}` uses syntax bash doesn't understand — maybe a typo or a feature from another shell.
fixes: Default value: `${var:-fallback}`.
Substring: `${var:0:3}`.
Length: `${#var}`. Check you're not in `sh` where some forms are missing.

patterns.match: bash: ([^:]+): cannot assign list to array member
patterns.title: array — wrong assignment
patterns.diagnosis: You tried to put a whole list into a single array slot `{1}`.
fixes: Assign the whole array: `arr=(a b c)`.
One element: `arr[0]=value`.
Append: `arr+=(more)`.

patterns.title: array — bad index
patterns.diagnosis: The index `{2}` for array `{1}` isn't valid — empty, or text where a number was needed for a numeric array.
fixes: Numeric arrays use integer indexes: `arr[0]`.
For string keys, declare an associative array: `declare -A map`.
Don't leave the index empty.

patterns.title: bad file descriptor
patterns.diagnosis: You redirected to/from descriptor {1} but it was never opened.
fixes: Open it first: `exec 3>file` before using `>&3`.
Standard FDs are 0 (stdin), 1 (stdout), 2 (stderr).
Close when done: `exec 3>&-`.

patterns.match: bash: warning: here-document at line [0-9]+ delimited by end-of-file \(wanted `([^`']+)'\)
patterns.title: heredoc — end marker missing
patterns.diagnosis: The heredoc never saw its closing word `{1}`, so it ran to the end of the file.
fixes: The closing `{1}` must be on its own line with no trailing spaces.
If you used `<<-`, the marker can be tab-indented (tabs only).
Match the marker exactly, including case.

patterns.match: bash: /dev/stdin: No such file or directory
patterns.title: /dev/stdin missing
patterns.diagnosis: This system or container doesn't expose `/dev/stdin`, so a command that reads it fails.
fixes: Pipe directly instead: `cmd <(other)` or a real pipe `a | b`.
Use `-` if the program accepts it for stdin.
On minimal containers, mount /dev or use a tmp file.

patterns.title: command not found in script
patterns.diagnosis: At a line in `{1}`, the shell couldn't find `{2}` — not installed, not on PATH, or a typo.
fixes: Check spelling of `{2}`.
Confirm it's installed: `which {2}` or `command -v {2}`.
If it's a local script, run it as `./{2}` or add its dir to PATH.

patterns.title: env — interpreter not executable
patterns.diagnosis: `env` found `{1}` but it isn't executable.
fixes: Make it runnable: `chmod +x $(command -v {1})` (if you own it).
The interpreter binary may be on a `noexec` mount.
Check the shebang points at the right path.

patterns.match: bash: ([^:]+): cannot execute: required file not found
patterns.title: missing interpreter for script
patterns.diagnosis: The script's shebang names an interpreter `{1}` that doesn't exist — or there's a `\r` in the shebang line.
fixes: Convert Windows line endings: `dos2unix script.sh`.
Verify the interpreter path in the first line is correct.
Reinstall the interpreter if it's truly missing.

patterns.match: bash: ([^:]+): cannot execute binary file: Exec format error
patterns.title: wrong-architecture binary
patterns.diagnosis: `{1}` is a binary built for a different CPU/OS (e.g. ARM vs x86, or a Mac binary on Linux).
fixes: Get the build matching your platform: `uname -m`.
On Apple Silicon, you may need Rosetta or an arm64 build.
Confirm the file type: `file {1}`.

patterns.match: bash: ([^:]+): cannot execute: Is a directory
patterns.title: tried to run a directory
patterns.diagnosis: You tried to execute `{1}`, but it's a folder, not a program.
fixes: Point at the actual script/binary inside it.
`cd {1}` if you meant to enter it.
Check for a name collision between a folder and a command.

patterns.title: disk full
patterns.diagnosis: The filesystem holding `{1}` is out of space, so writes fail.
fixes: See what's free: `df -h`.
Find big files: `du -sh * | sort -h`.
Clear logs, caches, or old downloads; watch out for a full `/tmp`.

patterns.match: df: ([^:]+): No such file or directory
patterns.title: df — path missing
patterns.diagnosis: df was pointed at `{1}`, which doesn't exist.
fixes: Run plain `df -h` to see all mounts.
Check the path spelling.
Use a real file/dir to query its filesystem.

patterns.match: du: cannot access '([^']+)': No such file or directory
patterns.title: du — path missing
patterns.diagnosis: du tried to measure `{1}` but it isn't there (or vanished mid-scan).
fixes: Verify the path exists.
Files deleted during the scan trigger this harmlessly.
`du -sh .` measures the current folder.

patterns.title: mount — needs root
patterns.diagnosis: Mounting `{1}` requires root privileges you don't have.
fixes: Use `sudo mount ...`.
Or add a user-mountable entry in `/etc/fstab` with the `user` option.
For removable media, a desktop file manager often mounts without sudo.

patterns.match: mount: ([^:]+): special device ([^ ]+) does not exist
patterns.title: mount — device not found
patterns.diagnosis: The device `{2}` you tried to mount on `{1}` doesn't exist.
fixes: List block devices: `lsblk` or `ls /dev/sd*`.
Plug in the device or check the correct name.
For images, add `-o loop`.

patterns.title: umount — filesystem busy
patterns.diagnosis: Something is still using files on `{1}`, so it can't be unmounted.
fixes: Find who's using it: `lsof +D {1}` or `fuser -m {1}`.
`cd` out of the mount point.
As a last resort, `umount -l {1}` (lazy unmount).

patterns.match: Failed to start ([^.]+)\.service: Unit ([^ ]+) not found
patterns.title: systemd — unit not found
patterns.diagnosis: There's no service unit named `{2}`. Wrong name, or the unit file isn't installed.
fixes: List units: `systemctl list-units --type=service`.
Check the exact name and `.service` suffix.
After adding a unit file, run `systemctl daemon-reload`.

patterns.title: systemctl — needs privileges
patterns.diagnosis: `systemctl {1} {2}` needs root (system services aren't user-controllable by default).
fixes: Use `sudo systemctl {1} {2}`.
For user services, add `--user`: `systemctl --user {1} {2}`.
Polkit may prompt for a password in a desktop session.

patterns.match: Job for ([^ ]+) failed because the control process exited with error code
patterns.title: systemd — service failed to start
patterns.diagnosis: The service `{1}` tried to start but its process exited with an error.
fixes: Read the logs: `journalctl -u {1} -n 50`.
Check the `ExecStart` command runs by hand.
Validate config files the service loads.

patterns.match: System has not been booted with systemd as init system \(PID 1\)
patterns.title: systemctl — no systemd here
patterns.diagnosis: This environment (a container, WSL1, or non-systemd distro) doesn't run systemd, so systemctl can't talk to it.
fixes: Start services directly: `service NAME start` or run the binary.
In Docker, run the process in the foreground as the container command.
On WSL, enable systemd in `/etc/wsl.conf` (WSL2) or manage manually.

patterns.title: crontab — bad day-of-week field
patterns.diagnosis: The 5th cron field (day of week) in `{1}` is invalid. It accepts 0-7 (0 and 7 both Sunday) or names.
fixes: Use 0-6 (or 7) or names like `mon`, `fri`.
A full line is `min hour dom mon dow command`.
`*` means every — `0 9 * * 1` is 9am Mondays.

patterns.title: crontab — none yet
patterns.diagnosis: User `{1}` doesn't have a crontab. This is informational, not really an error.
fixes: Create one: `crontab -e`.
List with `crontab -l` (shows this message until you add jobs).
Use `crontab -u {1} -e` to edit another user's (as root).

patterns.match: crontab: installing new crontab\n"([^"]+)":[0-9]+: premature end of file
patterns.title: crontab — incomplete line
patterns.diagnosis: A line in `{1}` is missing fields. Cron needs 5 time fields plus a command.
fixes: Each job: `min hour day month weekday command`.
Every line must be complete or a valid comment/blank.
Don't leave the last line half-written.

patterns.title: apt — lock held
patterns.diagnosis: Another apt/dpkg process is running and holding the package lock.
fixes: Wait for the other apt/unattended-upgrade to finish.
Find it: `ps aux | grep -E 'apt|dpkg'`.
Only as a last resort remove the lock files — and never while one is truly running.

patterns.title: dpkg — package config failed
patterns.diagnosis: Configuring `{1}` failed, leaving the package in a half-installed state.
fixes: Retry: `sudo dpkg --configure -a`.
Then `sudo apt -f install` to fix dependencies.
Read the lines above for the real cause.

patterns.title: apt — package not found
patterns.diagnosis: apt's index has no package called `{1}` — typo or the right repo isn't enabled.
fixes: Update the index first: `sudo apt update`.
Search for the real name: `apt search part-of-name`.
Some packages need a PPA or extra repo enabled.

patterns.title: yum — not on this distro
patterns.diagnosis: `yum` isn't here — you're likely on a non-RHEL distro or a newer one using `dnf`.
fixes: On modern Fedora/RHEL use `dnf`.
On Debian/Ubuntu use `apt`.
On Alpine use `apk`.

patterns.title: rpm — not an RPM
patterns.diagnosis: `{1}` isn't a valid `.rpm` file — wrong format or a truncated download.
fixes: Check the file: `file {1}`.
Re-download if it's truncated.
Use `dnf install` for repo packages rather than raw rpm files.

patterns.title: brew — not installed/on PATH
patterns.diagnosis: Homebrew either isn't installed or its bin dir isn't on PATH.
fixes: On Apple Silicon, add `/opt/homebrew/bin` to PATH.
On Intel Macs it's `/usr/local/bin`.
Run the eval line: `eval "$(/opt/homebrew/bin/brew shellenv)"`.

patterns.match: ping: ([^:]+): Name or service not known
patterns.title: ping — can't resolve name
patterns.diagnosis: DNS couldn't turn `{1}` into an address.
fixes: Check the spelling.
Try pinging an IP directly to test connectivity: `ping 8.8.8.8`.
Check DNS settings in `/etc/resolv.conf`.

patterns.match: nc: connect to ([^ ]+) port [0-9]+ \(tcp\) failed: Connection refused
patterns.title: netcat — connection refused
patterns.diagnosis: Nothing is listening on that port at `{1}`, so the connection was rejected.
fixes: Confirm the service is running on the target.
Check the port number.
See what's listening: `ss -ltnp` on the server.

patterns.match: telnet: Unable to connect to remote host: Connection refused
patterns.title: telnet — connection refused
patterns.diagnosis: The target port isn't accepting connections — service down or wrong port.
fixes: Verify the service is up and listening on that port.
Check a firewall isn't blocking it.
Use `nc -vz host port` for a cleaner port check.

patterns.match: dig: couldn't get address for '([^']+)': not found
patterns.title: dig — nameserver unresolved
patterns.diagnosis: dig couldn't resolve the nameserver `{1}` you pointed it at.
fixes: Use a known resolver: `dig @8.8.8.8 example.com`.
Check the spelling of the @server.
Drop the @server to use your system default.

patterns.match: curl: \(22\) The requested URL returned error: ([0-9]+)
patterns.title: curl — HTTP error status
patterns.diagnosis: With `-f`, curl treats HTTP {1} as a failure. The server returned an error response.
fixes: 4xx means your request was wrong (404 missing, 401/403 auth).
5xx means the server had a problem — retry later.
Drop `-f` to see the body, or add `-i` to view headers.

patterns.match: curl: \(3\) URL using bad/illegal format or missing URL
patterns.title: curl — malformed URL
patterns.diagnosis: curl couldn't parse the URL — missing scheme, stray spaces, or shell-eaten characters.
fixes: Include the scheme: `https://`.
Quote URLs with `&` or `?`: `curl 'https://x/y?a=1&b=2'`.
Check for hidden spaces or line breaks.

patterns.title: curl — timed out
patterns.diagnosis: curl gave up waiting: {1}. The server was slow, unreachable, or a firewall dropped packets.
fixes: Retry — it may be a transient hiccup.
Raise the timeout: `--max-time 60`.
Check connectivity and any proxy/firewall in the path.

patterns.title: curl — receive failure
patterns.diagnosis: The connection broke while receiving data: {1}. Often the server reset the connection.
fixes: Retry the request.
Check for a proxy or firewall interfering.
If it's HTTPS, a TLS mismatch can cause this — try `-v`.

patterns.match: wget: unable to resolve host address '([^']+)'
patterns.title: wget — DNS failed
patterns.diagnosis: wget couldn't resolve `{1}` to an IP.
fixes: Check the hostname spelling.
Test DNS: `nslookup {1}`.
Verify network/DNS settings.

patterns.title: basename — no argument
patterns.diagnosis: basename needs a path to strip down, but got nothing.
fixes: Pass a path: `basename /a/b/c.txt` → `c.txt`.
Strip a suffix too: `basename file.txt .txt` → `file`.
Quote variables that might be empty.

patterns.title: dirname — no argument
patterns.diagnosis: dirname needs a path to extract the folder from, but got nothing.
fixes: Pass a path: `dirname /a/b/c.txt` → `/a/b`.
Quote the variable: `dirname "$file"`.
Empty input yields `.` only if you pass an empty string explicitly.

patterns.title: date — can't parse
patterns.diagnosis: GNU date couldn't understand the date string `{1}`.
fixes: Use a clear format: `date -d '2024-01-15'`.
Relative works too: `date -d 'yesterday'`, `date -d '+1 day'`.
macOS `date` parses differently — use `-j -f` there.

patterns.title: date — bad format (BSD/macOS)
patterns.diagnosis: macOS/BSD `date` got a format it doesn't accept — it doesn't support GNU's `-d` the same way.
fixes: Install GNU coreutils for `gdate` if you want GNU behavior.
Output format strings start with `+`.

patterns.match: stat: cannot stat '([^']+)': No such file or directory
patterns.title: stat — file missing
patterns.diagnosis: stat can't read info about `{1}` because it isn't there.
fixes: Check the path with `ls {1}`.
On macOS, stat uses `-f` format strings (different from GNU `-c`).
Quote paths with spaces.

patterns.match: head: cannot open '([^']+)' for reading: No such file or directory
patterns.title: head — file missing
patterns.diagnosis: head couldn't open `{1}`.
fixes: Check the path with `ls`.
To read piped input, drop the filename.
`head -n 20 file` shows the first 20 lines.
